en: Oṃ, salutation to that Brahman which is Tat-Sat.
The Compendium of All Philosophical Systems.
The Cārvāka system of philosophy.
I bow to Śiva, the abode of eternal knowledge and the treasure-trove of supreme bliss;
by Him alone the earth and other elements were produced, and thus this entire world possesses a creator.

I daily take refuge in the son of the illustrious Śārṅgapāṇi, the teacher Viṣṇu, who has reached the further shore of the oceans of all philosophical systems, who has fulfilled the aims appropriate for himself and satisfied the entire world, and who knows all the scriptures.
The Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha is composed by the illustrious Mādhavārya, who is possessed of great splendor and is the Kaustubha jewel from the milk-ocean of the venerable Sāyaṇa.

Having thoroughly churned the scriptures of the ancients, which are exceedingly difficult to traverse, the illustrious Lord Sāyaṇamādhava has composed this work for the delight of the virtuous. Let the good people listen with minds free from envy; for to whom does a garland fashioned from variegated flowers not bring joy?
Now, how can the Supreme Lord’s status as the bestower of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) be asserted?
For that [status] has been cast far away by the Cārvāka, the crest-jewel of atheists, who follows the doctrine of Bṛhaspati. Indeed, the conduct of the Cārvāka is difficult to refute.
Generally, all living beings live for as long as they have life, seeking happiness; there is no one who is beyond the reach of death.
Once the body has been reduced to ashes, how can it ever return?

Thus, conforming to worldly verses and considering only wealth (*artha*) and pleasure (*kāma*) to be the human goals (*puruṣārtha*) according to the treatises on ethics and erotics, they are observed to follow the Cārvāka doctrine while denying any purpose pertaining to the next world.
For this very reason, that Cārvāka doctrine has another name, "Lokāyata," which is significant in its meaning. In that system, there are four elements (*tattva*) beginning with earth.

From those very elements, when they have transformed into the form of the body, consciousness arises—just as the power of intoxication arises from yeast and other ingredients—and when those [elements] perish, it perishes of its own accord. Thus they say: "This mass of consciousness, having arisen from these elements, perishes after them; there is no consciousness after death" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.12).
The self is simply the body qualified by consciousness,
because there is no evidence for a self distinct from the body;
for, as one who maintains that perception is the sole means of valid cognition, [such a person] does not accept inference and other means of knowledge due to their lack of validity.
The human goal (puruṣārtha) is indeed pleasure produced by such things as embracing a woman;
nor should it be thought that this cannot be a human goal because it is intermingled with suffering,
for one may enjoy pleasure alone by avoiding the suffering that has arrived unavoidably.
For example, one who desires fish takes the fish along with their scales and bones; having taken as much as is necessary, he desists.
Or, just as one who desires grain brings the grain together with its straw; having taken as much as is necessary, he desists.
Therefore, out of fear of suffering, it is not right to abandon pleasure that is experienced as agreeable.
For rice is not left unsown because deer exist; nor are cooking pots left unheated on the fire because beggars exist.
If some timid person were to abandon visible happiness, he would be as foolish as a beast.
As it has been said: "The pleasure arising from contact with sense objects is to be abandoned by men because it is beset with suffering"—this is the deliberation of fools.
O friend, what seeker of welfare would ever discard grains of rice rich with pure white kernels when they are accompanied by the husks and chaff?

If it be objected: "In the absence of happiness in the next world, how could those advanced in learning engage in the Agnihotra and other rites, which are accomplished only through the expenditure of great wealth and physical exertion?"—that too is unable to enter the ranks of valid proof. For the Vedic scriptures have been rejected by those very same deceitful crows who consider themselves learned in the Vedas—namely, those proponents of the authority of the *Karmakāṇḍa* who reject the *Jñānakāṇḍa*, and those proponents of the authority of the *Jñānakāṇḍa* who reject the *Karmakāṇḍa*. Thus, the Triple Veda is nothing but the prattle of deceivers; consequently, the Agnihotra and such rites serve merely as a means of livelihood.

And thus says the popular proverb: "The fire-sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff, and smearing oneself with ashes—Vṛhaspati says these are merely the livelihoods of those devoid of intelligence and manliness."
Therefore, hell is simply the suffering produced by thorns and the like;
the king established in the world is the Supreme Lord;
and liberation is the destruction of the body.
Furthermore, in the doctrine that the body is the self, the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in such expressions as "I am fat," "I am thin," or "I am dark" is logically established.
The conventional usage "my body" is merely figurative (aupacārika), like the expression "the head of Rāhu.
All of this has been summarized as follows: "The pleasure produced from the embrace of a woman is itself the human goal (puruṣārtha)."
Suffering produced by the pain of thorns and the like is called hell. ||1||
O King, the Lord of Beings is established by worldly consensus; no other supreme lord is recognized.
Liberation is the destruction of the body, and liberation is not held to result from knowledge. ||2||
In this regard, there are four elements: earth, water, fire, and air;
indeed, consciousness arises from these four elements. (3)

Just as the power of intoxication arises from substances such as fermenting agents when combined together, so too does the identification "I am fat" or "I am thin" arise through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). ||4||
"Furthermore, because it possesses bulk and other such qualities, the body itself is the self and nothing else;
the expression 'this is my body' would then be merely figurative. This might be so.
However, this wish would be fulfilled only if inference and the other means of valid cognition were not authoritative.
And there is indeed validity [of cognition].

Otherwise, how could the activity of discerning persons toward fire immediately after perceiving smoke be accounted for? Likewise, how could those seeking fruit proceed to the riverbank immediately upon hearing the statement, "There are fruits on the bank of the river"?
This is merely the manifestation of a daydream.

For those who maintain the validity of inference accept that a logical mark (*liṅga*) which possesses both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is the means of cognition.
And pervasion is a relationship free from both types of conditions (*upādhi*).
And that [object] does not function as a constituent part [of cognition] by virtue of its mere existence, as do the eyes and other sense organs;
rather, it does so by virtue of being known.
What, indeed, could be the means for such knowledge?
It is not, first of all, perception;
and that [perception] is intended to be either external or internal.
It is not the former.

Because it produces knowledge of an object associated with [the sense organ], even though there is the possibility of its functioning, it is impossible for past and future objects; thus, a universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) that encompasses all cases is difficult to know.

Nor should it be thought that the knowledge of concomitance has universals as its object, for that would entail the consequence that there is no inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) between two particular individuals.
Nor is the last [alternative] tenable;

for since the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is dependent upon the external sense organs, it is impossible for it to function independently with respect to an external object. As it has been said: "The mind (manas), when directed toward external objects, is dependent on the eye and other [senses]."
(Ta.Vi. 20) Thus, inference either is not a means for knowing pervasion (*vyāpti*),
because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress, as one would have to apply the same method in each and every instance.
Nor is verbal testimony (śabda) a means [to that knowledge],
because, according to the doctrine of Kaṇāda, it is included within inference (anumāna).

Or, even if it were not included, it would lack the capacity to avoid the previously mentioned defects, as it depends upon the apprehension of a logical mark (liṅga) in the form of the linguistic usage of elders.

Furthermore, because there would be no basis for trust— as in the case of Manu and others— merely on the basis of the statement that "there is an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) between smoke and fire," and because for a person who has not been taught the invariable concomitance, the absence of inference of one thing from the perception of another thing would result in the reduction of the very discourse on inference-for-oneself (svārthānumāna) to a mere fiction, what then can be said of inference-for-others (parārthānumāna)?
As for analogy (upamāna) and the other means of knowledge, they are cast far aside.

Because those [words] function to convey the relationship between a name and the named (saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha) and so forth, it is impossible for them to convey a relationship that is non-conditioned (anaupādhika).

Furthermore, the absence of conditions (upādhi) is also difficult to ascertain. Since there is no rule that conditions must be perceptible, even if the absence of perceptible things were perceptible, the absence of imperceptible things would remain imperceptible; thus, when one relies on inference and other means [to establish such absence], one does not escape the aforementioned defects.
Furthermore, its definition must be accepted as: "that which, while not pervading the probans (sādhana), is co-extensive with the probandum (sādhya).
As it has been said: "That which does not pervade the probans but is co-extensive with the probandum is called an *upādhi*.
For example, when "impermanence" is the probandum in the case of sound, "having a creator," "being a jar," and "being audible" [serve as such].
The three qualifiers are employed here in sequence to exclude [other possibilities];
therefore, this is faultless, as stated by the Teacher in the passage beginning with "having reached the compound" (*samāsam etya*).

In that case, since the determination of negation is preceded by the determination of affirmation, once the knowledge of the *upādhi* (limiting condition) has arisen, there arises the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāpti*)—which consists of a relation qualified by the absence of that [condition]—and the knowledge of the *upādhi* is dependent upon the knowledge of pervasion; thus, the flaw of mutual dependence, like a thunderbolt strike, becomes as indelible as adamantine glue.
Therefore, because the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is difficult to comprehend, there is no room for inference and the like.
The activity toward the cognition of fire and so forth following the cognition of smoke and so forth is either rooted in perception or is accounted for as an error.
In some cases, however, the attainment of a result is accidental, like [the effects of] jewels, mantras, or medicinal herbs;
therefore, even that which is to be accomplished by them, such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), does not exist.
If it is argued that, in the absence of the unseen force, the diversity of the world would be accidental—no, that is not correct.
For that [distinction] is established through intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone.
As it has been said: "Fire is hot, water is cold, and the wind is of neutral touch—who painted this? Therefore, the determination of these things arises from their intrinsic nature."
All of this has also been stated by Bṛhaspati: "Neither heaven nor liberation exists, nor does a self belonging to another world;
nor do the rituals of the castes and stages of life yield any fruit. (1)

The Agnihotra sacrifice, the three Vedas, the triple staff, and smearing oneself with ashes—these are merely means of livelihood devised by the Creator for those devoid of intelligence and manliness. 2.
If an animal, when slaughtered, goes to heaven in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, why then does the sacrificer not slaughter his own father there? (3)
If even for deceased beings a śrāddha ceremony were the cause of satisfaction,
then oil would increase the flame of an extinguished lamp.
For living beings departing from this world, the preparation of provisions for the journey is in vain;
satisfaction on the path is unimpeded by the śrāddha performed by those remaining at home. (5)
If those dwelling in heaven attain satisfaction there through giving, why is it not given here to those who stand upon the top of the palace? (6)
As long as one lives, let one live happily; having incurred debt, let one drink ghee.
Once the body has been reduced to ashes, how can there be a return? (7)
If he has departed from this body for the next world, why does he not return again, agitated by affection for his kinsmen? (8)
Therefore, the means of livelihood for Brahmins has been ordained here;
there exists nowhere else any other [means], such as the funeral rites for the deceased.
The three authors of the Veda are a jester, a rogue, and a night-stalker;
"jarpharī turpharī," and so forth, is recorded as the speech of scholars.
For in this rite, the horse's penis is declared to be taken by the wife;
likewise, the highest collection of objects to be seized is declared to be taken by the jesters.
Likewise, the devouring of those who possess pride was instigated by the night-stalker.
Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the Cārvāka doctrine should be adopted for the sake of favoring many living beings.
Thus ends the Cārvāka philosophy in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Mādhava, son of Sāyaṇa.
Now, the Buddhist philosophy.
On this point, the Buddhists state:

"What was asserted—that inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) is difficult to understand—is incorrect, because inseparable relation is easily known through identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*). As it has been said: 'The rule of inseparable relation arises from the causal relationship or from an essential nature as a regulator; it is not [known] from non-observation, nor from observation.'"
(Nyāyaviniścaya) Thus:

on the view that positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) are the determiners of inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*), the non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) between the probandum and the probans would be difficult to ascertain;
for doubt regarding deviation cannot be ruled out in the case of an object that was past, will be future, or is currently unperceived.
If it is objected that even in your own system, the suspicion of inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) is difficult to avoid in such cases, do not say so;

for a suspicion such as "let the effect arise even without a cause" is dispelled by its own inherent contradiction (*vyāghāta*). Indeed, one should only suspect that which, when suspected, does not give rise to contradictions and the like.
As it has been said: "Doubt extends only as far as the pervader" (*Nyāyakusumāñjali* 3.7).

Therefore, the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is determined by the ascertainment of that [effect's] origination from that [cause]. And the ascertainment of that origination is based on the fivefold process of perception and non-perception regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*).

The causal relation between smoke and fire is ascertained through five criteria: (1) the non-perception of the effect prior to its production; (2) its perception when the cause is perceived; and (3) its subsequent non-perception due to the non-perception of the cause.

Likewise, invariable concomitance is also ascertained through the determination of identity (*tādātmya*), because a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) operates against the contrary position: "If the *śiṃśapā* were to transcend the nature of being a tree, it would forfeit its very self."
But when no subverting factor has arisen, who can prevent the suspicion of deviation (vyabhicāra), even if coexistence is repeatedly observed?
Furthermore, the determination of identity between a *śiṃśapā* and a tree is established by the force of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the judgment "this tree is a *śiṃśapā*";
for such [coreferentiality] is not possible if there is absolute non-difference.
Because simultaneous application is impossible if they are synonyms,
nor is it possible if they are absolutely distinct, as is the case with a cow and a horse, since no such [simultaneous application] is observed.
Therefore, it is established that the nature of the effect and the nature of the cause lead to the inference [of one another].
If someone were not to accept inference as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), one should say to him:
"Is it merely stated that 'inference is not a means of valid cognition,' and in that case, is no proof adduced, or is one adduced?"
Not the first;
for if a statement lacking a conclusion (the thesis) is presented, the probandum remains unestablished,
since a mere proposition by itself cannot prove what has been proposed.
This follows from that principle.
Nor is the last [alternative] tenable;

for by asserting that inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) while refusing to accept verbal testimony as a valid means of knowledge, you fall into a contradiction—like saying "my mother is barren"—when you yourself employ in your own treatise a statement accepted as authoritative.

Furthermore, by stating that "the establishment of the distinction between valid cognition and its fallacies [is made] because of their belonging to the same class," you yourself have accepted inference based on essential nature (*svabhāvānumāna*).
By stating that "the misconception residing in another person is [known] through the mark of speech," you have accepted inference based on an effect (*kāryaliṅgaka-anumāna*).
And by negating some object through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), you have accepted inference based on the mark of non-perception (*anupalabdhiliṅgaka-anumāna*).

And so it has been stated by the Tathāgatas: "Because another cognition is understood through the persistence of a generality that is not [itself] another means of valid cognition, and because of the negation of something, there exists another means of valid cognition. Furthermore, since the learned have exerted themselves on this point, we shall desist here for fear of making the book too voluminous.
And those Buddhists explain the supreme human goal through a fourfold meditation.

These Buddhists, well-known by the names Mādhyamika, Yogācāra, Sautrāntika, and Vaibhāṣika, maintain respectively the doctrines of the emptiness of all things, the emptiness of external objects, the inferability of external objects, and the perceptibility of external objects.
Although the Blessed Buddha is one and the sole teacher, there is nevertheless a fourfold division due to the differences in the intellects of those to be enlightened.

Just as when it is said, "The sun has set," paramours, thieves, and Vedic scholars understand it as the time for their respective purposes—such as meeting a lover, stealing another's property, or performing daily rites—so too should the fourfold meditation be understood as taught:
"Everything is momentary, everything is suffering, everything is its own characteristic, everything is empty.

Among these, momentariness is to be inferred from the existence of moments such as the blue color and so forth, by the reasoning: "Whatever exists is momentary, like a mass of clouds; and these entities exist."
Nor is this reason unestablished (*asiddha*).
For the existence characterized by causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the case of moments such as blue and the like;

and because, according to the principle that "the exclusion of the pervader entails the exclusion of the pervaded," the exclusion of existence from the momentary is established by the exclusion of succession and simultaneity—the two pervaders—from it.
That capacity for causal efficiency is pervaded by succession and simultaneity;
nor is any other mode possible besides succession and simultaneity, for when two things are mutually exclusive, there can be no existence of a third alternative.
Nor can there be identity among contradictory things, because they are opposed by their very nature as distinct utterances.
This is because, according to the principle stated in *Nyāyakusumāñjali* (3.8), the contradiction is manifest.

Furthermore, since succession and simultaneity—being excluded from a permanent entity—also exclude its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), it is established that existence is determined only within the framework of momentariness.
If it is asked, "Why might a non-momentary entity not possess causal efficiency?", that is incorrect.
Because it cannot withstand critical analysis.
For instance, at the time when a permanent entity performs its causal function in the present, does it possess the capacity for past and future causal functions or not?
In the first case, there follows the undesirable consequence that those two [past and future functions] could not be excluded.
Because it is impossible for that which is capable to be delayed.

Furthermore, there is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-anumāna*): whatever is capable of performing a certain action at a given time must necessarily perform it at that time, just as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces its own effect; and this entity is capable [of acting].
In the second case [if it were incapable], it would never act, because the capacity to produce purposeful activity (*arthakriyākāritva*) is necessarily concomitant with mere capability.
Whatever does not produce a certain effect at a certain time is incapable of producing that effect at that time, just as a fragment of stone is incapable of producing a sprout.

Furthermore, this [permanent entity] does not produce the past or future causal efficiencies at the time it is performing its present causal efficiency; this follows from the very opposite of the definition of capacity.

If you argue that for a permanent entity, the successive production of past and future effects is possible through the acquisition of successive auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then you must answer this question: [If the permanent entity is already capable of producing the effect, what is the use of auxiliaries? If it is not capable, what can they do? Please explain this when you are questioned.
Do the auxiliary causes (sahakārin) assist the entity or not? If they do not, then they are not to be depended upon,
because it is impossible for them to serve that purpose if they provide no assistance whatsoever.
If it is argued that the nature of the entity is such that it performs the effect only together with those auxiliary causes, then, my friend, it should never abandon its auxiliaries;
on the contrary, even if they were fleeing, it should bind them by the neck with a noose and perform its task.
Because the intrinsic nature does not depart.
Regarding the position that it is an auxiliary factor (*upakāraka*), is this assistance distinct from the entity or not?
If it is the position of distinction, then causality would belong only to that adventitious factor.
An effect does not [arise] from a non-momentary entity, because it follows the presence and absence of adventitious excellence.
As it has been said: "What do rain and sun do to space? Their fruit is seen upon leather.
If that [entity] were like leather, it would be impermanent; if it were like space, its fruit would be non-existent."
Furthermore, does the excellence produced by the auxiliary causes (sahakārin) initiate another excellence or not?
In either case, there follows a rain of stones in the form of the previously mentioned refutations.
In the view that it initiates another excellence, there would also be the misery of a multi-faceted infinite regress.

If, in order to produce an excellence (*atiśaya*), there were a requirement for further auxiliary causes, then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result from that succession; thus, one must avoid such an infinite regress.
Likewise, when an excellence is imparted to a seed by a collection of entities such as water, wind, and other auxiliaries, the seed must be admitted as the producer [of that excellence];
otherwise, the excellence would manifest even in its absence.

Furthermore, the seed, while imparting a specific excellence (*atiśaya*), imparts it only in dependence upon auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). Otherwise, if this were not the case, the consequence would follow that the sprout would arise at all times; for even the sprout would then be produced constantly. Therefore, by those auxiliary causes which are required for the sake of the excellence, another excellence must be imparted to the seed.

Regarding that assistance as well, if the seed—being dependent on auxiliary factors according to the previous reasoning—is the producer [of the sprout], then the first infinite regress (anavasthā) is established regarding the excellence residing in the seed which is produced by those auxiliaries.
Now, even if that assistance, though required for the sake of the effect, produces the effect independently of the seed and so forth, or else dependent upon it:
in the first case, it would follow that the seed and other factors are not causes.

If, in the second case, a further excellence (*atiśaya*) must be produced in the seed and so forth by the assistance being required, then the same would apply at each subsequent stage; thus, there would result an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of excellences residing within the excellences produced by the seeds and so forth—this would be the second infinite regress. Likewise, if another assistance must be produced in the substrate (the seed and so forth) by the assistance being required, then there would result an infinite regress of excellences based on the seed that are produced by those successive assistances—this would be the third infinite regress, a truly wretched state of affairs.

Now, if it is accepted that an excellence (*atiśaya*) non-different from the entity itself is produced by the auxiliary causes, then it follows—just as my own tree of desire has borne fruit—that the original entity, which was devoid of such excellence, ceases to exist, and another entity, consisting of that excellence and designated by terms such as "the productive form" (*kurvad-rūpa*), comes into being.
Therefore, the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of a non-momentary thing is impossible either successively or simultaneously.
It is not established even through non-succession.
Because it cannot withstand logical analysis;
for instance,
does that nature which is capable of performing all its effects simultaneously persist at a subsequent time, or not?
In the first case, it would follow that the effect must be produced at all other times as well, just as it is at that specific moment.
In the second case, the hope for its persistence would resemble the prayer of one whose seeds have been eaten by mice for them to still produce sprouts.
Furthermore, whatever is superposed with contradictory properties is manifold, just like cold and heat.
Furthermore, the logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established in the case of a cloud because this [subject] is superposed with contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyasta*).

Nor is this reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*), because the capacity and incapacity [of a permanent entity] at different times are proven through reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) and its converse (*tadviparyaya*).
Among these, the reductio and its converse that prove incapacity have been stated previously.
The two [reasons] that establish capacity are stated as follows:
Whatever is incapable of producing a certain effect at a certain time, it does not produce that effect at that time, just as a piece of stone [does not produce] a sprout.
And this [entity], at the time of performing its present causal function, is incapable of past and future causal functions; such is the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
Whatever performs an action at a certain time is capable of that action at that time, just as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is capable of its own effect.

This entity, however, performs actions belonging to the past and future times while existing at those respective times; thus, the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅga*) is the contrapositive (*viparyaya*).

Therefore, it is established that existence—which possesses a negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) understood through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*) by excluding succession and simultaneity from the counter-example, and which possesses a positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) grasped through the force of the reductio and its contrapositive—will be restricted solely to the position of momentariness.
This has been stated by Jñānaśrī: "Whatever exists is momentary, like a rain-cloud; and these entities exist.
Here, existence is the capacity for purposeful action, which is established through valid cognition in those things that are proven.

It is not a single uniform kind, otherwise even an action performed by another would [be attributed to it]. Thus, in both ways, the connection with momentary destruction is established, and it finds its rest in the probandum."
Nor should it be thought that existence consists merely in being connected with the universal "existence" (*sattāsāmānya*), by accepting the positions of Kaṇabhakṣa (Kaṇāda) and Akṣacaraṇa (Gautama),

because this would entail the consequence that universals, particulars, and inherence would be non-existent. Furthermore, in those cases [of universals, etc.], the conventional usage of the term "existent" is not based on an intrinsic existence (*svarūpasattā*).
This is because it would entail the fault of overburdening the causal agent (*prayojaka*),
and because it is refuted by the dilemma of whether [the form] is pervasive (*anugata*) or non-pervasive (*ananugata*). Furthermore,

no form that is pervasive across diverse moments— such as mustard seeds, mountains, and so forth— is perceived, just as a thread is not seen in jewels or a quality is not seen in a collection of elements.
Furthermore, is the universal omnipresent, or is it omnipresent only within its own substratum?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of a confusion of all things,
and it would also entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets.
For it has been stated by Praśastapāda that [the universal] "pervades its own entire object.
Furthermore, when a jar exists, does the universal residing therein connect with another jar being produced by coming from that [original location], or without coming?
In the first case, there would be the consequence of its being a substance (*dravyatva*).

In the second case, the relation [of the universal] is untenable. Furthermore, when a jar has perished, does the universal remain, perish, or move to another location? In the first case, it would follow that it is without a substratum (*nirādhāra*).
In the second case, there is the illogicality of the assertion of eternality;
in the third, there is the consequence of its being a substance.
Because it is thus seized by the crocodile of such refutations, the universal (*sāmānya*) is unestablished by means of valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*).
As it has been said: "For that which exists elsewhere to have its occurrence in the birth of another place, while not moving from that location—that is extreme ingenuity!"
That entity exists where it is located and is connected with that very place;
yet it pervades the entire locus—this is truly a great wonder!
"It does not go there, nor was it there before, nor does it exist there afterwards, nor does it possess parts;
it does not abandon its former substrate—alas, what a succession of calamities!

If it is asked, "What is the objective support (ālambana) for the continuous cognition [of identity]?"—well, my long-lived friend, you should be content with the fact that its objective support is precisely the exclusion of others (anyāpoha). Enough of this over-elaboration.
That all of cyclic existence is of the nature of suffering is agreed upon by all the founders of philosophical systems;
otherwise, it would be impossible for them—who seek to escape from it—to engage in the means for its cessation.
Therefore, one should cultivate the meditation: "All is suffering, suffering."
If it is argued that when asked "What is it? one must provide an example, we say: not so.

Because particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are momentary, they lack any commonality of characteristic (*sālakṣaṇya*); therefore, it is impossible to say that another [moment] is similar to this one.
Consequently, one should contemplate each particular characteristic as being simply "particular characteristic."

In this way, even "emptiness" itself should be meditated upon as empty. For, in both dreams and waking states, we perceive a qualified negation such as, "This silver and so forth was not seen by me. If that [silver] had been seen, then there would have to exist the existence of the qualified perception of it, of the "this-ness" (idantā) which is its locus, of the silver-ness and so forth superimposed upon it, and of their relationship, such as inherence (samavāya).
And this is not accepted by any proponent of a philosophical school.
And the "half-old woman" approach is not appropriate;
for it is not conceived that one half of a hen should be intended for cooking while the other half for laying eggs.

Therefore, since among the superimposed object, the substratum, their relationship, the perception thereof, and the perceiver, the non-existence of even one or many would necessarily result in the non-existence of everything by virtue of being the object of negation—this being taught by the Blessed One—the Mādhyamikas, possessing supreme wisdom, spoke as follows: "By the maxim of the mendicant spreading out his feet, through the exposition of momentary destruction and so forth, and by dispelling the delusions regarding permanence, agreeable sensation, continuity, and the reality of all things, the ultimate conclusion rests precisely upon universal emptiness."
Therefore, reality is indeed emptiness alone, liberated from the four alternatives consisting of existence, non-existence, both, and neither.
For instance: if the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a jar or the like were existence, then the activity of causal agents would be futile.
If the position is that non-existence is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the very same fault previously mentioned would manifest.
As it has been said: "It is not held that dependence on causes is appropriate for what is non-existent, such as space and so forth;
for a cause cannot produce an effect that is non-existent, like a sky-flower."
The other two positions are untenable due to contradiction.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Laṅkāvatāra*: "When things are analyzed by the intellect, no intrinsic nature can be apprehended;
therefore, they are shown to be inexpressible and devoid of intrinsic nature."
This is what the wise declare as established by the force of reality:
"In whatever way objects are analyzed, they fall apart in that very same way.
And so it is said.
The meaning is that it does not abide in any position whatsoever.
Furthermore, the empirical activity of perceived objects is consistent with conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), just like the activity within a dream.
Therefore it has been said: "To an ascetic, a lustful man, and a dog, [the same] female body..."
"A corpse," "a woman," and "food"—these are the three conceptual constructions.

Thus, when all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have ceased through the power of these four meditations, the supreme nirvāṇa, which is of the nature of emptiness, will be accomplished; therefore, we have achieved our purpose and there remains nothing further for us to teach.
As for the disciples, they must practice two things: yoga and conduct (*ācāra*).
Among these, *yoga* is the inquiry for the sake of attaining that goal not yet attained.
Conduct consists in accepting the meaning as taught by the guru.
Because they accept what is taught by the guru, they are superior; and because they do not engage in critical questioning, they are inferior.
Therefore, they are renowned as Mādhyamikas (the "Middle Ones").

The reputation of certain [schools] as Yogācāra arises from their posing the challenge: "Having accepted the fourfold meditations taught by the Guru and the emptiness of external objects, how is the emptiness of the internal [mind] also accepted?
For this is their technical definition: self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) must indeed be accepted;
otherwise, the world would fall into total blindness.
This was stated by Dharmakīrti: "For one who does not perceive [the cognition] itself, the perception of the object is not established.
An external object of apprehension is simply not tenable, because conceptualization is untenable."
An object, in being graspable by cognition, must be either already arisen or not yet arisen.
It cannot be the former,
because that which has already arisen lacks duration.
Nor is it another [object],
because that which has not yet arisen lacks existence. If you should think that only a past object is graspable by cognition because it is its producer, that too is the talk of a child.
Because it would contradict the appearance of presentness,
and because it would follow that even the sense organs and so forth would be objects of apprehension by virtue of being generators of cognition.
Furthermore, is the object of apprehension (grāhya) something in the form of atoms or in the form of a composite whole?
It is not the latter,
because that has been refuted through the analysis of whether it exists as a whole or in part, and so forth.
Nor is it the former.
Because it is beyond the reach of the senses;
and because simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms] would contradict [the nature of] the hexad.
As it has been said: "Due to simultaneous conjunction with six [others], the atom would possess six parts."
"Even if those [atoms] were to occupy the same location, the aggregate would be no larger than a single atom.

Therefore, because there is no object of cognition distinct from itself, it is established that cognition, being of the nature of that [object], illuminates its own form by itself, like light. As it has been said: "There is nothing else to be experienced by cognition, nor is there another experience of it."
Due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] shines forth by itself.
Furthermore, the non-difference between the apprehended object and the apprehending subject must be inferred:
whatever is cognized by a particular cognition does not differ from that cognition, just as the self [does not differ] from its own knowledge;
and blue and other objects are thus cognized by those cognitions.
For if there were a difference [between the word and its object], the object would no longer possess a relationship with this [word],
because the cause of restriction— identity— is absent,
and because origination from that [object] is not a restrictive factor.
Furthermore, this appearance of the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness as distinct entities is an illusion, like the appearance of duality in a single moon.
In this case as well, the cause is nothing other than the beginningless and uninterrupted stream of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of non-difference.
As it has been said: "Because they are necessarily perceived together, there is no difference between the blue [object] and the cognition thereof."
And this differentiation would be perceived by erroneous cognitions, just as [duality] is seen in the case of the non-dual moon.

Although the nature of the intellect is without division, it appears as if possessed of the distinctions between the grasped object, the grasping subject, and self-awareness to those whose vision is distorted by error.
And so it is said.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the flavor, potency, post-digestive effect, and so forth, of a sweetmeat obtained through mere imagination would not be identical to those of a sweetmeat actually acquired. Although cognition is in reality devoid of the forms of the object and the subject, it nevertheless appears to possess distinct forms of apprehended and apprehender in accordance with the conventional understanding of ordinary people. This conventional status is established through the power of beginningless false conceptual impressions (*vāsanā*), just as those with eyes impaired by cataracts perceive a variety of hairs, nets, or fibers. Thus, no objection can be raised against this. As it has been stated: "Just as a delusion is perceived as having the forms of the object and the subject, though it is devoid of such forms..."
The delusion of the forms of the grasped and the grasper, whose characteristics are differentiated, has ceased.
Thus, when this distinction has been established— just as in the case of the difference between cognitions such as those of hair and so forth—
then it cannot be challenged that [consciousness] possesses the characteristics of the grasped and the grasper.
Therefore, it is established that consciousness alone appears in manifold forms due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Consequently, through the force of the accumulation of the aforementioned meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), there arises the dawn of pure cognition (*viśuddha-vijñāna*), in which all latent impressions have been eradicated and the impurities of various objective forms have dissolved.
Others, however, think as follows:

As for the claim that the external world of objects does not exist, that is incorrect because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). Nor should it be said that the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is the proof;

for that [rule], which is intended to establish the non-difference between the object of cognition and the cognizer, is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), as its exclusion from the contrary case (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*) is doubtful.
If it is objected that, in the case of difference, the proof consisting of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) would not hold, we say no;
for they appear as distinct due to cognition being inward-turned and the object of cognition being outward-turned,
and because a rule of simultaneity characterized by occupying the same location and existing at the same time is impossible.
Furthermore, if an object such as blue were of the nature of the cognition’s own form,
there would be an appearance of "I," rather than the apprehension of "this," because [the object] would not be distinct from the cognition.

Now it is argued that even though it has the nature of cognition, the form of blue appears through delusion as if external and distinct, and yet there is no mention of "I" therein. As it has been said: "This portion which, due to another determination [of the object], stands as if external, is a delusion—the appearance of distinction in cognition which is itself undivided."
And: "That which is the reality of the internal object of cognition appears as if it were external."
That is incorrect; for if external objects do not exist, it would be improper to state the simile "as if external," since that [simile] lacks the necessary basis for its application.
Indeed, no discerning person would say that Vasumitra appears like the son of a barren woman.

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*): if the appearance of difference is erroneous, then the appearance of non-difference is authoritative; and if the appearance of non-difference is authoritative, then the appearance of difference is erroneous.
Moreover, we observe a settled rule in the world: perceiving only blue and so forth through non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*), people adopt only the external and disregard the internal.
Thus, this reason intended to prove non-difference would fall into the fallacy known as the "logic of cow-dung and milk-porridge" (*gomayapāyasīyanyāya*).
Therefore, for one who says "as if external," it must be considered that the external object is indeed the apprehended (*grāhya*); thus, your own arrow would strike you.
If it is argued that it is untenable for an object existing at a time different from the cognition to be the apprehended, that is untenable.

For when a cognition is produced in relation to an object in sensory contact, that object is established as inferable through the fact that it imparts its own form to the cognition, and by means of the form thus imparted.
For this very reason, the objection and its resolution have been summarized: "How can that which exists at a different time be apprehended? To this, they reply:
"They know it to be apprehensible precisely because the manifestation [of the object] possesses the capacity to impart its form to the cognition; this alone constitutes its causality."

And so, just as food is inferred from its fullness, a country from its dialect, or affection from agitation, so too is the object of knowledge (jñeya) to be inferred from the form of the cognition (jñānākāra). As it has been said: "For nothing connects this [cognition] with the object except by assuming the form of the object; therefore, the conformity to the form of the object is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the apprehension of the object of knowledge."
For it is not logical that the mere existence of a cognition constitutes the awareness of an object,
since that existence is indistinguishable in all cases.
Rather, it is by entering into similarity with the object that the cognition is able to render itself similar to it and thereby apprehend it.

Likewise, regarding the existence of external objects, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which occur only occasionally (*kādācitka*), even when a certain [condition] is present, all depend upon something additional to that [condition].

For example, while I have no desire to speak (*avivakṣati*) nor desire to go (*ajigamiṣati*), the appearances of speech and movement depend upon the mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) of another person who does desire to speak and go.

And likewise, the cognitive states (*pravṛttipratyaya*) under dispute, although the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is present, only occasionally manifest blue and other such objects; therefore, the so-called storehouse-consciousness is the consciousness that serves as the locus of the "I" (*ahaṃkāra*).
And consciousness that delineates blue and so forth is the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
As it has been said: "That which serves as the locus of 'I' would be the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*);
that which delineates blue and so forth would be the active consciousness."

Therefore, it should be understood that there exists an external object, distinct from the continuum of the *ālayavijñāna*, which serves as the occasional cause for the functioning consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*); for their occasional arising occurs due to the occasional nature of the conditions for the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

In the system of the Vijñānavādins, what is called "latent impression" is the capacity of the *ālayavijñānas* occurring within a single continuum to produce their respective functioning consciousnesses.
And its "maturation" is its orientation toward the production of its own effect.
And its condition (*pratyaya*), that is, its cause, is accepted as the preceding moment existing within its own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*),
because dependence upon another continuum is not admitted.

Consequently, it must be stated that all moments existing within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are indeed capable with respect to the ripening of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) residing in the storehouse-consciousness which generates the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
If even one [moment] were not capable, [the result would never arise],
because there is no difference in their all existing within the continuum of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
On the other hand, if one holds the position that all [moments] are capable, the delay in time [before the result arises] would be untenable.

Furthermore, in order to account for their occasional occurrence, even a clear-minded person who does not wish to do so must acknowledge—without obscuring his own experience—that all six types of cognition, having as their objects sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and pleasure and so forth, arise in dependence upon four conditions.
These four well-known conditions are the objective (ālambana), the immediately preceding (samanantara), the contributory (sahakārin), and the dominant (adhipati).
Among these, for the mind—which is designated by the term "cognition" and manifests as blue and so forth—the state of having the aspect of blue arises from the blue objective condition.
From the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), which is the prior cognition, comes the nature of awareness;
from the auxiliary condition (sahakāripratyaya), which is light, comes clarity;
and from the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya), which is the eye, comes the specific determination of the apprehension of the object.
Since it would follow that the arisen cognition would be common to [all objects] such as taste and so forth, the eye ought to be the dominant condition (*adhipati*) for its restriction;
for in the world, that which acts as a restrictor is observed to be the dominant condition.
In this way, four causes are to be seen for pleasure and the rest, which consist of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
Thus, this aggregate consisting of mind and mental factors is fivefold, designated as form, consciousness, sensation, perception, and mental formations.

Among these, the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists of the sense faculties together with their objects, based on the etymological derivations that "objects are formed by these" (*rūpyante ebhiḥ*) and "they form [the objects]" (*rūpayanti*).
The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the stream of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

The aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is the stream of cognitions of pleasure, pain, and so forth, produced by the connection with the two previously mentioned aggregates. The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is the stream of consciousness that involves the verbal articulation of words such as "cow" and the like.

The aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as attachment and aversion, which are rooted in the aggregate of sensation, as well as the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as pride and arrogance, and merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
Having meditated upon all this as suffering, the locus of suffering, and the cause of suffering, one should accomplish the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), which is the means for its cessation.
Therefore it has been said: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—these four are the truths intended by the Noble Buddha.
Among these, suffering is well known;
the origin is the cause of suffering.

That [dependent origination] is twofold: dependent on conditions (*pratyayopanibandhana*) and dependent on causes (*hetūpanibandhana*). Regarding the dependence on conditions, the summarizing sutra states: "This is the fruit of conditions" (*idaṃ pratyayaphalam*). The meaning of the sutra is as follows: this effect arises from those other causes that "approach" or "converge"; the state of being a condition (*pratyayatva*)—that is, the collection of causes—is the fruit of that alone, and not of any conscious agent.
For example, the sprout, which has the seed as its cause, is produced from the convergence of the six elements (*dhātu*).
In that regard, the earth element produces the hardness and the odor of the sprout;
the water element produces its moisture and its taste;
and the fire element produces its color and its heat.
The wind element consists of tangibility and motion;
the space element consists of spatial accommodation and sound;
and the season element consists of earth and the other elements as appropriate.

And the sutra that summarizes the connection of causes is as follows: "Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the stability of phenomena (dharmasthititā), and the fixed order of phenomena (dharmaniyāmakatā)—that is, conformity with dependent origination (pratītyasamutpādānulomatā)—remains constant.

In the view of the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, that which is the nature of phenomena consisting of causes and effects—that is, the state of being cause and effect—remains established whether they arise or do not arise.
That which arises when something else exists, and does not arise when it does not exist, is the effect of that cause.
The explanation of "dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) is given by the phrase "dharma-sthititā" (the stability of phenomena), and so forth.
It refers to the stability of a phenomenon—that is, an effect—in its non-deviation from its cause.
The suffix *tala* is used here in its own sense (as a nominalizing suffix).
The restriction of the cause (dharma) with respect to its effect— namely,
that this causal relationship is not possible without a conscious agent— is addressed by the word "dependent" (pratītya).

When a cause exists, having depended upon— that is, having reached it— the conformity or accordance with the arising [of the effect] is itself the "nature of things" (dharmatā), which remains constant whether phenomena arise or do not arise.
And the meaning of the Sūtra is that no conscious presiding agent is perceived here.

The causal connection of dependent origination is as follows: from the seed comes the sprout, from the sprout the stalk, from the stalk the stem, from the stem the bud, from that the awn, from that the flower, and from that the fruit.

Yet, within this external collection, neither the cause, such as the seed, nor the effect, such as the sprout, is conscious; it does not think, "I am producing the sprout," or "I have been produced by the seed."
In this way, two causes should also be understood regarding internal [phenomena].
Following the principle that "one desists when the ocean of objects of knowledge stands before one," those who fear excessive prolixity in the text cease here.
Liberation is the cessation of both of those, or the arising of stainless knowledge immediately thereafter;
the means for that cessation is the path,
and that is the knowledge of reality.
And that [result] arises through the power of prior cultivation (*prācīnabhāvanā*); this is the supreme secret.
To those who asked about the end of the Sūtra, it was said: "Since you have asked about the end of the Sūtra, may you be Sautrāntikas.
Thus, by virtue of being so addressed by the Blessed One, the designation "Sautrāntika" came into being.

Certain Buddhists—describing themselves as Vaibhāṣikas—are known for characterizing this as a contradictory teaching. They argue that although external objects such as odors and internal aggregates such as form exist, the Blessed One taught "everything is empty" to beginners in order to produce detachment toward them; he taught "consciousness alone is real" to those second group who were obsessed with grasping at consciousness; and he taught "the object of cognition is inferable" to those third group who maintained that both [subject and object] are real.
This is their technical definition.

In the doctrine that [objects] are to be known through inference (*anumeya*), since there would be no object whatsoever that is perceptual (*pratyakṣika*), there would be no locus for the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and thus the operation of inference would be untenable; furthermore, this would contradict the experience of all people.
Therefore, objects are of two kinds: the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*).
Among these, apprehension in the form of non-conceptual [perception] (*nirvikalpaka*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).
Determination (*adhyavasāya*), which takes the form of conceptual cognition, is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*),
because it is a cognition consisting of conceptual construction (*kalpanājñāna*).
As it has been said: "Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*); it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Conceptualization (*vikalpa*), however, is a deception because it lacks correspondence with the appearance of the real object (*vastu-nirbhāsa*).
For the object to be grasped is indeed the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), provided that the act of grasping is otherwise [i.e., not deceptive].
That object does not exist, nor is that measurement produced by words, logical marks, the senses, and so forth.
And thus it is said.

If it is objected: "But if conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) lacks validity (*aprāmāṇya*), how can the attainment of the object and the correspondence (*saṃvāda*) for one who acts on its basis be possible?"—this is not sound.

For that is possible because the attainment of the object occurs through a mediated succession (*pāraṃparya*), according to the maxim of the conceptualization of a jewel regarding the luster of a jewel.
The remainder has been explained in detail in the section concerning the Sautrāntikas, and thus is not elaborated upon here.
Nor should it be said that a difference in instruction according to the inclinations of those to be trained does not belong to the tradition;
for it is stated in the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa*: "The teachings of the Lords of the World follow the power of the inclinations of sentient beings;
they are divided manifold in the world through many means."

"Through the distinction between the profound and the superficial, the teaching is indeed diverse, possessing both characteristics in some instances; yet the teaching is non-different [in its essence], characterized by the non-duality of emptiness.

It is well known in the Buddhist system that worship of the twelve sense-bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) brings about the highest good: "Having repeatedly acquired wealth, one should indeed [worship] the twelve sense-bases."
Since these are to be honored on all sides, what is the use of honoring anything else here?
The five organs of perception, as well as the five organs of action,
together with the mind and the intellect— these are declared by the wise to be the twelve sense-bases (āyatanas).
In the *Vivekavilāsa*, the Buddhist doctrine is stated as follows: "For the Buddhists, Sugata is the deity; the universe is momentary;
and this fourfold reality, known by the name of the Noble Truths, is respectively:
suffering, the bases [of perception], and then the origin."
Now, listen to the sequential explanation of this term "and the path."
The aggregates of one in saṃsāra are suffering, and they are proclaimed to be fivefold:
consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, and form itself.
The five sense-faculties, the objects beginning with sound, the fifth being the mind,
and the sphere of mental phenomena— these are the twelve spheres (āyatana).
Furthermore, that from which the group of afflictions such as attachment arises in the hearts of men—
known as the nature of "self" and "mine"— is the origin (samudaya).
That stable mental impression (vāsanā) which consists of the realization that "all conditioned phenomena are momentary" should be known as the Path; and that is designated as liberation.
Thus, there are two means of valid cognition: direct perception and inference;
likewise, the Buddhists are renowned as being of four schools, beginning with the Vaibhāṣikas.
The Vaibhāṣika does not highly regard an object that is conjoined with cognition;
the Sautrāntika does not maintain that an object is external and perceptible by direct perception.
The intellect accompanied by form is accepted by the Yogācāra;
however, the Madhyamikas consider consciousness alone to be self-abiding.

The liberation proclaimed by all four schools of Buddhism is said to arise from the eradication of the latencies within the continuum of consciousness that consist of passion and the other afflictions.

The Buddhist monks adopted the wearing of skins, the carrying of water-pots, the shaving of the head, the wearing of rags, eating during the forenoon, living in communities, and the wearing of red garments.
Now follows the doctrine of the Arhats. ||3||

Thus, unable to tolerate the doctrine of those who have loosened their waistbands (the Muktakas), the Nirgranthas (Jainas) somehow resort to the existence of a permanent entity and refute the position of momentariness.
They argue: "If no permanent self were admitted, then the accomplishment of the means for attaining results both in this world and the next would be fruitless;
for it is not possible that one person acts and another experiences the result."

Therefore, since the existence of a persisting entity that follows through prior and subsequent times—such that one might say, "I who performed an action in the past am now experiencing its fruit"—is established by clear evidence, momentariness (kṣaṇikatā), characterized as the subsistence in a temporal fraction devoid of prior and posterior parts, is not fit to be accepted by the discerning Arhats.
Now, you might think: "Who would prevent a stream that has arrived by virtue of being supported by valid means of knowledge?"

According to this principle, since momentariness has been established by such valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as "whatever exists is momentary," it follows accordingly that among those belonging to the same continuum (*saṃtāna*), the preceding cognition is the agent of the action and the subsequent cognition is the experiencer of the fruit.
Nor does there follow an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
because the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) serves as the restrictive factor.

Just as when mango seeds impregnated with sweet juice are sown in well-prepared soil, there is a certainty of sweetness in the fruit through the sequence of sprouts, stalks, trunks, branches, and shoots;
or just as when cotton seeds and the like are sprinkled with lac-dye juice, there is a certainty of redness in the cotton and so forth through the succession of sprouts and so on—as it has been said:
"For in whichever very continuum the latent impression of karma is deposited..."
It bears fruit right there, just as redness appears in cotton.

When lac-dye and other substances are sprinkled upon a citron flower or the like on Mount Kūṭaśaila, a certain potency is imparted to it; do you not see that? Even that [argument] is merely a resort to a blade of kāśa grass or a blade of kuśa grass.
Because it cannot withstand critical analysis:
is momentariness in the case of the example, such as a cloud, established by this very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) or by another?
Not the first.
The first [alternative] is not tenable, because since the momentariness favored by you has never been observed anywhere, this inference cannot arise due to the lack of an established example.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for by that very same logic, if momentariness were established everywhere, the inference based on existence would result in being redundant.

If it is accepted that existence (*sattva*) consists in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), then even a false snake-bite and the like would result in being considered existent by virtue of their causal efficiency.
For this very reason it has been said: "That which is endowed with origination, destruction, and persistence is existent.
Now, if it is argued that its [existence] is established through the superimposition of contradictory properties characterized by capacity and incapacity, that is incorrect.
Since the proponents of *syādvāda* accept the doctrine of non-absolutism (*anekāntavāda*), no contradiction is established [in their position].
As for what was said regarding the example of cotton and so forth, that is mere assertion,
because no supporting reasoning has been stated.
Furthermore, even there, the destruction of things without leaving a trace (niranvaya-nāśa) is not admitted.
Nor can a "series" (saṃtāna) be established as an object of valid cognition apart from the members of that series.
As it has been said: "Those [moments] which are of the same class, produced in succession, and mutually proximate..."
The individuals are those [moments], and their continuity is said to be one.
Nor can it avoid the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the restriction regarding the relationship between cause and effect.
For instance, the disciple's intellect might remember what was experienced by the teacher's intellect, or experience the fruit of the karma accumulated by that [teacher].
In such a case, there would follow the fallacies of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).

This has been stated by the author of the *Vākyakāra*, Siddhasena: "Alas! This other person is a great adventurer who, disregarding the faults of the destruction of what was done, the experience of the fruits of deeds not yet performed, the impossibility of liberation from cyclic existence, and the violation of the continuity of memory, directly desires momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*)."
(Vī.stu.18).

Furthermore, on the view of momentariness, since the object of cognition does not exist at the time of the cognition and the cognition does not exist at the time of the object, the relationship between the grasped and the grasper would be untenable, and consequently, all worldly activity would come to an end. Nor should one entertain the possibility that they exist simultaneously.

Because the relationship of cause and effect is impossible—like that between the left and right horns [of a cow]—it is untenable for that which is ungraspable to serve as an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
If it is argued that even though it belongs to a different time, it is graspable by virtue of imparting its form (*ākāra*) [to the cognition], that too is unsatisfactory;
for since it is difficult to maintain that a momentary cognition can be the locus of the imparting of a form, the theory of cognition with form (*sākāra-jñāna-vāda*) is thereby refuted.
Even in the theory of formless cognition (*nirākārajñānavāda*), the determination of specific objects for each respective action is established by virtue of *yogyatā* (causal capacity).

For instance, through perception, cognition is experienced as being devoid of the form of the object, grasping jars and other things for each individual person in a competitive "I-first" manner, and not as being overlaid with a reflection like a mirror. Furthermore, if cognition were to bear the form of the object, the practical distinction between distance and proximity regarding the object would be abandoned.
Nor should this be considered an instance of proving what is already accepted,

for the conventional usage [of terms] such as "the mountain is more distant," "this arm is closer," and "it is long" remains unimpeded and fully operative. Furthermore, it should not be argued that such usage occurs because the cause of the form [of the cognition] possesses properties such as being more distant.
Because it is not perceived as such in a mirror or similar surfaces.
Furthermore, if cognition, which arises from an object, were to imitate its insentience just as it imitates its blue form, then that cognition would also be insentient.
And in that case, for you who desired to gain growth, even your very root would be destroyed—thus a great calamity has befallen you.

Now, if you say that knowledge does not imitate insentience in order to avoid this fault, then—alas!—there would be no apprehension of it; thus, the logical fallacy arises that "while one seeks to secure something, another is lost. [Objection: Let there be no apprehension of insentience; what is that to us? [Response: Nothing at all. However, if you maintain that knowledge is distinct from insentience, then its apprehension must be admitted. And if that is so, then since it is impossible for knowledge to be both distinct from and non-distinct from insentience, the aforementioned fault remains unavoidable. Furthermore, if knowledge were non-distinct from insentience, then just as insentience is never perceived, knowledge too would never be perceived. Therefore, because it is impossible for knowledge to be either distinct from or non-distinct from insentience, the conclusion is that knowledge is simply non-existent. Thus, the position of those who hold that consciousness is self-proven is untenable. Consequently, the view of the venerable Śaṅkara—that the Self is established by the very nature of its existence—is alone correct. This is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The Self is established by the very nature of its existence (*siddhasvabhāvāt*). This means that the Self is established merely by its own existence, without depending on any other means of proof. This is because the Self is the witness of all means of knowledge, and because it is impossible for the Self to be unknown. For even when one says, "I do not know myself," it is the Self itself that is the knower of that very negation of knowledge. If the Self were not known, then the statement "I do not know myself" would be impossible, just as the statement "I do not know Devadatta" is impossible if Devadatta himself is not known. Moreover, the Self is not an object of knowledge like a pot or the like, which are perceived through the senses. Rather, the Self is the very nature of the knower. It is said: "The Self is not an object of knowledge; it is the nature of the knower. And: "The Self is not perceived by the senses; it is perceived by the witness of the senses.
