Even if that [consciousness] is not apprehended, when there is the apprehension of the form of blue, there would either be a difference between the two or an inconclusiveness [regarding their identity].
Furthermore, if its insentience is not apprehended while the form of blue is apprehended, how could that [insentience] be its own nature?
Otherwise, even the unapprehended three worlds would become the nature of a pillar that has been apprehended.

This entire collection of objects of knowledge has been elaborated upon in treatises such as the *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa* by followers of the Arhat’s doctrine, beginning with Prabhācandra (see *Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa*, p. 27). For fear of excessive length, it is not presented here.
Therefore, persons desiring the goals of human life should not follow the Buddhist path; rather, only the path of the Arhats is worthy of being followed.
And the true nature of an Arhat was defined by the venerable Hemacandra Sūri in the *Āptamīmāṃsā-alaṃkāra*: "The Lord Arhat,
the Supreme Sovereign, is omniscient, has conquered defects such as passion, is worshipped by the three worlds,
and speaks of things exactly as they are."

Now, it may be argued that no particular person designated by the term "omniscient" falls within the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the fivefold set of means of valid cognition that could apprehend his existence is not found to apply there.
Thus it has been stated by the Tautātitas: "An omniscient being is certainly not perceived at present by people such as ourselves."
Neither a single part nor a mark is perceived that might lead to inference.
Nor is there any scriptural injunction that eternally establishes an omniscient being;
nor can the intended meaning (tātparya) of explanatory passages (arthavāda) be postulated in that regard. ||2||
Nor is its existence established by those [scriptures] whose primary purpose is something else;
nor can it be restated, since it has not been previously understood through other means. (3)
The subject matter of the beginningless tradition has no beginning, nor does the Omniscient One have a beginning;
how, then, could he be established by means of a fabricated and unreal [scripture]? (4)
If the omniscient one is recognized by those who know him solely on the basis of his own words, how can the establishment of these two be achieved, given that they are mutually dependent? (5)
The word is true because it was spoken by the Omniscient One; therefore, his existence [is established].
How could both of these be proven without another established foundation? (6)

But those who, from a statement composed by one who is not omniscient and devoid of a [valid] foundation, understand that [the speaker] is not omniscient, do not recognize the nature of their own verbal expression. (7)
If we were now to see anyone at all who resembles the Omniscient One,
then we could know the Omniscient One by means of that analogy.
Even the Buddha’s teaching concerning the domain of dharma, adharma, and so forth,
would not be possible if omniscience did not exist.

Likewise, even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not applicable here as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the truth of the teaching is not perceived through direct perception (*adhyakṣa*). ||10||
To this, the following reply is given.

As for what was stated—that there is no perception of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could establish its existence—that is incorrect. This is because there exists inference and other such means that inform us of its existence. For instance, there is a certain self (*ātman*) who is the direct perceiver of all objects, because, while possessing the nature of apprehending them, his obstructing conditions have been eliminated.

If something possesses the nature of apprehending an object and its obstructing conditions have been eliminated, it directly perceives that object—just as visual consciousness, when free from obstructions such as cataracts, directly perceives color-form—and the Self possesses the nature of apprehending all objects and has its obstructing conditions eliminated; therefore, it directly perceives all things. Thus, the fact that the Self possesses the nature of apprehending all objects is not unestablished.

Furthermore, because the arising of knowledge of all objects through the force of *codanā* (Vedic injunction) would otherwise be inexplicable, and because the knowledge of the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*) that "whatever exists is multiform in nature" arises [from it];

for the teachers of the *Adhvaramīmāṃsā*, who maintain that "injunction indeed makes known such objects as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, the concealed, and the remote," accept that the self possesses the nature of apprehending all objects, based on their investigation into injunctions and prohibitions which results in knowledge whose scope encompasses every object.
Nor is there any impossibility regarding the destruction of the veil that obstructs all objects [of knowledge],
for the specific causal complex characterized by the triad beginning with right vision (samyagdarśana), which serves as the cause for the destruction of the veil, is well-established.
By this same principle, minor obstacles should also be dispelled.
If it is argued that it is incorrect to say that clear, primary perception arises as a cognition whose object is entirely free from limitation by virtue of the destruction of obstructions—
because for such an omniscient being, being eternally liberated, an obstruction is simply impossible— that is not so,
because the very state of being eternally liberated is unproven.
The Omniscient One is not one who was liberated at the beginning;
because he is liberated, he is like one who was not previously liberated. Furthermore, the designation "liberated" is made in relation to those who are bound.
And in the absence of that [cause], this [world] would also be non-existent, like space.
But surely, its existence is established by its being the agent of the beginningless succession of effects such as the earth;
for instance: "The earth and so forth have an agent, because they are effects, like a pot."
That too is incorrect,
because the very nature of being an effect is unestablished.
Nor should it be asserted that this is proven by the fact of having parts.
For this web of conceptual constructions arises as follows:

Is "having parts" (sāvayavatva) the state of being conjoined with parts, the state of inhering in parts, being produced by parts, being a substance that inheres [in others], or being the object of a cognition of something having parts?
It is not the first.
Because it is inconclusive with respect to space and so forth;
nor is the second [alternative] correct,
because of its deviation in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and the like.
Not the third,
because it is indistinguishable from the probandum;
nor the fourth.
Because it is subject to being seized by the bolt of the pair of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*),

"substantiality" (*dravyatva*)— whether intended as mere substantiality through the relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha-mātra*), or as substantiality inherent [in something] (*samaveta-dravyatva*), or as substantiality inherent elsewhere (*anyatra-samaveta-dravyatva*)— is made the reason (*hetu*). In the first case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to space (*gagana*) and so forth.
For in that case as well, the properties of being an inherence (samavāyatva) and being a substance (dravyatva) would be possible [in the reason].
In the second alternative, there is non-difference from the probandum (sādhyāviśiṣṭatā),
because one would be proving the inherence in the parts which constitute the inherent cause (samavāyakāraṇa) of the referents of other words.
Even though it is the object of a cognition of something possessing parts, it lacks the nature of being an effect.

Nor should it be accepted that, despite its partlessness, its status as the object of a cognition of something possessing parts is merely figurative due to its connection with objects that possess parts;
for if it were partless, it would contradict its omnipresence, just like an atom.
Furthermore, is it being established that there is one creator or many?
In the first case, there is a deviation [from the rule] regarding palaces and the like,
because many individuals, such as architects and others, are observed to be the creators therein.

In the second case, if many were the creators of the universe, it would be impossible to prevent the possibility of mutual disagreement among them; consequently, if each one were to create an object with a different form from the others, everything would fall into disorder.
Furthermore, since all possess equal capacity, if the entire world were produced by even one of them, the others would be rendered useless.
As it has been said in the *Vītarāgastuti*: "There is some creator of the world; he is one, he is omnipresent, he is independent, and he is eternal."
These would indeed be mere mockery of the gods for those who do not have you as their instructor.
(Vīrastuti 6).

Also elsewhere: "Furthermore, no agent whatsoever is seen here acting according to his own will; otherwise, the same consequence would apply even to a mat-maker. Moreover, what effect could a person produce here by directly striking the three worlds with axes and such tools?"
Thus.
Therefore, it is logical that omniscience arises upon the destruction of the veils through the power of the three previously mentioned causes.
Nor should it be argued that the triad beginning with right vision is untenable due to the absence of another teacher for him;
for his knowledge of all things originates from the scriptures composed by a previous omniscient being.

Nor is there any fault such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), because we accept that the lineage of the scriptures and the omniscient ones is beginningless (*anādi*), like the seed and the sprout; enough of this digression.

The triad of right view (*samyagdarśana*) and so forth, well-known as being denoted by the term "Three Jewels" (*ratnatraya*), has been elucidated in the *Paramāgamasāra*, which is devoted to summarizing the teaching of the Arhat, as follows: "Right view, knowledge, and conduct constitute the path to liberation."
And it has been explained by Yogadeva:

when the reality of the objects such as the soul (*jīva*) is established in its true form and taught by the Arhat, the state of conviction—synonymous with being free from perverse attachment—is right vision (*samyagdarśana*).
As stated in the *Tattvārthasūtra*: "Right vision is conviction in the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*)."
Furthermore: "Interest in the truths taught by the Jina is called right faith;
it arises either by nature or through a teacher. Thus [it is said].
*Nisarga* (natural acquisition) is the essential nature of the self independent of instruction from others.
*Adhigama* (attainment through learning) is knowledge produced by instruction from others in the form of explanations and the like.
Right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) is the comprehension, free from delusion and doubt, of the categories such as the soul (*jīva*) and so forth, according to their actual nature as they exist.
As it has been said: "The wise call that right knowledge (samyagjñāna) which is the comprehension, either in brief or in detail, of the principles (tattva) as they truly exist."
That knowledge is fivefold, distinguished by the divisions of *mati*, *śruta*, *avadhi*, *manaḥparyāya*, and *kevala*.
As it has been said: "Knowledge consists of *mati*, *śruta*, *avadhi*, *manaḥparyāya*, and *kevala*.

The meaning of this is as follows: when there is the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), that which, being operative while relying upon the senses and the mind, cognizes an object as it truly is, is *mati*.

When there is the subsidence-cum-destruction (*kṣayopaśama*) of the veil of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇa*), the clear knowledge produced by sensory perception (*mati*) is *śruta* (scriptural knowledge). *Avadhi* (clairvoyance) is that knowledge which has a delimited object and is caused by the subsidence-cum-destruction produced by qualities such as right vision (*samyagdarśana*). When there is the subsidence-cum-destruction of the veil of knowledge and the obstruction of the mind (*manahparyāya-antarāya*), the clear discerning knowledge of an object residing in another's mind is *manaḥparyāya* (telepathy). That knowledge for the sake of which ascetics practice specific ascetic disciplines (*tapaḥkriyā*), being unmixed with other forms of knowledge, is *kevala* (omniscience).

Among these, the first is indirect (parokṣa) and the other is direct (pratyakṣa). As it has been said: "Valid cognition (pramāṇa), which illuminates both itself and its object and is free from contradiction, is twofold—direct and indirect—due to the determination of the object of knowledge."
The internal subdivisions, however, should be understood in detail from that very scripture (*āgama*).

For one who is endowed with faith and knowledge and is striving for the destruction of the karma of transmigration, the cessation of activity that causes the movement toward sin is right conduct (*samyak-cāritra*).
This has been explained in detail by the Arhat: "Conduct is said to be the renunciation of all forms of association with what is blameworthy."
That has been proclaimed as fivefold, according to the distinctions of the vows beginning with non-violence.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness:
that which does not involve the taking of life through the influence of negligence,
whether toward mobile or immobile beings, is considered the vow of non-violence.
Speech that is pleasant, beneficial, true, and kind is said to be the vow of *sūnṛta*.
Even that which is true is not "truth" if it is unpleasant and harmful;
the vow of non-stealing is declared to be the non-taking of what is not given. For wealth is the external life-force of men; by seizing it, one indeed kills them.

The renunciation of divine and worldly sensual pleasures through mind, speech, and body— whether performed by oneself, permitted by others, or caused to be done by others— is considered the eighteenfold Brahma-faring.

The relinquishing of infatuation toward all things constitutes non-possessiveness; for even toward non-existent things, infatuation gives rise to the corruption of the mind. These [five senses] are cultivated in five ways through the five meditations in successive order.
The great vows accomplish for the world the imperishable state.

And the elaboration of the fivefold cultivation has been explained: "By constantly refraining from joking, greed, fear, and anger, and by speaking only after careful reflection, one should cultivate the vow of truthful speech."
By such statements [as these],
it is shown that these— right vision, right knowledge, and right conduct— are the cause of liberation when combined, not individually,
just like an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Likewise, in this context, knowledge, faith, and conduct together accomplish the fruit, not individually.
Here, in brief, there are two principles known as the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva). Among these, the living is characterized by consciousness.
The non-soul (ajīva), however, is characterized by a lack of consciousness.

As it was stated by Padmanandin: "The two supreme principles are the conscious and the unconscious; discrimination is the discernment between them, consisting of determining what is to be accepted as acceptable and what is to be rejected as rejectable."
For that which is to be abandoned is the agent, passion, and so forth, along with their effect, non-discrimination;
that which is to be accepted is the supreme light, characterized solely by pure awareness. Thus it is said.

Upayoga is the state of knowledge and perception when they undergo transformation into the nature of self-aware consciousness (*sahujacidrūpa*). It serves as the cause for the soul—which has become one with karma through the bondage of its own constituent parts (*pradeśabandha*)—to realize its distinctness from that karma. Furthermore, when there is an intention to describe the specific modes (*paryāya*) of the soul, which is a universal characteristic of all living beings, it constitutes the soul's essential nature (*jīvasvarūpa*) as it transforms through the states of *aupaśamika*, *kṣāyika*, and *kṣāyopaśamika* by virtue of subsidence, destruction, or destruction-cum-subsidence, and through turbid or other forms due to the rise of karma.

As the Vācakācārya stated: "The subsidential (aupaśamika), the destructive (kṣāyika), the mixed (miśra), the emergent (audayika), and the transformational (pāriṇāmika) states are the inherent nature of the soul" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 2.1).
When there is subsidence (upaśama) of karma in the form of its not reaching the state of fruition, the state that arises in the soul is the subsidential (aupaśamika).
It is like the clarity of water when it has fallen to the bottom after the mud that was making it turbid has settled due to contact with a substance such as *kataka*.
The *kṣāyika* state is that which brings about purity by washing away the mud of passion and other defilements through the investigation of the reality of the Arhat.
A state arising when karma has been destroyed is *kṣāyika*, just as there is clarity in water contained within a clean vessel of crystal or the like, once it has been separated from the mud;
as is liberation (*mokṣa*).
A mixed state (miśra) is one that possesses both natures;
for example, the partial transparency of water.
A state that comes into being when there is the emergence of karma is called "emergent" (audayika).
The innate state (*sahaja-bhāva*), such as consciousness (*cetanatva*) and so forth, which does not depend on the subsidence of karma and the like, is the transformative (*pāriṇāmika*) nature.
This is the meaning of the aphorism: that this [nature] constitutes the essential selfhood (*svarūpa*) of the soul (*jīva*), whether it be capable of liberation (*bhavya*) or incapable (*abhavya*).
As it is stated in the *Svarūpasaṃbodhana*: "It is neither different from knowledge, nor non-different; it is in no way both different and non-different."
Knowledge, existing as a continuous sequence of prior and subsequent moments, is proclaimed to be this very Self.

If it is argued that since difference and non-difference exist by mutually excluding one another, only one of them can be real, and therefore their coexistence as a dual nature is illogical—this is incorrect.
For there is a lack of evidence for sublation (*bādha*). Indeed, non-perception (*anupalambha*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that effects sublation.
It does not exist;
for in all things, the nature of manifoldness (*anekāntātmakatva*) is well-established according to the doctrine of the Syādvādin—so much for that.

Others, however, describe another elaboration of the categories of the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*), based on the division into the five astikāyas: *jīva*, space (*ākāśa*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and matter (*pudgala*).
Regarding these five principles (*tattva*), the designation "existence" (*asti*) is applied because they are connected with the three periods of time.
The designation "body" (*kāya*) is applied because they possess multiple spatial points (*pradeśa*), like a physical body.
In that regard, souls (*jīva*) are of two kinds: those in the cycle of existence (*saṃsārin*) and those who are liberated (*mukta*).
Those who undergo the transition from one existence to another are transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*).
They are of two kinds: those with minds (*samanaska*) and those without minds (*amanaska*). Among them, those possessing consciousness (*saṃjñin*) are those with minds.
Perception (saṃjñā) consists of the grasping of the forms of training, actions, and speech; those devoid of these are the mindless (amanaska).
These mindless beings are of two kinds, distinguished as mobile (trasa) and stationary (sthāvara).
Among those, the fourfold mobile beings (trasas) consist of those with two sense-faculties and so forth, such as the conch-shell, the snail, and the like;
the immobile beings (sthāvaras) consist of earth, water, fire, air, and plants.
Among these, the dust found on a path is earth.
Bricks and the like constitute the earth-body (*pṛthivīkāya*).
One who has grasped [the earth] as an earth-body is an earth-bodied being (*pṛthivīkāyika*).
One who will grasp the earth as an earth-body is an earth-living being (*pṛthivījīva*).
In this same manner, the fourfold division should also be applied to water and the other elements.

In that context, "immobile beings" (sthāvara) refers to those who have taken up or will take up earth and the other elements as their bodies; it does not refer to the earth-element itself or the "earth-body" (pṛthivīkāya), because those [latter] lack sentience (ajīvatva).
And those immovable beings possess only the sense of touch;
they are liberated, being devoid of the attainment of another existence.
The categories of dharma, adharma, and space possess unity and are inactive, yet they are the causes for the movement of substances to other locations.
In this regard, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are well known.
They reside everywhere in the unobstructed light within the space designated by the term "world-space" (*lokākāśa*).
Their function is to assist in motion and stability.
For this very reason, the category of motion (dharmāstikāya) is inferred from movement;
the category of rest (adharmāstikāya) is inferred from stability;
and immersion (avagāha) is the entry of one substance into the space occupied by another substance.
That is the function of space.
*Pudgalas* possess touch, taste, smell, and color (*Ta.sū.* 5/24).
They are of two kinds: atoms (*aṇu*) and aggregates (*skandha*).
Atoms (aṇu) cannot be consumed;
they are aggregates (skandha) such as dyads (dyaṇuka) and so forth.
In that regard, atoms and the like are produced from the disintegration of aggregates such as dyads and so forth.
From the aggregation of atoms (*aṇu*) and so forth, dyads (*dyaṇuka*) and other compounds arise.

In some cases, the production of aggregates (*skandha*) occurs through both division and aggregation (Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.26). For this very reason, they are called *pudgala* because they "fill" (*pūrayanti*) and "dissolve" (*galanti*).
Although time lacks the status of an ontological category (*astikāya*) due to its lack of multiple spatial points (*pradeśa*), it nonetheless possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*).
This is because of its association with the characteristic of extension (*tallakṣaṇayoga*).
As it has been stated: "Substance possesses qualities and modes" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.38), and "Qualities reside in substance and are themselves devoid of qualities" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 5.39).

For example, in the case of the soul (*jīva*), there are attributes such as the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*), and in the case of matter (*pudgala*), there are general natures such as the nature of form (*rūpatva*).

The qualities (*guṇas*) of substance (*dravya*)—namely *dharma*, *adharma*, space (*ākāśa*), and time (*kāla*)—are its common characteristics, such as being the cause of motion, rest, accommodation, and the passage of time, respectively, according to their possibility.
The manifestation of that substance in the form described above is its mode (*paryāya*).
Origination, the state of becoming that [substance], transformation, and mode are synonyms for *paryāya*.
Just as the knowledge of jars and so forth, pleasure, and affliction belong to the soul (jīva);
as the lump of clay, the jar, and so forth belong to the person (pudgala);
and as the specific states of motion and so forth belong to the categories beginning with dharma—therefore, there is the well-known doctrine that there are six substances (dravyas).

Some describe seven principles (*tattva*). As it is said: "The principles are the soul (*jīva*), the non-soul (*ajīva*), influx (*āsrava*), bondage (*bandha*), stoppage (*saṃvara*), dissociation (*nirjarā*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). (Tattvārthasūtra 1.4).
Therein, the soul (jīva) and the non-soul (ajīva) have been defined.
Now, influx (āsrava) is defined: the movement of the self (ātman) by way of the vibration of the body, such as the gross physical body and so forth, which is designated by the term "yoga," is influx.
Just as a door submerged in water is called "influx" because it is the cause for the inflow of water and other substances.
It is thus stated that since karma flows [into the soul] by means of the channel of yoga, that yoga is the influx (*āsrava*).

Just as a wet cloth catches the mass of dust brought from all sides by the wind, so too the self, moistened by the water of passions (*kaṣāya*), receives the karma brought by yoga through all its parts.
Or, just as a red-hot iron ball thrown into water absorbs the water from all sides, so too the living being, heated by passions, takes up the karma brought by yoga from every direction.
*Kaṣāya* (passion) is so called because it "grinds" or destroys the self by leading it to an evil rebirth; it consists of anger, pride, deceit, and greed.
It is twofold, distinguished as auspicious (*śubha*) and inauspicious (*aśubha*). Among these, the auspicious bodily yoga (*kāyayoga*) consists of non-violence and the like.
Auspicious vocal activity (*vāgyoga*) consists of speaking the truth, that which is beneficial, and so forth.

Auspicious mental activity (*manoyoga*) consists of devotion to the five supreme beings (*pañcaparameṣṭhin*)—namely the Arhat, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, and Sādhu—as well as delight in austerity, scriptural knowledge, humility, and so forth.
Conversely, inauspicious activity is also threefold.
This entire collection of the various divisions and sub-divisions of the influx (āsrava) is the activity (yoga) of body, speech, and mind;
that is the influx.
When it is auspicious, it leads to merit (puṇya).
This was stated with great emphasis in the sequence of sūtras beginning with "The impure [leads] to evil" (Ta.Sū. 6.1–4).
Others, however, held this view: "Influx" (āsrava) is the activity of the senses toward objects, for it causes the person to flow [into them].
For the light of the self (pauruṣaṃ jyotiḥ), through the gateway of the senses, touches the objects and transforms itself into the form of cognitions such as color-and-shape (rūpa-jñāna).

Bandha is that which the soul performs—namely, the taking up (*ādāna*) or adherence (*upaśleṣaṇa*) of matter-particles (*pudgala*) that are capable of forming karma, which consist of infinite space-points (*ananta-pradeśa*), occupy a single subtle space-point (*sūkṣma-eka-kṣetra-avagāhin*), and are influenced by false view (*mithyā-darśana*), non-restraint (*avirati*), negligence (*pramāda*), passions (*kaṣāya*), and activity (*yoga*).
As it has been said: "Because of its state of possessing passions (*sakaṣāyatva*), the soul takes up matter-particles suitable for the state of karma; that is bondage" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.2).
In this context, the mention of "passion" (*kaṣāya*) is intended as an indicator for all causes of bondage.

The teacher Vācaka enumerated the causes of bondage: "False view, non-restraint, negligence, passion, and yoga are the causes of bondage" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.1). False view (*mithyādarśana*) is of two kinds: one is innate, consisting of a lack of faith in the principles arising from the maturation of false karma (*mithyākarma*) without depending on the instruction of others;
the other is born from the instruction of others.
Non-restraint (*avirati*) consists of the appropriation of the six objects beginning with earth and the lack of self-control over the six sense organs.
Negligence (*pramāda*) is the lack of enthusiasm for the five careful conducts (*samiti*) and the three restraints (*gupti*).
Passion (*kaṣāya*) refers to anger and the other afflictions.

In this regard, the distinctions are as follows: those ending with the *kaṣāyas* (passions) are the causes for the bondage of duration (*sthiti*) and intensity (*anubhava*), while *yoga* (activity) is the cause for the bondage of nature (*prakṛti*) and quantity (*pradeśa*).
It has been stated that "bondage is fourfold; its types are nature, duration, intensity, and quantity" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 8.3).

Just as the neem tree and molasses possess the inherent natures of bitterness and sweetness respectively, so too does the obscuring karma (*āvaraṇīya*) have the nature of obscuring knowledge and perception—like a cloud covering the light of the sun, or like a jar obstructing the light of a lamp.
The capacity of karma to be experienced as both pleasant and unpleasant to produce pleasure and pain is like licking honey from the edge of a sword.
The capacity of deluding karma (*darśanamohanīya*) to cause lack of faith in the true meaning of reality is like association with wicked people.
The capacity of deluding karma (*cāritramohanīya*) to be a cause of non-restraint is like the intoxication of liquor.
The function of *āyus* (vitality) is to bind the body, like water;
the function of *nāman* (name) is to produce various names, like a painter;
the function of *gotra* (lineage) is to determine high or low status, like a potter.
The nature of an obstacle (*antarāya*) is to be the cause of hindrance to generosity and the other virtues, like a treasury official.
This natural bondage (*prakṛti-bandha*) is of eight kinds, to be understood as the primary categories of substance-karma (*dravya-karma*) with their internal subdivisions.

Thus spoke the venerable teacher Umāsvāti: "The first [category] consists of knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, life-span-determining, name-determining, status-determining, and obstructive karmas" (Tattvārthasūtra 8.4).
And he has summarized its divisions as follows: "There are five, two, nine, eight, twenty-six, four, two, forty-two, and five divisions, respectively" (Ta. Sū. 8.5).
Since all of this has been explained by Vidyānanda and others, it is not presented here for fear of prolixity.

Just as the milk of goats, cows, buffaloes, and so forth remains established without deviating from its nature of sweetness for such a long duration, so too, for the three primary *prakṛtis* beginning with knowledge-obscuration (*jñānāvaraṇa*) and for the obstructive karma (*antarāya*), there is a state of non-deviation from their own respective natures for a period of thirty *koṭi-koṭis* of *sāgaropamas*, which constitutes their maximum duration (*parāsthiti*), as stated in the *Tattvārtha-sūtra* (8.14). This is a state of stability like that of the aforementioned examples.

Just as there is a specific capacity for performing their respective functions—characterized by degrees such as intense or mild—in the milks of goats, cows, buffaloes, and so forth, which is termed *anubhāva* (potency), so too is the specific capacity of the *karmapudgala* (karmic matter) for performing its own function called *anubhāva*.

The entry of the infinite number of spatial points (*pradeśa*) of the aggregates of *pudgala* that have transformed into the state of karma into the spatial points of the self (*ātman*) is *pradeśabandha* (bondage of spatial points).

*Saṃvara* is the cessation of influx (*āsrava*). That by which karma entering the self is obstructed—namely, the vows of restraint (*gupti*), the codes of conduct (*samiti*), and so forth—is *saṃvara*.
Gupti is the concealment of the self through the impossibility of its movement;
it is threefold, distinguished by the restraint of body, speech, and mind.
Samiti is the correct proceeding by avoiding injury to living beings.
It is fivefold according to the distinctions of *seryā*, *bhāṣā*, and so forth,
as elaborated by the master Hemacandra:
"On a path traversed by the world, kissed by the rays of the sun..."
Having observed [the path] for the sake of protecting living beings, such a mode of movement is considered "right conduct" (īryā) by the virtuous.
Speech that is blameless, immortal, beneficial to all people, and measured—
this pleasant speech of those who restrain their words is called the restraint of speech (bhāṣā-samiti).
When a sage accepts food that is always untainted by the forty-two faults of begging, this is considered the restraint of seeking (eṣaṇā-samiti).
Having carefully inspected seats and other such items,

and having avoided those that are infested with insects on the surface of the earth— abounding in phlegm, urine, and excrement— one should take them up, set them down, and contemplate them; this is known as the *ādāna-samiti*.
When a virtuous person discards [food] with care, that constitutes the samiti of utsarga (the carefulness regarding disposal).

"An influx (āsrava) is the gateway of the stream; that which closes it is restraint (saṃvara). Thus they say. As it has been stated by the learned: "Influx is the cause of existence; restraint is the cause of liberation."
Thus, this is the creation of the Arhatas; everything else is its elaboration.
The principle known as *nirjarā* (dissociation) is the wearing away of accumulated karma through practices such as austerity (*tapas*).

Tapa is defined as that which causes the body to "waste away" (*jarayati*) or destroys the collection of long-standing passions (*kaṣāya*), merit, pleasure, and pain; it consists of acts such as the plucking out of hair.
This *nirjarā* is of two kinds, distinguished as *yathākāla* (natural) and *aupakramika* (induced).

Among these, the first is that which occurs when a karma intended to yield its fruit at a specific time actually bestows that fruit at that very same time; it is celebrated as "nirjarā" (exhaustion) arising from the ripening of desire and so forth. That which enters the sequence of emergence through the power of austerity (*tapas*) by one's own will is "upakramika-nirjarā" (voluntary exhaustion).
As it has been said: "In this world, [it is the exhaustion] of those karmas which constitute the seed of *saṃsāra*."
Nirjarā is considered to be of two kinds: nirjarā with desire (sakāma) and nirjarā without desire (akāma).
"It is remembered that for those who practice self-restraint, it is accompanied by desire, whereas for other embodied beings, it is without desire."

Liberation (*mokṣa*) is the absolute release from all karma through the cessation of the causes of bondage—such as false view (*mithyādarśana*) and the rest—which results in the non-occurrence of new karma, and through the removal of accumulated karma by means of the presence of the causes of dissociation (*nirjarā*).
As it is said: "Liberation is the complete liberation from all karma through the absence of the causes of bondage and through dissociation" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.2).
Immediately thereafter, [the soul] ascends upwards to the end of the universe (*ālokāntāt*) (Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.5).

Just as a potter’s wheel, set in motion by the whirling of the hand, staff, and so forth, continues to spin even after that [motion] has ceased due to the force of its momentum (*saṃskāra*) until that momentum is exhausted, so too, the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) which was repeatedly made by the self while dwelling in *bhava* for the sake of attaining liberation results in the liberated one’s movement to the end of the world (*ālokānta*) through the force of prior momentum, even in the absence of that [aspiration].

Or, just as a gourd substance, having become heavy by being coated with clay, sinks in water, but rises upward once it is freed from the bond of the clay, so too the self, being devoid of karma, moves upward because of its lack of attachment (*asaṅga*).
Due to the nature of upward motion, like the seed of the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*) after its binding is severed, and due to the nature of [flaming] upward like a crest of fire;
"bondage" (*bandha*) is the state of existing without separation when there is mutual interpenetration of spatial points (*pradeśa*),
whereas "contact" (*saṅga*) is merely mutual reaching.
Thus it has been said: "Due to previous application, due to non-attachment, due to the severance of bonds, and likewise due to the transformation of the state of existence" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.6);
and "like a potter's wheel that has been set in motion, like a gourd freed from its coating, like a castor-oil seed, and like a flame of fire" (Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.7).
For this very reason, they recite:
The planets, such as the sun and the moon, return again and again after they have gone;
but those who have reached the space of the world of Brahmā do not return even today.
(Thus ends the *Pañcārtha-bhāṣya*.

Others, however, maintained that liberation is the abiding of the self in the upper region—an self whose afflictions and their latent impressions have all been eliminated, whose knowledge is unobstructed, and which is solely intent upon bliss.
Some have accepted these nine categories as previously described, together with merit and demerit, which are the means for happiness and suffering.

Thus it is stated in the Siddhānta: "The soul (jīva) and the non-soul (ajīva), along with merit (puṇya) and demerit (pāpa), influx (āsrava), stoppage (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarana), bondage (bandha), and liberation (mokṣa)—these are the nine principles (tattvas). We have desisted from further elaboration here, as we have already engaged in a general summary. In all these matters, the Jains apply the logic known as the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅginaya).

"It may be that it exists, it may be that it does not exist, it may be that it both exists and does not exist, it may be inexpressible, it may be that it exists and is inexpressible, it may be that it does not exist and is inexpressible, and it may be that it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible. Anantavīrya established all of this: "When there is the intention to express its affirmation, the understanding should be 'it may be that it exists';
when its negation is intended to be expressed, the application should be 'it may be that it does not exist'."
When there is a desire to express both [truth and falsity] successively, the formulation pertains to the whole [set of propositions].
When there is a desire to express them simultaneously, it would be inexpressible due to incapacity.
When there is a desire to express the first two [truth and falsity] as inexpressible, the fifth alternative (bhaṅga) is accepted.
When there is the intention to express both the last [alternative] and the inexpressible, the sixth proposition arises.
And the seventh alternative is said to be joined by a conjunction.
The word *syāt* is indeed an indeclinable (*nipāta*) that resembles a finite verb (*tiṅanta*) and indicates non-absolutism (*anekānta*).

As it has been said: "In sentences, the indeclinable *syāt* indicates non-absolutism; it is a qualifier with respect to what is to be understood. Because it possesses a specific meaning, it is an indeclinable resembling a finite verb."

If, however, this word *syāt* were indicative of an absolute certainty (*ekānta*), then in the sentence "it exists" (*syād asti*), the word *syāt* would be redundant. But since it indicates non-absolutism (*anekānta*), the meaning "in some way it exists" (*kathaṃcid asti*) is obtained from the word *syāt*; thus, there is no redundancy. As it has been said: "The doctrine of *syād-vāda* [arises] from the abandonment of absolute one-sidedness; for what kind of existence is there [without it]?"
"Dependent upon the method of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅginaya), it effects the distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted."

If a thing exists absolutely—existing in every way, at all times, in all places, and with its entire essence—then one would never, at any time, or for any purpose, engage in activity toward it or withdraw from it through the desire to acquire or the desire to avoid.
This is because there would be nothing to be attained that has not already been attained, and it would be impossible to abandon what cannot be abandoned.

However, under the view of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda), since a thing exists in some respect, in some place, at some time, and in some manner, the abandonment and acquisition of things are logically possible for those who act with discernment.
Furthermore, one must ask whether the nature of a thing is its existence or its non-existence, and so forth.
First of all, it is not the case that existence is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of a thing.
Because "the pot exists" and [the pot] are synonyms, their simultaneous employment is improper;
furthermore, it would contradict the employment of the term "does not exist.
This should be applied similarly in other cases as well.
As it has been said: "One should not say 'the jar exists,' because the jar is indeed existent;
nor should one say 'it does not exist,' because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence."
And so forth.

Therefore, it should be stated as follows: opponents are of four types based on the distinctions of the doctrines of existence (*sat*), non-existence (*asat*), both existence and non-existence (*sadasat*), and the indescribable (*anirvacanīya*). Furthermore, there are three types who hold views of existence, non-existence, and so forth, mixed with the doctrine of the indescribable. When these [opponents] are questioned as to whether a thing exists and so forth, since it is possible for them to reply "it exists in some way" and so on, all those disputants become despondent and remain silent; thus, for one who accepts the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects) which determines the complete meaning, victory is achieved in every instance—this is entirely logical.

As the Teacher stated in the *Syādvādamañjarī*: "The object of all cognitions is a reality consisting of manifold aspects (*anekāntātmaka*). An object qualified by a single aspect is considered the domain of a *naya*.
This occurs when various logical systems (*nyāya*), each fixed upon a single point, proceed along the path of scripture."
That which determines the complete meaning is the entity called "scripture" (śruta). Thus it is said.
Just as other doctrines are characterized by the state of mutual thesis and counter-thesis among those who are envious,
so it is not with the system of the Arhat, for he desires all methods of reasoning without distinction and is thus free from partiality.

Violence, attachment and aversion, passion and hatred, lack of restraint, lust, grief, and false belief—He who is free from these eighteen defects is [the Lord]. 2.
The Jina is the God and the Guru, the teacher of the instruction of the true knowledge of reality;
knowledge, vision, and conduct are the path to liberation. ||3||
For the Syādvāda, there are two means of valid cognition: perception and inference.
Everything consists of the nature of both the eternal and the non-eternal; there are either nine or seven categories. (4)
The soul and the non-soul, merit and demerit, as well as influx, restraint, bondage, shedding, and liberation—their explanation is now stated. (5)
The soul is characterized by consciousness; that which is other than it is non-soul.
Merit consists of the atoms of virtuous karma, while demerit is its opposite. (6)
An influx (āsrava) is the stream or gateway; restraint (saṃvara) is that which closes it.
The entry [of matter] is the bondage of karmas; shedding (nirjarā) is the separation from them.
Liberation results from the destruction of the eight karmas; furthermore, some maintain that merit is included within restraint (saṃvara) and evil within influx (āsrava). ||8||

For the self that has attained the fourfold infinity, is hidden from the world, and has exhausted the eight karmas, liberation is proclaimed by the Jina as the irreversible state beyond the ocean [of rebirth]. 9.
Wearing dust-sweeping brooms, subsisting on alms, with shaven heads, clad in white garments, patient by nature, and free from attachments—such are the Jaina ascetics. 10.

With their hair plucked out, carrying peacock-feather brooms in their hands, using their palms as bowls, and naked, they subsist on food gathered from above; these are the second kind of Jina-sages who dwell in the house of a donor. (11)
"One who eats does not become a Kevalin, nor does a woman attain liberation while naked;
this, they say, is the great difference between them and the Śvetāmbaras. (12) Thus it is said.
This doctrine of the Ārhats deserves the censure of those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

For when a single entity exists as an ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is impossible for mutually contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence—which are themselves ultimately real—to coexist within it simultaneously.
Nor should it be argued that, since a conjunction of existence and non-existence, which are mutually contradictory, is impossible, there must instead be an alternation (*vikalpa*) between them.

For according to the principle that "it is action (kriyā) that is subject to conceptual differentiation (vikalpyate), not the real entity (vastu)," it should not be maintained— on the strength of supporting examples such as Heramba and Narasiṃha— that the entire world is non-absolute (anaikānta).

In one place there is elephant-hood or lion-hood, while in another there is human-hood; thus, because there is no contradiction due to the difference in location, the illustration fails when used to assert that a single entity is non-absolute (anekānta) by virtue of having existence and non-existence in the same place. If it is argued that both are tenable—existence in the form of substance (dravyātman) and its absence in the form of mode (paryāyātman)—this is not so. For if existence and non-existence were the nature of something at different times, there would be no fault.
Nor should it be argued that, like shortness and length, the world would possess a state of non-exclusivity (anekāntatva) for a single entity;
for there is no contradiction when the counter-correlates (pratiyogin) differ.
Therefore, due to a lack of evidence, it is not logical for mutually contradictory properties such as simultaneous existence and non-existence to reside in a single object.
In this manner, the refutation of other modes of expression (*bhaṅgī*) should also be understood.

Furthermore, is this *saptabhaṅginaya*, which is the root of all this, itself one-sided (*ekānta*) or non-one-sided (*anekānta*)? In the first case, there is a contradiction with the proposition that "everything is non-one-sided."
In the second case, the intended meaning is not established,
because it is non-conclusive (anaikāntika) and therefore lacks probative force. Thus, for the proponent of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvādin), this would be a rope with snares on both ends.

Moreover, if there were no fixed determination regarding the number nine or seven as the result, nor the knower who determines it, nor the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by which it is determined, nor the object of knowledge (*prameya*) such as the number nine itself, then the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Lord), the founder of the Arhat doctrine, would have most effectively established his own status as a *tīrthaṅkara*.

Likewise, if one accepts that the soul (*jīva*) possesses a dimension corresponding to the body, then for a yogi who assumes multiple bodies through the power of yoga, it would follow that the soul is divided within each individual body.
A soul the size of a human body would not be capable of entering the entire body of an elephant.
Furthermore, when [the soul] abandons the body of an elephant or similar creature and enters the body of an ant, the destruction of the previous bodily configuration would necessarily follow.

Nor should it be maintained that the soul, like a particular light of a lamp, undergoes contraction and expansion within the interior of wells, palaces, and so forth, as it does in the bodies of humans, elephants, and the like.

If [the self] were subject to change like a lamp, it would follow that it is impermanent; this, in turn, would entail the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
Thus, following the maxim of "overthrowing the chief wrestler," one should infer refutations in other cases as well by way of the critique directed at the category of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Therefore, because it contradicts the eternal and faultless Śruti, this [doctrine] is not to be accepted.
This was stated by the venerable Vyāsa: "On account of the impossibility [of contradictory attributes] in one [substratum]" (Brahma-sūtra 2.2.31).
And Rāmānuja explained this very sūtra as being intended for the refutation of the Jaina doctrine.

For his established position is that there are three categories of reality, established through the distinctions of the conscious, the unconscious, and the Lord, and through the distinctions of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller.
As it has been said: "Hari is the triad of categories—Īśvara, Cit, and Acit.

Īśvara is declared to be Cit, while the individual soul (jīva) and the visible world are Acit. Others, however, maintain that Brahman alone—which is pure consciousness (cinmātra) and opposed to all distinctions—is the ultimate reality.

And that reality, although its very nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and free, is bound and liberated as the oneness with the individual soul (jīva), as understood through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in such passages as "That thou art" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).

They maintain that the entire manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of various enjoyers, objects of enjoyment, and so forth, which exceeds that [Brahman], is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) within it, on the authority of a collection of scriptural passages such as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1). Thus, by virtue of hundreds of statements from the crest-jewels of the Vedas, such as, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.3), they accept the cessation of beginningless ignorance through the knowledge of the non-dual identity of the self and the attributeless Brahman.

"Death after death he attains who perceives here as if there were multiplicity" (Katha Upanishad 2.1). Hearing this censure of difference, those who consider themselves wise reject this distinction, asserting that ultimate difference is non-existent. To this, the following resolution is stated: This would indeed be so if there were any valid means of knowledge for ignorance.

Is it not the case that this ignorance—which is beginningless, positive in nature, and removable by knowledge—is established by the means of direct perception through such experiences as "I am ignorant" and "I do not know myself or another"?
As it has been said: "The wise declare that to be ignorance which is beginningless, positive in nature, and dissolved by knowledge; such is its definition."
(Citsukhī 1.9).
Nor should it be suspected that this [statement] has as its object the absence of knowledge;
for who would say such a thing—one who leans on the hand of Prabhākara, or one who is supported by the hand of Bhaṭṭa?

Not the first [alternative]: in an entity that is eternally of the nature of both existence and non-existence by virtue of its own form and the form of others, some aspect is known by someone at some time;
for non-existence is indeed just another state of being (bhāva) from a particular perspective.
"Non-existence is not something other than a different state of existence, because it cannot be defined as such. Since one who says this does not admit a non-existence distinct from existence,
the second [alternative] is not tenable.

Since non-existence is the object of the sixth means of knowledge (non-apprehension) and cognition is always inferable, it is impossible for its absence to be an object of perception. However, if some proponent of the theory that perception apprehends absence were to speak thus, one should refute him as follows: "In the experience 'I am ignorant,' is there or is there not an awareness of the self as the locus of the absence and of cognition as its counter-positive?"

If [the opponent argues] that there is indeed no experience of the absence of knowledge precisely because of contradiction, then if the experience of the absence of knowledge were dependent upon the knowledge of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it would be even more impossible. Since that ignorance is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*), and because the aforementioned defects do not apply, this experience must be admitted as having for its object only positive ignorance.
This is like chewing the cud upon the sky;
for positive ignorance (bhāvarūpājñāna) shares the same fate as the mere absence of knowledge (jñānābhāva).
To explain: is the inner self (pratyagartha) apprehended as the differentiator of ignorance by way of being its object or its locus, or not?
If that ignorance is something to be removed by the knowledge of its own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*), then once that [nature] is realized, how could that ignorance remain?
If, on the other hand, it is not realized, how can ignorance—which lacks a defining characteristic, a locus, and an object—be experienced?

Now, if you argue that it is the clear manifestation of the nature itself that is opposed to ignorance, and that it does not manifest simultaneously with ignorance; therefore, even when there is knowledge of the locus and the object, there is no contradiction in the experience of ignorance—alas, then this would apply equally even in the absence of knowledge, were it not for your dogmatic attachment [to the contrary].
Therefore, one must admit that the very absence of knowledge accepted by both parties—namely, "I am ignorant" and "I do not know another"—is the object of experience.

Let it be, then, that inference is the means of knowledge: "The knowledge in question, which is the subject of dispute, is preceded by another entity located in its own locus, which is distinct from its own prior non-existence, which veils its own object, and which is removed by itself; because it illuminates an object already present [but unmanifest], like the light of a lamp first produced in the dark.
That too cannot withstand scrutiny.
For even in the case of ignorance, [the reason] would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets by proving another form of ignorance that is not intended;
because if it does not prove that [intended ignorance], it is inconclusive;
and because the illustrative example is devoid of the probans.
For it is not possible for the light of a lamp to illuminate objects that have not been illuminated,
because illumination belongs exclusively to cognition;
even when a lamp is present, the illumination of an object occurs only through cognition.

As for the light of a lamp, its assistance to the visual faculty in producing cognition consists merely in its being an auxiliary by way of dispelling the opposing darkness; enough of this excessive detail. Furthermore, the counter-argument is as follows: the ignorance under dispute does not reside in Brahman, which is mere consciousness, because it is ignorance, like the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and similar objects.
If it is argued that the inner self, which is the substratum of the ignorance regarding mother-of-pearl and so forth, is indeed of the nature of mere consciousness, do not entertain such a doubt.

Experience (*anubhūti*)—which has other names such as cognition (*jñāna*), apprehension (*avagati*), and consciousness (*saṃvit*)—is by its very existence a specific attribute of the experiencing self (*ātman*), which is transitive (i.e., directed toward an object) and whose nature is to bring about the suitability for linguistic usage (*vyavahārānuguṇatva*) of some entity.
This is because one accepts that the selfhood of the experiencer consists in being the substratum (*āśraya*) of the specific quality of knowledge (*jñānatva*) residing within the self.

If it is asked, "How can the self, whose very form is knowledge, possess knowledge as its quality?", that is groundless. For just as a luminous substance such as a gem or the sun, while existing in the form of light, is the substratum of the quality consisting of the form of that light.

Just as light, although it is a substance by virtue of existing elsewhere than its own substrate and possessing color, is designated as a "quality" based on its dependence upon that [substance], so too this Self, though its very nature is self-luminous consciousness, possesses consciousness as its quality. And thus says the Śruti: "As a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a single mass of cognition..."
"In this state, this person becomes his own light" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9).

"For there is no loss of consciousness for the knower" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30). "Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.4). "This person, consisting of consciousness among the vital breaths, is the light within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7).

For there are such scriptural passages as: "This indeed is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the agent, the person consisting of consciousness" (Praśna 4.9).
Nor can it be maintained that the Śruti passage, "They are indeed veiled by untruth" (Chāndogya 8.3.2), serves as proof for the existence of avidyā;
for the word *anṛta* refers to that which is other than *ṛta* (truth).
The word *ṛta* denotes action (*karman*), as seen in the statement,
"the two who drink the *ṛta*" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 3.1).
*Ṛta* refers to that [action], while *anṛta* is action other than that— namely, worldly action yielding meager fruits— which is opposed to the attainment of Brahman.
This is because of the scriptural statement: "Those who do not find this world of Brahman are indeed obstructed by untruth" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.3.2).

Furthermore, in passages such as "One should know Māyā to be Prakṛti" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.10), the word *māyā* denotes the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), which produces a manifold creation; it does not denote an indefinable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*).
Therefore, [it is said]: "With his swift-moving [arrows], he destroyed that thousandfold *māyā* of Śambara."
While protecting the body of a fool, it has been destroyed by a single part [of that very body].

In passages such as these (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 1.19–20), we observe that the term *māyā* denotes specifically the supreme power (*pāramārthika-śakti*) of Śiva, which is capable of creating a manifold universe and is distinct from the weapons of the Asuras and others.
Therefore, the Śruti never propounds an indefinable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*),
nor does it do so through the necessity of otherwise explaining the teaching of non-duality (*aikyopadeśa*).

Because the two words *tat* and *tvam* denote Brahman with attributes, the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), which are thus contradictory, cannot be apprehended; consequently, the fallacy of the non-arising of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) vitiates [the Advaitin position]. To explain: the word *tat* denotes Brahman, who is free from all defects, the locus of infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities, and whose sport consists in the creation, sustenance, and dissolution of the universe.
This is because He alone is the subject under discussion in such passages as, "He thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate'" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).

The word *tvam*, being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with that [word *tat*], denotes Brahman as having the individual soul (*jīva*)—which is itself qualified by non-conscious matter—as its body;
for grammatical apposition has as its purport a single reality qualified by two modes.

Now, one might object: why could the meaning of the apposition not be the oneness of the self as a featureless essence, through the abandonment of contradictory parts (*bhāga-tyāga-lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of the expression "This is that Devadatta"?
Just as in the expression "this is that" (*yathā so 'yam*), by the word "that" (*tat*) a person connected with another place and another time is perceived,
and by the word "this" (*idam*) one connected with the present time and the proximate place;
through their grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), their identity is understood.

In that case, since the simultaneous cognition of contradictory space and time for a single entity is impossible, it is possible to apprehend the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) when both words refer to that very nature.

If you argue that here too, by discarding the contradictory elements such as partial knowledge and omniscience, the undivided essential nature is indicated through *lakṣaṇā* (indication)—this is an unequal comparison. For even in the example cited, there is no possibility of even a trace of *lakṣaṇā*, because of the absence of contradiction.
First of all, the connection of a single [entity] with two times—the past and the present—is not contradictory.

Furthermore, the contradiction regarding the connection with different locations—namely, that its residence in another location was past while its residence in a proximate location is present—is to be resolved by means of the difference in time. Moreover, even when resorting to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), since the contradiction can be resolved by relying on the figurative sense of only one word, it is not appropriate to accept that both words possess a figurative meaning.

Otherwise, if one does not accept the validity of recognition—which apprehends a single object as being qualified by both "that-ness" and "this-ness"—then permanence would remain unestablished, and the Buddhist proponent of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*) would triumph.
Thus, it has been demonstrated here as well that the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) through the relationship of body and self is not contradictory;
for the individual soul, being a mode (*prakāra*) of Brahman by virtue of being its body, is essentially identical with Brahman.

"Abiding within the self, yet distinct from the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self"—from this other scriptural passage [Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22]. To say that this is the case is to state too little;
for all words are denotative of the Supreme Self alone.
Nor is there synonymy [between the terms], because a difference in modality is possible.

For just as the various forms such as gods and humans— which constitute the modes of the individual soul (jīva) by way of being its bodies— all things are identical with Brahman, as they are of the nature of Brahman.

Therefore— whether it be a god, a human, a yakṣa, a piśāca, a serpent, or a rākṣasa; a bird, a tree, a creeper, wood, stone, grass, a jar, or a cloth— all such words, well-known in the world as denoters through the combination of roots and suffixes, are expressive of the entire complex beginning from the object perceived with its respective form, up to the individual soul (jīva) identifying with it, and finally the Supreme Self (paramātman) dwelling within it.

The fact that words such as "deva" (god) and others ultimately refer to the Supreme Self is stated in the fourth chapter of the *Tattvamuktāvalī*: "The word 'deva' and others denote the individual soul (*jīva*) because they express an entity that is not established separately from it; this is due to the absence of any extraction [of the soul from the body], and there is abundant and firm usage of these terms here in both worldly and Vedic practice.

At a time when the Self is not associated [with a body], the existence of forms such as gods or mortals is not perceived; yet, through the entry of the individual soul, the All-pervading Lord manifested names and forms in the world."
(Tattvamuktākalāpa 4.82).

By this [verse], having established that words such as "deity" (deva) and so forth extend up to the individual soul (jīva) as qualified by a body, and having shown the definition of a body through the verse beginning with (Tattvamuktākalāpa 4.83)—stating that it lacks uniformity of configuration and so on—and having demonstrated that the universe is not established as separate from the Lord through the verse beginning with (Tattvamuktākalāpa 4.84)—using terms such as "body," "limb," and "form"—the fact that all words ultimately refer to the Supreme Self is established by the verse beginning with (Tattvamuktākalāpa 4.85), which expresses the underlying intent of the final conclusion (*niṣkarṣākūta*). All of this is to be understood from that very [text].
This very point was established by Rāmānuja in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha* at the occasion of explaining the scriptural passages concerning name and form (*nāmarūpa*).

Furthermore, since every means of valid cognition has for its object that which possesses attributes (*saviśeṣa*), there exists no means of valid cognition whatsoever regarding a reality devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*).
Even in indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*), only an entity possessing attributes is apprehended.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for there to be a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) in the form "this is that," which involves the apprehension of an object as qualified by a mode previously established.
Furthermore, a sentence such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) cannot be a sublater of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*),
because it is rooted in error, like a statement regarding a rope-snake prompted by delusion.

Nor is the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self the sublater [of the world], since the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that has already been established. Furthermore,
in the view that establishes the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), there is no contradiction of the promise that "by the knowledge of one, all is known."

Since the entire effect—consisting of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the individual self (*puruṣa*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the gross elements (*bhūta*), the sense organs (*indriya*), the fourteen worlds (*bhuvana*), and all the various forms of existence within that cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) such as gods, animals, humans, and stationary beings—is indeed Brahman alone, the knowledge of everything arises simply from the knowledge of Brahman, which is the cause; thus, the claim that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" is most appropriately established.
Furthermore, if everything other than Brahman were false, then because everything would be non-existent, the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known" would be contradicted.

Brahman, whose body consists of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the individual soul (*puruṣa*) in a subtle state that is not yet fit for the differentiation of name and form, is in the causal condition.
Dissolution (*pralaya*) is simply the attainment of that [causal] state by the world.
Brahman, whose body consists of the gross conscious and unconscious entities differentiated by the distinction of name and form, is in the effected condition.

And such a gross state of Brahman is designated as "creation" (sṛṣṭi). In this way, the non-difference between cause and effect, which was established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa*, becomes even more convincingly demonstrated. Furthermore, the doctrines concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇavāda*) are to be understood as having the purpose of negating those qualities that are un-natural and subject to rejection.

The doctrines refuting plurality are established by accepting that they aim to negate the existence of any entity separate from Brahman—which is the Self of all—on the grounds that everything consisting of sentient and insentient things is a mode (*prakāra*) of the one Brahman alone as its body, and thus Brahman alone exists in every form as the Self of all.
What is the reality here: difference, non-difference, or both?
All of these are the reality.
In this regard, non-difference (*abheda*) is accepted on the grounds that Brahman alone exists in every way as the entire body.

Difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*) consists in the fact that the one and only Brahman exists in a manifold manner through its various modes of sentient (*cit*) and insentient (*acit*) matter.
Furthermore, difference arises from the distinctness of the essential nature and characteristics of the sentient, the insentient, and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as their lack of confusion.

In this regard, the essential natures of the conscious selves (*jīvātman*), who are of the nature of consciousness and consist of uncontracted, unlimited, and pure knowledge, but are enveloped by beginningless ignorance in the form of karma, include: the contraction and expansion of knowledge according to various karmas; association with non-conscious objects that serve as objects of experience; the state of being an enjoyer consisting of the dual experience of pleasure and pain corresponding to that [association]; the realization of the Lord; the attainment of the state of the Lord; and so forth. As for non-conscious entities, which serve as objects of experience, their essential natures include: insentience, the state of not being the human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*), being the locus of modification, and so forth.

The Supreme Lord’s abiding as the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of both the enjoyer and the enjoyed; His possession of a multitude of countless, incomparably excellent, and auspicious qualities such as immeasurable knowledge, sovereignty, valor, power, and splendor; His being the source of the entire collection of all sentient and non-sentient entities other than Himself, which proceed according to His own volition; and His possessing a single, uniform, divine form that accords with His will, adorned with various, unsurpassed, and infinite ornaments—these and others [are His attributes].

Veṅkaṭanātha has thus established the classification of categories: "The knowers of reality declare that the principles (tattva) are measured as twofold, divided into substance (dravya) and non-substance (adravya). Substance is divided into two: the first is the insentient (jaḍa), consisting of the unmanifest (avyakta) and time (kāla); the latter [the sentient] is both internal (pratyak) and external (parāk). Of these, the former is twofold due to the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa); the latter is eternal manifestation (bhūti) and cognition (mati). Here, some say that the first of these [the insentient] is itself non-eternal."

(Tattvamukta-kalāpa 1.6) Therein, substance (*dravya*) is of ten kinds; here, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is endowed with the qualities beginning with *sattva*; time (*kāla*) has the form of years and so forth; the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic and possesses cognition; the Lord (*īśvara*) is another self (*ātman*). Eternal existence (*nityabhūti*) is declared to be distinct from the three qualities and likewise endowed with *sattva*. Furthermore, the manifestation of the object of knowledge to the knower is called the intellect (*mati*). Thus, the definition of substance has been stated in brief.
As stated in [Tattvamuktākalāpa 1.7] and other passages:
therein, the individual selves (*jīvātman*), which are denoted by the term *cit*, are distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and eternal.
And thus says the Śruti: "Two birds, inseparable companions... (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.6), and so forth.

For this very reason it has been stated: "The selves are manifold on account of their distinct dispositions" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 3.2.20). Their eternity is also well-known from the Śruti: "The wise one is neither born nor does he die; having come to be, he will not cease to be again.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, he is not slain when the body is slain."
(Kārikā 2.18).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
For this very reason it was said: "Because birth is not observed for one who is free from passion" (Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.25).

Its atomicity is also well-known from scripture: "The individual soul (jīva) should be known as a part of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold; yet it is capable of infinity."
Thus it is said: "The Person is the size of the tip of an awl" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 5.9), and "The subtle Self is to be known by the mind" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.9).

The visible, insentient, and inert world, denoted by the word *acit*, is threefold, distinguished as the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), the instruments of enjoyment (*bhogopakaraṇa*), and the locus of enjoyment (*bhogāyatana*).
The ontological cause and material substratum of that world is the entity known as Īśvara, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), who is designated by such terms as Vāsudeva.
This has also been stated: "Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, endowed with auspicious qualities;
he is the material cause of the worlds, the agent, and the controller of individual souls."

That very Vāsudeva—the Supreme Person, supremely compassionate and affectionate toward His devotees—in order to bestow fruits upon His worshippers according to their fitness, abides in five forms by His own divine play (*līlā*): as the *arcā*, the *vibhava*, the *vyūha*, the *sūkṣma*, and the *antaryāmin*.
Among these, the *arcā* refers to images and the like;
the *vibhava* refers to incarnations such as Rāma and others.
The manifestation (vyūha) is fourfold, known as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
The supreme Brahman, called Vāsudeva, is subtle and possesses the six complete attributes.
These attributes are freedom from sin and so forth.
"His evil has been destroyed; he is free from old age, death, sorrow, hunger, and thirst; his desires are true and his resolves are true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.3).
According to this Śruti, He is the Inner Ruler (Antaryāmī), the controller of all individual souls.
"He who, dwelling within the self, controls the self from within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad Mādhyaṃdina 3.7.22). According to this Śruti.

In this regard, when the accumulation of sins that obstruct the goals of human life has been destroyed through the worship of each preceding form, one gains the qualification for the worship of each subsequent form.
As it has been said: "Out of affection for His devotees, Vāsudeva bestows abundant fruit upon their various desires in accordance with their respective qualifications."
For that purpose, He indeed assumes His own five forms through His divine play.
An image and the like are the *arcā* (worshipable) form; the incarnations (*avatāras*), however, are the *vaibhava* (manifestation) forms.
These are Saṃkarṣaṇa, Vāsudeva, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
The array is to be known as fourfold: subtle, and complete with the six qualities.
That alone is declared to be the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva;
it is called the Inner Controller (Antaryāmī), residing within the individual soul (jīva) and impelling the jīva.

He who has been defined by the networks of Vedānta statements as "that which is in the self" becomes qualified [for higher knowledge] once his impurities have been cast off through the worship of the syllable *oṃ*.
After the worship of the manifest form, and thereafter the worship of the cosmic manifestation (vyūha),
one should subsequently become capable of perceiving the Inner Controller within the subtle.

And that worship is fivefold—approach (*abhigamana*), procurement (*upādāna*), sacrifice (*ijyā*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and yoga—as stated in the *Śrīpañcarātra*. Among these, "approach" refers to the sweeping, smearing with cow-dung, and other such acts regarding the path to the deity's abode. "Procurement" is the gathering of the materials for worship, such as fragrances, flowers, and so forth.
Sacrifice (*ijyā*) means the worship of the deities.

Self-study (*svādhyāya*) means the recitation of mantras preceded by reflection on their meaning, the chanting of Vaiṣṇava hymns and praises, the proclamation of the Lord’s names, and the study of scriptures that establish the ultimate reality. Yoga means the constant contemplation of the deity.

Thus, when the seer and the seeing have perished through the knowledge accumulated by the combination of meditation and ritual action, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)—who is affectionate toward His devotees and supremely compassionate—bestows upon the devotee who is fixed in Him His own station, which consists of infinite bliss corresponding to the experience of His true nature and from which there is no return. Accordingly, the Smṛti says: "Having come unto Me, the high-souled ones, having attained supreme perfection, do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering."
(Bhagavad Gītā 8.15): Thus, Vāsudeva also, having attained His own imperishable bliss,
bestows upon His devotee His own abode from which there is no return.
And thus it is said.

Keeping all this in mind and relying on the philosophical tradition of the Mahopaniṣad, Rāmānuja, having observed the extensive commentary (*vṛtti*) on the *Brahmasūtra* composed by the venerable teacher Bādarāyaṇa-Dhaumya, authored the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*.

Regarding that, the meaning of the first sūtra, "Then, therefore, the inquiry into Brahman" (*atha ato brahmajijñāsā*, BS 1.1.1), is as follows: here, the word *atha* signifies immediate succession to the prior study of ritual action (*karman*). As stated by the author of the *Vṛtti*: "After the study of ritual action has been completed, one desires to know Brahman."
The word "ataḥ" (therefore) signifies a reason.

Because one who has studied the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*sāṅga*) and understood their meaning becomes detached from ritual action—which yields perishable results—and consequently desires the stable liberation (*mokṣa*), there arises in him the desire to know Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), which is the means to that end.
By the word "Brahman," the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) is denoted, who by his very nature is free from all defects and possesses infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities.

Thus, since ritual action (*karma*) and its performance serve as means toward the knowledge of Brahman—by way of generating dispassion (*vairāgya*) and by way of removing the impurities of the mind—the two stand in a relationship of cause and effect; consequently, the Pūrva and Uttara Mīmāṃsās constitute a single scripture.
For this very reason, the authors of the *Vṛtti* have stated: "This is indeed one single scripture, together with the sixteen-chapter [work] of Jaimini."
