Having examined the perishability of the fruit of action and the imperishability of the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman, [the scripture] has established this through such Vedic texts as, "A Brahmin, having become disillusioned with the worlds acquired by karma, should turn away [from them], for there is nothing uncreated that can be obtained by means of the created" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 1.2.12), which are reinforced by inference and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). By censuring each [of the two paths] individually, the Śruti shows that it is knowledge qualified by action that is the means to liberation: "Into blinding darkness enter those who worship ignorance;
into a darkness even greater than that, as it were, enter those who delight in mere knowledge."
"Whoever knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality by means of knowledge. (Īśa Upaniṣad 11), and so forth.
Thus it is said in the *Pāñcarātrarahasya*: "That very Lord, the ocean of compassion who is affectionate toward his devotees, assumes five forms in accordance with the needs of his worshippers."
That which is designated as the manifestation of its light (arcā-vibhava), the cosmic array (vyūha), the subtle (sūkṣma), and the inner controller (antaryāmin)—
it is by depending solely upon this that the group of conscious beings attains each respective object of knowledge.
One whose impurities have been worn away by the specific meditations mentioned previously becomes qualified for the meditation upon each successive form.
Thus, day after day, in accordance with the duties prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, [one should proceed].
Through the aforementioned worship, Vāsudeva becomes gracious toward men;
Hari, with his self pleased by devotion in the form of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation),
immediately removes ignorance in the form of the accumulation of karma.

Then, those auspicious qualities of men, such as omniscience and the rest, which are innate but obscured by saṃsāra, become manifest. In this way, the qualities of the liberated souls and those of the Lord would be identical.
Among them, O God, the sole quality of being the creator of all is what distinguishes you.
"But those who are liberated, while remaining as subordinate parts within the Supreme Brahman—their ultimate Remainder—attain all desires together with that All-knowing One. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, it is stated that those afflicted by the threefold suffering must desire to know Brahman—which is to be known through such terms as "Puruṣottama" (the Supreme Person)—for the sake of immortality.

According to the rule that "the base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix primarily," and because the sense of desire (*icchā*) is subordinate to the object desired (*iṣyamāṇa*), it is knowledge (*jñāna*)—the object desired—that is the thing to be enjoined here.
Furthermore, this is that realization denoted by terms such as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and "worship" (*upāsana*), and not a superficial cognition produced merely by a sentence.
For one who hears the composition of words and possesses the necessary proficiency, [the knowledge] is already attained even without an injunction, as evidenced by such scriptural passages as:

"The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5); "One should meditate [on the Self] as the Self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7); "Having known [It], let him practice wisdom" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21); and "Having understood [It] through hearing, he realizes [It]" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.1).
In this context, the term "is to be heard" (*śrotavya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Since the study of the Veda together with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga-svādhyāya*) is undertaken through the injunction for formal study (*adhyayanavidhi*), and since a person who has thus studied the Veda naturally engages in hearing (*śravaṇa*) for the purpose of determining its meaning upon perceiving that it possesses a purposeful goal, such hearing is already established [as a duty].
Furthermore, the term "it should be reflected upon" (*mantavya*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*),
because reflection is also already established as being for the sake of stabilizing what was heard.
This is because of the logical principle that "the scripture is purposeful when [its goal] has not yet been attained.
Furthermore, meditation (*dhyāna*) consists of an uninterrupted stream of mindfulness (*smṛti*), like a continuous flow of oil.
This is because it is heard in scripture that steadfast mindfulness alone is the means to liberation: "When there is the attainment of steadfast mindfulness, there is the loosening of all knots."
And that memory has a form identical to direct perception.
"The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut away,
and his karmas are exhausted when That, which is both the high and the low, is seen."
This is because it forms a single syntactical unit with the statement [Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8].
Likewise, by the passage "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5), its nature as a form of seeing is enjoined.
And through the intensity of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), memory attains the nature of direct perception.
The author of the *Vākya* has explained all this in detail through such passages as, "Knowledge (*vedana*) would be worship (*upāsana*)," and so forth.
The Śruti itself qualifies that very meditation (*dhyāna*): "This Self is not to be attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing;
only he whom this [Self] chooses, by him is it attained. To him alone does the Self reveal its own form."
(Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.23).
For it is only the most beloved who is worthy of being chosen.
Thus, the Blessed One Himself has declared that He Himself strives so that this most beloved may attain the Self: "For those who are ever steadfast and worship Me with love... (Bhagavad Gītā 10.10).
I bestow upon them that yoga of discernment by which they come unto Me.
(Bhagavad Gītā 10.10);
and also: "That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable by unswerving devotion" (Bhagavad Gītā 8.22).
Devotion (*bhakti*), however, is indeed a particular state of knowledge characterized by supreme bliss, love, having no other purpose, and freedom from desire for everything else.

And its attainment occurs through discernment (*viveka*) and other means, as stated by the author of the *Vākya* (Bodhāyana): "Its attainment arises from discernment, detachment, practice, action, auspiciousness, lack of despondency, and lack of exultation, because of their occurrence and their etymological definitions.
Among these, "discernment" (*viveka*) refers to the purification of the *sattva* [of the mind] resulting from food that is not [unwholesome].
The etymological explanation here is as follows: "From purity of food comes purity of the mind; from purity of the mind, steady mindfulness.
Liberation is freedom from attachment to desires.
"One should meditate in a state of tranquility"—this is the etymological explanation.
Practice (*abhyāsa*) is repeated cultivation.
And the etymological definition has been cited by the Commentator from the *Smṛti*: "Always permeated by the contemplation of That" (*Gītā* 8.6).
Performance of action consists of the practice of *śruti*-based and *smṛti*-based duties according to one's capacity.
"He is an active practitioner, the most excellent among the knowers of Brahman"—this is the etymological definition.
Truthfulness, uprightness, compassion, charity, and other such virtues are auspicious qualities.
"It is attained through truth," and so forth—this is the etymological definition.
The opposite of dejection is non-depression;
its scriptural definition is: "This Self is not to be attained by one who is devoid of strength" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.4).
Arrogance is the satisfaction born from the opposite of that [non-depression].
The opposite of that is the absence of elation;
this is the etymological definition of one who is "peaceful" (śānta) and "self-controlled" (dānta).

Thus, it is established that the state of the Supreme Person (puruṣottama-pada) is attained through devotion (bhakti)—which consists of meditation characterized by the manifestation of a clear cognition of the Self as an incessant and unsurpassed object of love, free from other purposes—wherein the darkness of the heart has been destroyed by the grace of the Supreme Person obtained through such specific disciplines.
This was stated by Yāmuna: "The yoga of exclusive and ultimate devotion is attainable by one whose mind has been refined by both [paths].
This means: by one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified through the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action.

Furthermore, in response to the inquiry as to what Brahman is that ought to be investigated, the definition is stated: "From which the origin and so forth of this [world proceed]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2).
"Janmādi" means creation, maintenance, and dissolution. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the inclusion of its own attributes (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*).

The meaning of the Sūtra is this: from whom—from that Supreme Lord, whose nature is opposed to all that is to be discarded, who possesses true resolve and other infinite, unsurpassed, and innumerable auspicious qualities, who is omniscient and omnipotent—proceed the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of this world, which has an inconceivable and manifoldly diverse structure, which is interspersed with individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) ranging from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, and which is subject to experiences determined by specific place and time.

When the inquiry arises as to what is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman as it thus exists, it is stated [in the Brahma Sūtras] that scripture alone is the means of valid knowledge, in the sūtra: "Because [Brahman] has scripture as its source" (1.1.3).
That which has scripture as its *yoni*—meaning its cause or its means of valid knowledge—is "śāstrayoni. The state of being such is "śāstrayonitva"; [the sūtra says] "because of that."
The meaning is that because the scripture is the cause of the knowledge of Brahman, Brahman has that [scripture] as its source (*yoni*).
Nor can it be suspected that Brahman is cognizable through other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
since perception cannot operate there due to its being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
Nor is there the inference that "the great ocean and so forth have a creator because they are effects, like a pot," for such an argument is like a rotten pumpkin [useless and fallacious].
It is established, therefore, that the scripture beginning with "From which indeed these beings... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1.1) propounds Brahman as characterized by those [qualities].

Although Brahman does not fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, in the absence of a focus on activity (*pravṛtti*) or cessation from activity (*nivṛtti*), the scripture would not be capable of establishing Brahman as an already established entity (*siddharūpa*). To resolve this objection, it is stated: "But that [is established] because of the harmony [of the texts]" (*brahmasūtra* 1.1.4). The word "but" (*tu*) serves to set aside the doubt that has arisen. Thus, it is indeed possible for Brahman to have the scripture as its means of valid cognition.

"Because of the connection with that [Brahman]" means because Brahman, which is indeed the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), is connected as the subject matter (*abhidheya*). Nor is there a lack of purpose for that which is devoid of either engagement (*pravṛtti*) or withdrawal (*nivṛtti*);

for even in cases where the words refer to the thing-in-itself (*svarūpa-parāḥ*), such as "A son is born to you" or "This is not a snake," we observe that they possess purposes consisting of the attainment of joy or the cessation of fear. Thus, nothing is untenable.
Only a mere indication has been shown here; however, the details should be understood from the original sources themselves. Fearing prolixity, I shall desist, so all is clear.
Now begins the exposition of Pūrṇaprajña. ||5||

Disregarding this system of Rāmānuja—despite its similarities with his own views regarding the atomicity of the individual soul (*jīva*), its servitude (*dāsya*), the non-human authorship of the Vedas, the capacity of established facts to convey meaning, the self-validity of knowledge (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), the triad of means of valid cognition, the reliance upon the *Pañcarātra*, and the reality of the difference within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—Madhva (Ānandatīrtha), accepting three mutually contradictory positions such as absolute difference (*bheda*), composed a different system under the guise of a commentary on the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, establishing that the collection of Vedānta passages beginning with "That [is] the Self, Thou art That" (*tat tvam asi*) has a different intended meaning through a different method of interpretation.
For in that system, reality is indeed twofold, distinguished as independent (*svatantra*) and dependent (*paratantra*).
As it is stated in the *Tattvaviveka*: "Reality is held to be twofold: independent and dependent.
The independent is the Lord Viṣṇu, who is faultless and possesses all excellent qualities."

If it is objected: "Since the Vedāntas—which establish that Brahman is the reality devoid of internal, external, and homogeneous diversity—are awake and active, how can it be said that [Brahman] possesses all auspicious qualities? Do not say so.
For those [Vedāntic texts] cannot be authoritative in that regard, as they contradict many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish difference.
To explain: perception (*pratyakṣa*), for its part, directly perceives the difference between blue, yellow, and so forth, in the form "this is different from that."

Now, you might think: does perception apprehend difference alone, or as constituted by the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)? It cannot be the first, because difference—which is dependent upon them—cannot be determined without the cognition of the locus and the counter-correlate.

As for the second, is the apprehension of difference preceded by the apprehension of the locus and the counter-correlate, or is there a simultaneous apprehension of all these? It cannot be the former, because the intellect does not function by pausing [between operations], and because it would lead to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because of the absence of simultaneity between the cognitions of the effect and the cause;
for the cognition of the substratum (dharmin) is the cause of the cognition of difference,
and likewise, the cognition of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is as well.

If it is argued that, even when the locus (*dharmin*) is present, difference (*bheda*) remains unknown in the absence of the cognition of the remote counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and that therefore—through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—the causal relation between them is understood, and consequently the perception of difference does not easily prevail;

[we reply: are these objections being voiced against the proponent of difference as the very nature of the thing (*vastu-svarūpa-bheda-vādin*), or against the proponent of difference as a distinct attribute (*dharma-bheda-vādin*)? In the first case, there is the fallacy of punishing Māṇḍavya for the crime of a thief.
Because the objections being asserted by you do not have that [entity] as their object.

Now, it might be argued that if difference were the very nature of the thing itself, its dependence upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) would be untenable, just like the jar [which does not depend on another jar for its existence].
If it is replied that "difference is everywhere perceived as dependent upon a counter-correlate," we say no.

First, when the nature of an object is known through its distinction from everything else, the application of specific designations becomes possible in relation to its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
For instance, the nature of an object constituted by dimension is first apprehended;
subsequently, in relation to a specific counter-correlative, that very same object becomes the locus of specific usage as "short" or "long."
This has been stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya*: "Nor is difference established through the relation of qualifier and qualified;
for the relation of qualifier and qualified presupposes difference.
Difference is established only in dependence upon a substratum (*dharmin*) and a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)."
Furthermore, since the state of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) depends upon difference, difference is untenable due to mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*),
as stated in the passage beginning with "because difference is the very nature of the category (*padārtha*).
For this very reason, those seeking a cow do not act upon seeing a *gavaya*, nor do they recall the word "cow."
Nor should it be said that when the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of milk, water, and so forth is being apprehended, there would also be a manifestation of difference (*bhedapratibhāsa*).
For the non-occurrence of the manifestation and linguistic usage of difference is established by the force of obstructions such as the proximity of similar substances (*samānābhihāra*).
As it has been said: "Due to extreme distance, due to extreme proximity, due to injury to the sense organs, and due to instability of the mind..."
Due to subtlety, obstruction, suppression, and intermixture with similar objects.

The meaning is that there is no correct apprehension [of an object] due to excessive distance—as in the case of a mountain peak or a distant mountain; due to excessive proximity—as in the case of collyrium applied to the eyes; due to the impairment of the sense organs—as in the case of lightning; due to the instability of the mind—as in the case of a jar situated in bright light for one whose mind is overwhelmed by passion and the like; due to subtlety—as in the case of atoms; due to obstruction—as in the case of something hidden behind a wall; due to being overpowered—as in the case of the light of a lamp during the day; and due to the blending of similar things—as in the case of water and milk.
Alternatively, even if one maintains the doctrine of the distinction between properties (*dharmabheda*), there is still no fault.
For when the substratum and the counter-correlative are apprehended, the subsequent apprehension of the difference constituted by them is logically possible.
Nor does this entail the fallacy of mutual dependence;
because once a thing possessing non-difference is apprehended independently of anything else, the manifestation of the difference between its attributes becomes possible.

Furthermore, it should not be maintained that in the theory of the differentiation of phenomena (*dharmabheda*), there would be an untenable infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because each particular difference would itself be differentiated by further differences; for if further differences were required, there would be no foundational basis (*mūlābhāva*). Moreover, we do not observe such linguistic usage as "the difference and the thing differentiated are distinct."
Nor can one particular instance be inferred from the strength of another particular instance;
for there is no fault in its arising provided it does not contradict the distinction of the corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
This is like someone who has gone to beg for a mere scrap of oil-cake being promised a *khārikā* measure of oil.
But when the distinction between the example and [the thesis] is refuted, there is simply no further arising;
for one does not marry off a daughter in order to destroy the bridegroom.
Therefore, since there is no destruction of the root, infinite regress is not a fault.
The difference is also determined by inference:
the Supreme Lord is distinct from the individual soul,
because He is the object of service for that soul.
Whoever is to be served by another is distinct from that other,
just as a king is distinct from his servant.

For men who seek the goals of human existence— thinking, "May there be happiness for me, and may there not be even the slightest suffering"— would not be recipients of honor if they merely desired the status of a master builder.
On the contrary, they become vessels for all misfortune.
He who speaks of his own inferiority and the excellence of another's virtues is worthy of praise; being pleased, he grants the desired object to that speaker.
Thus it is said: "Kings indeed put to death those who say, 'I am the king.'"
And they bestow every desired object upon those who speak of the excellence of their own virtues.

Thus, by asserting that the excellence of Viṣṇu’s qualities is like a mirage out of a longing for non-difference from the Supreme Lord, one emulates the cutting off of one's own tongue in the desire to obtain a large plantain fruit;
for such hatred toward Viṣṇu results in the consequence of entering into blinding darkness.
This very point was established by Madhyamandira in the *Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*: "The Daityas, who have been enemies from time immemorial, had their hatred for Viṣṇu further increased."
By his final resolve, he casts the Daityas into blind darkness at the end.
Thus [it is said in] the *Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya* (1.111).
And that service (*sevā*) is threefold, distinguished by branding (*aṅkana*), naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), and worship (*bhajana*).
Among these, branding consists of marking oneself with the weapons and other attributes of Nārāyaṇa, for the purpose of remembering His form and for the attainment of desired goals.

And so says the *Śākalyasaṃhitā-pariśiṣṭa*: "The man who bears the well-heated discus—the strength of the gods, of the immortal Viṣṇu—he goes to the celestial realm, shaking off his misdeeds, just as the passionless ascetics enter it. By that Sudarśana, held in the arm, the gods went forth to their destination."
Marked by which the Manus expand the creation of the world, and the Brahmins carry it forth.
"May we become fortunate in this world, marked by the signs of the wide-striding Viṣṇu, by which those who are branded go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

And also the Taittirīya Upaniṣad states: "One whose body has not been heated [by austerity] does not attain that, being raw; only those who have taken refuge and carry it [the fire] together partake of it. (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.11).

The specific placement [of the symbols] is also demonstrated in the Āgneya Purāṇa: "A Brahmin should wear the Sudarśana on his right hand and should wear the Śaṅkha with his left; thus the knowers of Brahman understand."

Elsewhere, regarding the wearing of the discus, a specific mantra is shown: "O Sudarśana, of great radiance, with a brilliance equal to ten million suns! Constantly show the path to me, who am blinded by ignorance, O Viṣṇu!"
O Pāñcajanya, you were born from the ocean and held in the hand by Viṣṇu;
you are saluted by all the gods—homage be to you!
Naming refers to the practice of addressing one's sons and others by names such as Keśava and so forth, for the purpose of constant remembrance of that name.

Devotion (*bhajana*) is tenfold: through speech—truthfulness, benefit, kindness, and sacred study; through the body—giving, protection, and preservation; and through the mind—compassion, longing, and faith.
In this context, devotion consists of accomplishing each of these individually and offering them to Nārāyaṇa.
As it has been said:
"Marking, naming, and worship—these constitute the tenfold [process].
In this way, the distinction [between the Lord and the individual soul] is also to be inferred through such qualities as being the object of knowledge."
Likewise, difference (*bheda*) is to be understood from scripture (*śruti*) as well:

"All rejoice after this Truth, receiving the gift of the generous Lord. "His greatness, His power, is praised as Truth at the sacrifices in the kingdom of the wise. "The Self is Truth, the individual soul (*jīva*) is Truth, difference is Truth, difference is Truth, difference is Truth; let it not be spoken against, let it not be spoken against, let it not be spoken against"—from such scriptural passages which establish the distinction between liberation and bliss. "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained My own nature."
Even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer.

This is also established by such [scriptural statements] as "excluding the activity of the world" (*jagadvyāpāravarjam*) and "because of the context and because of the lack of proximity" (*prakaraṇādasaṃnihitatvācca*) from the *Brahma-sūtras* (4.4.17–18).

Nor can the supreme sovereignty of the individual soul (*jīva*) be suspected on the strength of the Śruti text, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself" (*brahma veda brahmaiva bhavati*, Muṇḍaka 3.2.9);
for that passage has the sense of "he becomes expanded" (*vṛṃhito bhavati*), just like the statement, "Even a Śūdra may become a Brāhmaṇa by worshipping a Brāhmaṇa with devotion."
If indeed the manifold world (prapañca) existed, it would undoubtedly cease;
this duality is mere illusion (māyāmātra), for non-duality (advaita) is the ultimate reality (paramārtha).

If it is argued that the unreality of duality is understood from the statement in the *Māṇḍūkya-kārikā* (1.17), "It is true; however, this is stated without intending to affirm its positive existence.
For it is said: 'If this were to arise, it would undoubtedly cease.'"
Therefore, this fivefold expansion of differentiation is indeed beginningless and preeminent;
yet it is not non-existent,
because it is merely an illusion (*māyāmātra*).
"O Infinite One,
what is called 'māyā' is Your will; it is called Mahāmāyā, Avidyā, Niyati, Mohinī, Prakṛti, and Vāsanā."

It is called *prakṛti* because it performs the most excellent creation (*prakṛṣṭakaraṇāt*), and it is called *vāsanā* because it perfumes (*vāsayet*). By the word "A," Hari is denoted; by that which is named after Him, namely "Māyā" or "Vidyā."
She is called "Māyā" because she is preeminent; for the name "Māyā" is applied to that which is most excellent. Only the singular wisdom of Viṣṇu is expressed by these various words.
For Hari is of the nature of conceptual designation (prajñapti), and that [designation] has self-bliss as its characteristic;
by the force of the authority of such a collection of statements,
that very wisdom (prajñā) which acts as both the means of knowledge and protection— of whom that is merely illusion (māyāmātra).
Consequently, because it has been known and protected by the Supreme Lord, duality is not imagined through delusion;
for delusion is impossible in the case of the Lord,
since delusion is based upon the perception of specific distinctions.
To the question, "In that case, how is there a designation for it? the answer is: "Non-duality from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
By "from the perspective of ultimate reality," it is meant with reference to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus, it is stated that the reality of Viṣṇu, which is superior to everything, is devoid of any equal or superior.

And thus says the supreme Śruti: "The difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as the difference between the insentient (jaḍa) and the Lord; the mutual difference between individual souls, and likewise the difference between the insentient and the individual soul."

The mutual difference between the insentient, which is the phenomenal world consisting of the fivefold division, is both real and beginningless; for if it had a beginning, it would necessarily meet its destruction.
It does not undergo destruction, nor is it imagined through delusion;
for if it were imagined, it would cease, yet it does not cease.
"Duality does not exist"—this is the view of the ignorant;
for this is the measured and protected doctrine of the wise, established by Viṣṇu.
"Therefore, He alone is proclaimed as Mātra, for Hari is indeed supreme," and so forth.
Thus, the intended purport of all the Āgamas is precisely the pre-eminence of Viṣṇu.
With this very intention, it was said by the Blessed One: "There are these two persons in the world, the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are the perishable; the one who stands at the peak (the immutable) is called the imperishable."
But there is another, the Supreme Person, declared to be the Supreme Self;
the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable,
therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
He who, undeluded, thus knows me as the Supreme Person—
O Bhārata, that all-knowing one honors me with his whole being.
Thus has this most secret teaching been spoken by me, O sinless one;
having understood this, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done, O Bhārata.
Thus [it is said in Gītā 15.16–20].
Also in the Mahāvarāha Purāṇa: "The primary purport of all the Vedas is upon the Supreme Lord;
however, their purport toward anything other than Him would be merely secondary."
And it is fitting that there is a great purport regarding Viṣṇu’s supreme excellence;
for liberation is indeed the highest of all human goals. While dharma, artha, and kāma are all non-eternal, liberation alone is eternal.
"Therefore, a wise man should strive for that [liberation] which is eternal.
Thus says the Bhāllaveya Śruti.
Furthermore, liberation is not attained without the grace of Viṣṇu.
By whose grace one is liberated from this supreme form of saṃsāra and not by any other—
He is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme, who should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation from these bonds of karma.
Thus says the Nārāyaṇa-śruti:

"When He is pleased, what is there in this world that is unattainable? Enough with dharma, artha, and kāma, for they are but trivial things. From the infinite Tree of Brahman, those who have taken refuge in Him attain, without doubt, the fruit of right reasoning."
And as stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa (Vi.Pu.
1.17.61): "Grace [arises] only from the knowledge of the excellence of qualities, not from the knowledge of non-difference.
Nor is there any contradiction with such texts as "That thou art" regarding identity.
This is due to the manifestation of a failure to understand the intended meaning of the scripture.

For the word "that" (tat) refers to that which is eternally beyond perception, while the word "thou" (tvam) refers without distinction to that which is immediate; how then can there be identity between the two?
That scriptural statement is intended for the purpose of similarity, like the expression "the sacrificial post is the sun.

And thus says the supreme scripture: "The absolute identity of the individual soul (jīva) with the Supreme is merely a similarity of intellect, or it is a state of being situated in the same place, with respect to the location of manifestation."
Even for that which is joined, there is no identity of essential nature because of its dissimilarity;
independence and fullness, as well as limitation and dependence, constitute this dissimilarity.

Alternatively, in the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it is that very Self which possesses qualities such as sovereignty; whereas "Thou art not That" (*atatvamasi*) means that you do not exist as That because you are devoid of those qualities. Thus, identity is emphatically rejected. As it has been said: "Or rather, there is a word-break as *a-tattvam*; by this, oneness is thoroughly refuted."

Therefore, even in the nine illustrations, such as "Just as a bird is bound by a string" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.3), since only difference is expressed through these examples, this is not an instruction on non-difference; such is the secret of the Tattvavāda [the Doctrine of Reality].
And so says the Mahopaniṣad: "As the bird and the string, as the juices of various trees, as rivers and the ocean, and as the individual soul and the tree."
Just as the power of atomization (aṇimā) and a grain of rice [are distinct], just as pure water and salt [are distinct],
and just as a thief and his victim, so too are the soul and the objects of the senses.
Just as the multitude of individual souls is ignorant while the vital breath is the controller,
so too are the individual soul and the Lord distinct and always characterized by difference.
Nevertheless, because of His subtle nature, Hari, though He is the supreme impeller,
is not perceived as distinct from the individual soul by those of dull vision.
"Having understood the distinction between those two, one is liberated; otherwise, one is bound.
Brahmā, Śiva, and the gods and others are perishable because their bodies are subject to decay;
Lakṣmī is imperishable because her body is imperishable; and Hari is beyond even her.
By virtue of all their qualities— such as the power of absolute sovereignty, consciousness, bliss, and so forth—
they are all, by being limitless, eternally under His control.
Having known Viṣṇu, who is complete with all auspicious qualities, one becomes free from the cycle of worldly existence;
eternally enjoying sorrowless bliss, he rejoices in His presence.
Viṣṇu is the support of the liberated ones, as well as their superior overlord;
they are all entirely under his control, for he is forever the Lord.
And thus:
the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is consistent with [the latter being] the primary cause and so forth, but not with the falsity of all things;
for a false cognition cannot arise from a true cognition.
Just as the designation "the village is known" or "the village is unknown" is observed based on the knowledge or ignorance of its principal inhabitants;
and just as when the father, who is the cause, is known, one knows his son;
or just as through similarity, from the knowledge of one woman, there arises the knowledge of another woman.

In this case as well, it is that very similarity which is intended to be expressed, as shown by the passage beginning, "Just as, my dear, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay would be known" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4). Otherwise, the words "one" (*eka*) and "lump" (*piṇḍa*) in the phrase "by means of one lump of clay, my dear, all that is made of clay is known" would be rendered redundant; for the sentence would be complete simply by saying "by means of clay being known."
Nor should it be accepted that the passage, "The modification is a verbal handle, a mere name; 'clay' alone is true" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.5), teaches the falsity of the effect.
This is because the meaning accepted here is that the name—such as "clay" and so forth—which belongs to that unmodified, eternal entity whose modifications are merely verbal handles, is what is true.
Otherwise, the redundancy of the words "name" and "mere" would result.
Therefore, the falsity of the world is not established anywhere.

Furthermore, regarding the claim that "the phenomenal world (prapañca) is false," is this falsity itself real or unreal? In the first case, there is the consequence of the collapse of true non-duality (advaita). In the latter case, it follows that the phenomenal world is real.
"Is impermanence itself permanent or impermanent?
In either case, there is an inconsistency"—this too would be a variety of the *nityasama* (balancing the permanent) fallacy, like the objection [just mentioned].

As it was stated by the Creator of Nyāya: "The *nityasama* occurs because, since impermanence exists as something impermanent, permanence is established for the impermanent thing" (*Nyāyasūtra* 5.1.35).

And in the *Tārkikarakṣā*: "Because the conceptualization of the property (*dharma*) and its various forms is untenable, the destruction of the substratum’s (*dharmī*) being qualified by it would constitute the *nityasama* [fallacy].

Intending that this name is merely indicative (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is stated in the *Prabodhasiddhi* that it is called *uparañjakadharmasama* because the name is etymologically significant (*anvarthitva*).
If it is argued that, therefore, this is an incorrect response—this is merely the intimidation of one who is untrained, because the root of its fallacy has not been identified.
That [fallacy] is of two kinds: common and uncommon.
Among these, the first is self-contradictory (*svavyāghātaka*).

The second is threefold: deficiency of necessary members (*yuktāṅgahīnatva*), superfluity of unnecessary members (*ayuktāṅgādhikatva*), and occurrence outside the proper scope (*aviṣayavṛttitva*). Of these, the common [defect] is simply impossible.
Because the objection raised does not apply to itself;
likewise, it is also non-common (*asādhāraṇa*).
For when the non-existence of a jar is stated, its existence is implied; this is applicable to the present case as well.

If it is argued that the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is accepted, but not its non-existence (*asattva*), this would merely imitate the story of the cart-driver who, even when his head was about to be cut off, refused to give up a hundred [coins] but readily gave twenty-five.
This is because "falsity" and "non-existence" are synonyms; enough of this prolixity.
In this regard, the meaning of the first aphorism, "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*atha ato brahma-jijñāsā*, *Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.1), is as follows:
In this context, the word *atha* is accepted as having the sense of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and the sense of immediate succession to a topic (*adhikārānantarya*).
The word *ataḥ* has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).
As it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*: "All sūtras whatsoever are preceded by the words *atha* and *ataḥ*."
They are commenced by destiny alone; what, then, is the regulating factor in this matter?
O learned one, what is the purpose of those two, and how is their superiority established?
Tell me this, O Brahmin, so that I may understand it according to the truth.
Thus addressed by Nārada, the most excellent Brahmā spoke concerning the section on immediate succession (ānantarya) and likewise for the sake of auspiciousness.
The word "atha" (then/now), however, and the word "ataḥ" (hence) are declared to have the sense of a reason (*hetvartha*).
Since liberation is not obtained without the grace of Nārāyaṇa, and grace [is not obtained] without knowledge, it is established that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken.
The definition of Brahman, the object of this inquiry, has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "That from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]" (Brahmasūtra 1.1.2).
The meaning of the statement is that Brahman is that from which creation, maintenance, and so forth, arise.

And thus says a passage from the Skanda Purāṇa: "Since birth, maintenance, destruction, destiny, knowledge, concealment, bondage, and liberation proceed from the Person, He is Hari, the sole sovereign."
This is also established by such scriptural passages as "From which these [beings arise]," and so forth.
Regarding this, the means of valid cognition has also been stated in the Brahma Sūtra: "Because He has the scripture as His source" (1.1.3).

Through such scriptural texts as "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.12.9.7) and "Him, however, one knows through the Upaniṣads" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.26), His being inferable is refuted.
Furthermore, inference does not possess independent authority.
As it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Inference devoid of the assistance of Śruti can never establish an object with certainty, nor can it function as an independent means of valid knowledge."
That other supreme means of valid knowledge which is assisted by Śruti and Smṛti shall attain the status of a valid authority; no deliberation is required on this point.
The nature of the scriptures is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, the Mahābhārata, the Pāñcarātra, and the Mūla-Rāmāyaṇa are designated as the scriptures."
"And that which is conducive to this [realization] is proclaimed as the scripture;
any other expansion of texts is not scripture at all, for it is a wrong path.

By this, the hope of the Advaitins—that according to the maxim "the meaning of a scripture is that which cannot be obtained otherwise," since difference is already established by other means, the Vedas do not intend to teach difference but rather have their purport solely in non-duality—is refuted.
Since there is no establishment of God through inference and other means, His distinctions likewise cannot be established by them.
Therefore, [the scripture] does not merely restate distinctions; rather, it is understood to have Him as its primary subject.
For this very reason it has been said: "He who is to be known solely through the authentic scriptures, and who transcends both the perishable and the imperishable."
I ever revere Nārāyaṇa, who is free from all defects and possesses every perfect virtue.

Thus [it is said]. The authority of the scripture (*śāstra*) in that regard has been established by the sūtra: "But that [Brahman is known] from the harmony [of the texts]" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.4). "Harmony" (*samanvaya*) refers to the evidence consisting of the introductory passages and so forth.

And it is said in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*: "The introduction, the conclusion, repetition, novelty, the fruit, the explanatory praise, and the corroboration—these are the marks for determining the intended meaning (*tātparya*).
Thus, by virtue of the intended meaning of the Vedānta, it is stated that Brahman alone is what is to be known through the scripture.
Only a mere indication has been shown here;
the remainder should be sought in the commentaries on Ānandatīrtha’s Bhāṣya and other works.
I desist for fear of excessive prolixity.
And this secret has been described by Pūrṇaprajña Madhyamandira as the third incarnation of Vāyu, distinct from the others:
"The first was Hanumān, and the second was Bhīma;
the third was Pūrṇaprajña, the accomplisher of the Lord’s work."

Intending this very point, the following verse is written at the conclusion of various works: "In the Vedic scripture, three divine forms of the Great Splendor (Bhargas) of that God are proclaimed: 'Baṭ' is the first, manifest form; 'Darśata' is the second, the form of Vāyu; and 'Mahat' is the third, the form of Madhu. This book has been composed by Keśava [using] these [words]: 'Baṭ' as the first, consisting of Rāma’s words; 'Darśata' as the second, the body of Pṛkṣa; and 'Mahat' as the third, which is Madhu."

The meaning of this verse is understood by reflecting upon such Vedic scriptures as: "Truly, that beautiful splendor of the God was established for His body, from which He was born through His power" (*Ṛgveda* 1.141.1).
Therefore, the purport of the entire scripture is that the reality of Viṣṇu is the supreme of all; thus, everything is faultless. Now begins the Nakulīśa-Pāśupata system. (6)

Finding this Vaiṣṇava doctrine—which is characterized by dependence known through terms such as "servitude"—unappealing because it brings about suffering and is not a locus for the desired cessation of suffering, certain followers of Maheśvara, desiring supreme sovereignty (*pāramaiśvarya*), accept the Pāśupata scripture as their authority. This scripture is devoted to the exposition of the five categories (*pañcārtha*) as the means to achieve the supreme human goal. They establish their position through such inferences as: "Those held to be liberated by others are not truly liberated, because they are dependent and lack supreme sovereignty, just like ourselves"; and "The liberated souls are connected with the qualities of the Supreme Lord, because, while being persons, they are devoid of all seeds of suffering, just like the Supreme Lord. It is these who take refuge in the Pāśupata teaching.
In this regard, the opening sūtra is: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the rule for the yoga of Paśupati.
Its meaning is as follows: here, the word *atha* (now) refers back to what has been previously discussed.
And what was previously discussed is the question posed by the disciple to the teacher.
The nature of the Guru is described in the *Gaṇakārikā*:
"The five groups are to be known as eight, and the group consisting of three is one;
he who knows this group of nine and is its purifier is called the Guru."
The gains, the impurities, the means, the places, the states, the purifications, the initiations, the powers—these are the eight; the pentads are five, and the modes of conduct are three.

Where "three modes of activity" (*tisro vṛttayaḥ*) ought to have been used, the Vedic form "three modes of activity" (*trīṇi vṛttayaḥ*) is employed. In that context, the fruit of the means being prescribed is "attainment" (*lābha*).
It is fivefold, distinguished by knowledge (*jñāna*), austerity (*tapas*), constancy (*nityatva*), steadiness (*sthiti*), and purity (*śuddhi*).
Regarding this, Haradattācārya says: "Knowledge, austerity, constancy, stability, and purity as the fifth—these are the qualities inherent in the self.
Impurity (mala) is a defective state residing in the self;
it is of five kinds, distinguished by false knowledge and the rest."

Regarding this, it is said: "False knowledge, demerit, attachment, as well as falling [from one's state], and the condition of being a bound soul— these five, which are the root of bondage, are to be abandoned through discernment in the Tantra" (Gaṇakārikā, 8).

The means for the purification of the practitioner is fivefold, distinguished by types such as dwelling (vāsa) and conduct (caryā). This too has been stated: "Dwelling, conduct, recitation (japa), constant mindfulness of Rudra, and surrender (prapatti)—these five are determined to be the means for attaining the [spiritual] gains."

That place—such as the presence of the teacher and so forth—by means of which one attains the increase of knowledge and austerity preceded by the investigation of the meaning, is the "place" (*deśa*).
As it is said: "The teacher, the cave, the cremation ground, and Rudra himself.

That state of remaining established within a single boundary until the attainment of the goal is the "state" (*avasthā*), characterized by specific distinctions such as the manifest (*vyakta*) and so forth.

As it has been said: "The manifest, the unmanifest, victory, giving, and fifthly, steadfastness—these constitute purity, which is the absolute removal of false knowledge and the rest. It is fivefold according to the distinction of its opposites."

As it has been said: "The removal of ignorance, the removal of unrighteousness, the removal of that which causes attachment, the removal of the state of transmigration, and the removal of the state of being a bound soul—this is remembered as the fivefold purification."

The five factors that constitute initiation have been stated: "Substance, time, ritual action, the form, and the guru as the fifth. And the fivefold power is: "Devotion to the guru, grace, the dualistic method of the mind, righteousness, and vigilance; this is remembered as the fivefold power. Thus it is said.

The means of acquiring food that do not contradict the scriptures, intended for the purpose of lightening the five impurities, are called the modes of livelihood (*vṛtti*), namely: begging (*bhaikṣya*), eating what is discarded (*utsṛṣṭa*), and accepting whatever is obtained (*yathālabdha*).
The remainder in its entirety should be understood from the source itself.
By the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*), the end of suffering (*duḥkhānta*) is indicated.
This is because that [question] has as its purpose the inquiry into the removal of the threefold suffering, beginning with internal suffering;
because the word *paśu* (the bound soul) expresses the effect (*kārya*) as being dependent on another; and because the word *pati* (the Lord) expresses the cause (*kāraṇa*).

Because the term "Īśvara" signifies the Lord who is the cause of the universe—as in "the Lord, the Master, the Ruler"—and because the methods of yoga are well known, [it is established]. In that regard, the end of suffering (duḥkhānta) is of two kinds: that which is without self (anātmaka) and that which is with self (sātmaka).

In this context, that which is *anātman* (devoid of self) consists in the absolute cessation of all suffering. That which is *sātman* (possessing a self), however, is sovereignty characterized by the powers of vision and action.
Therein, although the power of vision (*dṛk-śakti*) is one, it is figuratively described as fivefold due to the distinction of its objects: seeing, hearing, thinking, discerning, and omniscience.
In that context, *darśana* is the knowledge whose objects are all visual and tactile things—whether subtle, concealed, or distant;
*śravaṇa* is the perfected knowledge whose object is the entirety of sound;
and *darśana* is the knowledge whose object is every conceivable thought.

The perfected knowledge whose object is all sounds without exception is hearing (*śravaṇa*). The perfected knowledge whose object is all thoughts without exception is reflection (*manana*). The perfected knowledge whose object is the entirety of the scriptures, both in terms of their textual form and their meaning, is higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
That by which one's own treatise is proclaimed—

wherein there is the knowledge of established truth that is ever-arisen, pervasive, and characterized by the attainment of the reality of all things, both those already stated and those yet unstated, through concise, detailed, and specific divisions— is omniscience.
This is the power of intellect (*dhī-śakti*).

The power of action (kriyā-śakti), though single, is treated as threefold: swiftness like thought (manojavitva), the ability to assume any form at will (kāmarūpitva), and the state of being free from the need for instruments (vikaraṇadharmitva). Among these, swiftness like thought is the quality of acting with unsurpassed rapidity. The ability to assume any form at will is the capacity, independent of karma and other factors, to preside over the creation of infinite forms—whether identical or distinct—in accordance with one's own will.
Even for one whose organs have been withdrawn, the state of being connected with unsurpassed sovereignty is the quality of possessing the power of action (vikaraṇadharmitva).
This is the power of action (kriyāśakti). Everything that is an effect is dependent.
In that regard, there are three categories: Vidyā (knowledge), Kalā (limited agency), and Paśu (the bound soul).
Through the knowledge of these, doubt and other such afflictions are removed.
Among them, Vidyā is the attribute of the Paśu.
That [nature] is also twofold, due to the distinction between the natures of consciousness and non-consciousness.
That which has the nature of consciousness is twofold, due to the distinction between the activities of discernment and non-discernment;
it is called the mind (*citta*).

For every living being, by means of the mind, cognizes objects—both those distinguished and those not distinguished—insofar as they are generally sustained by the light whose nature is awakening (*bodha*). Among these, the activity of discrimination is manifested solely by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, the ignorance (*avidyā*) which consists of non-awakening pertains to the objects of cattle and to merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*).
While being dependent upon consciousness (*cetanā*), the insentient (*acetana*) constituent is called *kalā*.

That too is of two kinds: that termed "effect" (*kārya*) and that termed "cause" (*kāraṇa*). Among these, the one termed "effect" is tenfold: the five elements beginning with earth, and the five qualities beginning with form (*rūpa*).

The category called the "causes" (kāraṇa) is of thirteen kinds: the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, and the three internal organs characterized as intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (manas), which are distinguished by their functions known as determination, self-consciousness, and volition. A "bound soul" (paśu) is one who is connected with the state of being bound. That too is of two kinds: with impurity (sāñjana) and without impurity (nirañjana).
In this context, the "stained" (sāñjana) is that which is connected with the body and the senses;
the "unstained" (nirañjana), however, is devoid of those.
The detailed exposition of this should be sought in the *Pañcārthabhāṣyadīpikā* and other such works.
The Cause is that which effects the creation, destruction, and grace of the entire universe.
Although it is one, its division has been described through the passage beginning with "the Lord, the primordial," etc., in consideration of the distinctions among its qualities and actions.
Among these, lordship (*patitva*) consists in possessing unsurpassed power of knowledge and action; by virtue of that sovereignty, it possesses an eternal connection therewith.

The state of being primordial (*ādyatva*) and the connection with sovereignty that is non-adventitious (*anāgantuka*) have been defined by the founders of various systems (*tīrthakara*), such as the author of the *Ādarśa*.
Yoga is the cause for the connection with the Lord (*īśvara*) through the medium of the mind (*citta*) (Pāśupata Sūtra 5.2).
And it is of two kinds: characterized by action (*kriyā-lakṣaṇa*) and characterized by the cessation of action (*kriyoparama-lakṣaṇa*).
In this context, that which is characterized by action consists of recitation, meditation, and so forth;
whereas that characterized by the cessation of action is designated as "niṣṭhā," "saṃvit," "gati," and so on.
A *vidhi* (injunction) is an operation that accomplishes dharma and artha.
And that is twofold: primary and secondary.
Among these, the primary is conduct (*caryā*), which is the direct cause of dharma.
It is twofold: vows (*vrata*) and the gates (*dvārāṇi*).
In this context, the vow (*vrata*) consists of bathing with ashes, lying on ashes, making offerings (*upahāra*), recitation (*japa*), and circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇā*).
This was stated by the venerable Nakulīśa: "One should bathe with ashes three times a day; one should lie on ashes" (Pāśupata Sūtra 1.8).
Here, the offering (*upahāra*) refers to the restrictive observance (*niyama*).
And that [offering] consists of six limbs.
As stated by the author of the Sūtra: "One should attend upon [the deity] with an offering consisting of six limbs: laughter, song, dance, the *huḍukkāra* sound, prostration, and recitation.
Among these, "laughter" (*hasita*) refers to a loud, boisterous laugh (*aṭṭahāsa*) preceded by the opening of the throat and the lips.

Song (*gīta*) is the contemplation of the qualities, attributes, and other characteristics related to Maheśvara, performed in accordance with the conventions of the science of music (*gāndharvaśāstra*).

Dance (*nṛtya*) also, following the rules of dramaturgy (*nāṭyaśāstra*), should be executed by the raising and other movements of the hands, feet, and so forth, together with the major limbs (*aṅga*), minor limbs (*pratyaṅga*), and secondary parts (*upāṅga*), as well as the internal emotional states (*bhāva*) and their absence.
The *huḍukkāra* is a holy sound produced by the contact of the tongue and palate, resembling the bellowing of a bull.
*Huḍu* is an imitation of sound, like *vaṣaṭ*.
Where common people are present, all of this should be employed cryptically;
the rest is well known.

The gateways, however, are yawning (krāthana), twitching (spandana), coquetry (mandana), affectation (śṛṅgāraṇa), doing what one should not do (avitarkakaraṇa), and speaking what one should not speak (avitarkabhāṣaṇa).
Among these, "yawning" is the display of the signs of sleep while one is actually not asleep.
"Twitching" is the trembling of the limbs of the body as if one were overcome by speechlessness.

*Śṛṅgāraṇa* (coquetry) is that by which one displays amorous gestures, like a lover upon seeing a woman endowed with beauty and youth, as if one's own movement were slow, like that of one whose faculty of feet has been impaired.
*Avitarkakaraṇa* (inappropriate action) is the performance of deeds censured by the world, like one who is devoid of the discrimination between what ought and ought not to be done.

The utterance of words that are contradictory, meaningless, and so forth, constitutes improper speech (*avitadbhāṣaṇa*). However, the prescribed rule (*vidhi*) regarding post-bath activities (*anusnāna*) and the like is subordinate; it is intended to assist in the practice by removing the impression of unfitness caused by such things as eating alms-food or consuming remnants.
This too has been stated by the author of the Sūtras: "One who wears the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) and the sectarian mark (*liṅga*) after the bath."
In this context, "conciseness" (samāsa) refers to the designation of the mere subject (dharmin), which has already been accomplished in the very first aphorism.
"Detailed exposition" (vistara) is the designation of the five categories according to their means of valid cognition;
that indeed is to be seen in the *Rāśīkāra-bhāṣya*.
The "classification" (vibhāga) is the designation of these [categories] according to their respective characteristics without confusion;
that has indeed already been established.
The "distinction" (viśeṣa) is the description of these [categories] as possessing superior qualities compared to other treatises.
For instance: elsewhere, the end of suffering is merely the cessation of suffering;
here, however, it is the attainment of supreme sovereignty.
Elsewhere, the effect is something that did not previously exist but comes into being; here, however, it is eternal, such as cattle and so forth.
In other cases, the cause is dependent;
here, however, the Blessed One alone is independent. In other cases, yoga has fruits such as Kaivalya and so forth.
But here, however, the injunction has as its fruit the end of suffering characterized by supreme sovereignty;
whereas elsewhere, the injunction has as its fruit heaven and the like, which are subject to return. Here, moreover, it has as its fruit proximity and so forth, which are characterized by non-return.
Now, one might object: "Is this not a great magical illusion, that the Supreme Lord is the cause while being independent?
If that were so, two defects would manifest: the futility of karma and the simultaneous production of all effects.
Do not think thus.
Because they have different substrates (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*).

If the Lord were the cause independently [of karma], then what would follow from the fruitlessness of karma? If you say it is the "absence of a purpose"—but whose absence of purpose is the cause for the fruitlessness of karma? Is it that of the agent of the action (*karmī*), or that of the Lord? Not the first, because it is logically established that an action favored by the will of the Lord is fruitful.
Furthermore, for one who has not been so favored, there is the possibility that [the action] might sometimes be fruitless, just like the actions of Yayāti and others; yet,
this does not entail a lack of engagement in ritual acts,
as such engagement is logically justified, as in the case of farmers and the like.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because the activity of bound souls (paśu) is dependent upon the will of the Lord; furthermore,
since the Supreme Lord possesses all desires fulfilled, he has no need for any purpose to be accomplished through karma.
As for what was stated—that there is a simultaneous arising (*samasamayasamutpāda*)—that too is incorrect.
For it is accepted that the Supreme Lord, who possesses inconceivable power, brings about effects through His unimpeded power of action (*avyāhatakriyāśakti*), which conforms to His will.
As it has been said by those who know the tradition: "Since He acts according to His own will, being independent of karma and other such factors..."
Therefore, for that reason, it is stated in the scripture: "The cause of all causes.

Now, one might ask: "Since liberation is indeed obtained through the knowledge of God even in other philosophical systems, what is the distinction of this [system]? Do not speak thus; for such an objection is untenable due to the impossibility of the alternatives.

Is the cause of liberation merely knowledge concerning Īśvara, or is it direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), or rather the ascertainment of reality as it truly is? Not the first, because if liberation were established by the mere arising of the cognition "Mahādeva is the lord of the gods"—just like ordinary people—even without the scripture, it would follow that the study of the scripture is futile.
Nor is it the second.

For animals whose eyes are fleshly and who are accumulated through a multitude of various impurities, the direct realization of the Supreme Lord is impossible. In the third case, there would be the consequence of falling into our own position; for without the Pāśupata scripture, the determination of reality as it truly is is impossible.
As it has been said by the Teachers: "In mere theoretical knowledge, scripture is in vain; direct perception is difficult to attain.
There is no determination of reality as it truly is other than through the *Pañcārtha*."
Therefore, it is fitting that those foremost of men who desire the goals of human life should take refuge in the Pāśupata scripture, which is devoted to the exposition of the ultimate goal.
Now begins the Śaiva philosophy. ||7||

Rejecting this position—that "the Supreme Lord is the cause independent of karma and other factors"—because it is vitiated by the defects of partiality and cruelty, certain Māheśvaras who correctly perceive the established tenets of the Śaiva Āgamas accept the alternative position that "the Supreme Lord is the cause dependent on karma and so forth. They propose another view, stating that there are three categories of reality (padārthas) based on the distinction between the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu), and the fetter (pāśa).
As it has been said by those who know the truth of the Tantras: "The Great Tantra, which consists of three categories and four feet, was taught by the Teacher of the World."
"Some [teachers] do not summarize it by means of a sutra, but rather speak of it at length."

The meaning of this is as follows: that in which the three categories (padārtha) mentioned exist is "tripadārtha"; that in which the four feet (pāda)—known as Vidyā, Kriyā, Yoga, and Caryā—exist is the "four-footed" (catuścaraṇa) Mahātantra.
Among these, because the bound souls (paśu) lack independence and the fetters (pāśa) lack consciousness, the Lord (pati), who is distinct from them, is mentioned first.
Because they share the common characteristic of being conscious, the bound souls are mentioned immediately after him.
The rule of sequence is that the remaining *pāśas* (fetters) are placed at the end.

Because initiation (*dīkṣā*) is the cause of the supreme human goal, and because it cannot be accomplished without the knowledge (*jñāna*)—which determines the greatness of the Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and so forth, and serves as the means for ascertaining the true nature of the bound soul (*paśu*), the fetters (*pāśa*), and the Lord (*īśvara*)—the *Vidyāpāda*, which conveys that [knowledge], comes first. Following that is the *Kriyāpāda*, which demonstrates the various types of initiation rituals along with their auxiliary components.
The realization that the desired goal cannot be attained without yoga establishes that the *yogapāda*, which teaches yoga with its constituent parts, follows those preceding sections.

Furthermore, since even yoga does not succeed without conduct (*caryā*)—consisting of the performance of prescribed duties and the avoidance of prohibited ones—the *caryāpāda*, which explains such conduct, is placed last; this is the distinction.
In this context, Śiva is the intended object of each individual term.
Although the liberated souls, such as the Vidyeśvaras and others, possess the state of Śiva, they nevertheless lack absolute autonomy due to their dependence on the Supreme Lord.
Consequently, because entities such as bodies, organs, and worlds are characterized by a specific arrangement, they are understood to be effects.
And since they are effects, it is inferred that they must have been preceded by an intelligent agent; thus, the existence of the Supreme Lord is established through the force of inference.
[Objection: But surely, the fact that the body itself is an effect is unestablished;
for nowhere, by no one, at any time, has a body ever been seen being produced.
[Reply: True; nevertheless, it is not accepted that the body is not being produced by anyone, and therefore the denial of the perception of an agent is not tenable.

For that [the world] can also be established as being inferable. To explain: the body and so forth must be an effect, because they possess a specific configuration or because they are perishable, like a jar.
And by means of that quality of being an effect, it is indeed easy to infer that they are preceded by an intelligent agent.
The subject of dispute possesses a creator, because it is an effect, like a pot.

Whatever possesses the aforementioned probans possesses the aforementioned probandum, as in the case of objects and so forth. That which does not possess [the probans] does not possess [the probandum], as in the case of objects and so forth.
The proof for the validity of the inference of the Supreme Lord has been established elsewhere, so I shall desist here.
"This ignorant creature is not its own master over pleasure and pain;
impelled by God, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell."
According to this principle, since the agency of the Supreme Lord is established in dependence upon the karma performed by living beings,
it should not be argued that his sovereignty is impaired;
for we do not observe a loss of a creator’s sovereignty merely because he depends upon instruments.
Just as a king who depends on his treasury gives gifts through his favor and so forth;

as it has been stated by the Siddha-gurus: "The independence of an agent consists in being the instigator of the instruments and so forth, not in being independent of the object and other factors. Thus it is said.

And thus it is established that the agent—who, by virtue of those respective latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*), knows the specific details of experience, the means of experience, and their material causes—is proven through inference and other means.

This very point was stated by the venerable Bṛhaspati: "In this world, he who understands the objects of enjoyment, the means of enjoyment, and their material causes—apart from him, there would be no one else who knows the ripening of the latent impressions of human action."
Elsewhere it is also stated: "Everything under dispute is preceded by an intelligent agent, because it is an effect, just like a pot or other effects established for both of us."
From His being the creator of all, His omniscience is established, because it is impossible for one who is ignorant to act as a creator.
And it has been stated in the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra: "He is omniscient because He is the creator of all, together with the means, the auxiliaries, and the results."
Whoever knows what, he performs that very thing; this is well-established.
Let it be, then, that God is an independent creator;
however, He is not bodiless,
because we observe that effects such as jars are produced by embodied agents like potters.
If it be argued that, being possessed of a body, the Lord would— like ourselves and others—
be subject to afflictions, lack omniscience, and possess limited power, do not think thus;
for we observe that even the bodiless Self is an agent with respect to the movement of its own body and so forth.
Even granting this for the sake of argument, we say:
even if the Blessed One possesses a body, the aforementioned defects do not follow.
For the Supreme Lord, since the web of bonds such as impurity (*mala*) and karma is impossible, his body is not material (*prākṛta*), but rather consists of power (*śākta*).

Through the five mantras beginning with Īśāna, which are the forms of His powers (*śakti*), there is the conceptualization [of the Lord's body] starting from the head: Īśāna is the head, Tatpuruṣa the face, Aghora the heart, Vāmadeva the private parts, and Sadyojāta the feet. Thus, according to the well-known tradition, the Lord is the cause of the fivefold cosmic functions characterized by grace (*anugraha*), concealment (*tirobhāva*), withdrawal (*ādāna*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and manifestation (*udbhava*). His body, assumed for the sake of His own will, is not like our bodies. As it is said in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Because of the impossibility of impurity and the like, the body of the Lord is empowered (*śākta*) and not of such a nature."
Elsewhere it is also said: "That body [of Śiva] consists of five mantras suitable for the fivefold acts—namely Īśa, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Ādya—located in the head and other parts."

If it is argued that in the Āgamas, such as "the five-faced one with fifteen eyes," the Supreme Lord's connection with a body, senses, and so forth is heard of as being primary indeed—the answer is: true. However, since meditation, worship, and the like are impossible for one who is formless, there is no contradiction in His assuming various forms for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees.
As it is said in the venerable Pauṣkara: "This form of His is traditionally taught for the protection of the practitioner.
And elsewhere: "By rule, that which possesses form is to be worshipped; the intellect does not reach a reality that is formless."

And the fivefold activity has been elaborated upon by King Bhoja: "The fivefold nature of that activity consists of creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and likewise the bestowing of grace; this is declared to belong to Him who is eternally manifest."

And regarding this fivefold task, the distinction is that in the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*) it is performed directly by Śiva as the agent, whereas in the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) it is performed through Ananta and others.
As it is said in the venerable *Karaṇa*: "In the pure path, Śiva is declared to be the agent; in the [impure] path, Ananta is the agent of the Lord."

Thus, it should be understood that by the term *śiva*, there is an inclusion within the category of the Lord (*pati*) of all those who possess the nature of Śiva—namely, the mantras, the lords of mantras (*mantreśvara*), the great lords (*maheśvara*), and the liberated souls (*muktātman*)—along with their designations, together with the collection of means such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) which serve as the instruments for attaining that state of Śiva-nature.
In this manner, the category of the Lord has been defined.

Now, the category of the bound soul (*paśu*) is defined: the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which is not an atom (*anaṇu*) and is known by terms such as "knower of the field" (*kṣetrajña*), is the bound soul.
But it is not of the nature of the body and so forth, as held by the Cārvākas and others, because—
according to the principle that "one person does not remember what was seen by another"— the recognition [of past experiences] would otherwise be impossible.
Nor is it something to be illuminated, as held by the Naiyāyikas and others.
Because it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress.
As it has been said: "If the self were an object of cognition, there would have to be another as its cognizer;
if that other self were seen, then there would have to be yet another."
Nor is it non-pervasive like that of the Jainas,
nor is it momentary like that of the Buddhists,
because it is unconditioned by space and time.
This has also been stated: "That entity whose existence is unconditioned by space and time is held to be eternal and all-pervading; thus, the self is both all-pervading and eternal."
Nor is it one, as the Advaitins maintain,
because the specific determination of experience— which serves as proof for the plurality of puruṣas— is possible; nor is it a non-agent, as the Sāṃkhyas maintain.
Because it is heard in scripture that Śiva-hood consists of consciousness whose nature is eternal and unsurpassed vision and action, once the net of bonds has been removed.
As it is stated in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "Because Śiva-hood is heard [to exist] when the bonds have ceased.
Consciousness, whose nature is vision and action, exists in the Self at all times.
And because liberation is heard of as being "facing all directions" (sarvatomukha) from every side, it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "The liberated souls are also Śivas;
however, he by whose grace they are liberated—he alone is to be known as the eternally liberated one, whose body consists of the five mantras."
The bound soul (*paśu*) is of three kinds, distinguished as *vijñānākala*, *pralayākala*, and *sakala*.

Among these, the first is designated as *vijñānākala* because, when karma is exhausted through knowledge (*vijñāna*), yoga, renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), or experience (*bhoga*), there is an absence of the bondage of the *kalās* and so forth—which exists for the sake of exhausting karma—and he is joined only with impurity (*mala*).

The second, however, is conventionally termed *pralayākala* because, due to cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), the *kalās* and other factors are withdrawn, and he remains joined with both impurity and karma.
The third, however, being accompanied by the threefold bondage consisting of impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and action (*karman*), is designated as "sakala" (the conditioned).
Among these, the first is of two types, distinguished as those whose impurities are exhausted and those whose impurities are not exhausted.
Therein, having graced those foremost of men who possess the ripening of their impurities and are fit for authority, [the Lord] leads them to the state of the eight lords beginning with Ananta.
That group of eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) is specified in the Bahudaivatya: Ananta, Sūkṣma, and likewise Śivottama;
Ekanetra, as well as Ekarudra, and Trimūrtika.
Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin—these are declared to be the Vidyeśvaras.
It ordains other seventy million mantras that bestow grace.
As it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "Bound souls (*paśu*) are declared to be of three kinds: the *sakala* in the states of consciousness and dissolution;
among these, the first is possessed of impurity (*mala*), and the second is joined with both impurity and karma."
Among them, the Sakala is endowed with impurity (mala), māyā, and karma; he is of two kinds.
The first has completed his impurity, while the second has not completed his impurity.
Having favored the first eight, Śiva appoints them to the state of Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśatva);
he also creates other mantras, which are said to number seven crores.
Somaśambhu has also stated: "In the scripture, the recipient of grace is considered to be of three kinds: the first is named Vijñānākala, the second is Pralayākala, and the third is Sakala."
Among them, the first is joined with impurity alone, while the other is joined with both impurity and karma.
The Sakala [subject] is endowed with the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā and ending with Bhūmi.
The *pralayākala* is also of two kinds: one whose two bonds have matured (*pakvapāśadvaya*) and one distinct from that (*tadvilakṣaṇa*).
Among these, the first attains liberation.
The second, however, joined with the *puryaṣṭaka*, undergoes various births under the influence of karma.

This too has been stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "Among the *pralayākalas*, those whose impurity (*mala*) and karma (*karman*) are unripened go, endowed with bodies consisting of the eightfold group of *mūrtis*, into all wombs by the power of their karma."

The *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city) is also specified in that very same work: "The *puryaṣṭaka* consists of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the intellect (*dhī*), and the instruments of action (*karmakaraṇa*).

This has been explained by the teacher Aghoraśivācārya: "The so-called *puryaṣṭaka* is fixed for each individual; it exists from the beginning of creation until the end of a kalpa or until liberation. It is a subtle body composed of thirty principles, beginning with earth and ending with *kalā*. Thus it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*: "This group of principles, beginning with earth and ending with *kalā*, is fixed for each person."
And by the power of karma, this [individual] wanders through all the bodies born within the worlds.

And thus the meaning is established as follows: by the term *antaḥkaraṇa* (internal organ), which denotes the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*), there are also indicated the other seven principles (*tattva*) that are internal to the person's process of experience—namely, *kalā*, *kāla*, *niyati*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *prakṛti*, and the *guṇas*.

By the term *dhīkarma* (intellect and action), the five knowable gross elements (*bhūta*) and their causes, the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), are intended. By the term *karaṇa* (instrument), the ten organs of knowledge and action are comprised.
Indeed, it is stated in the venerable Kālottara: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—this pentad, along with intellect, mind, and ego, is declared to be the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city)."
Thus it is heard [in scripture].
How then can it be stated otherwise? Indeed, for this very reason, the venerable Rāmakaṇḍa has explained that sūtra as referring to thirty principles; so enough with excessive elaboration.

Nevertheless, how does this [puryaṣṭaka] possess the nature of being an "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka)? There is no contradiction, because it is composed of five groups—namely, the elements, the subtle elements, the organs of cognition, the organs of action, and the internal organ—along with their cause, Pradhāna, and the group consisting of the pentad beginning with Kalā.

In that regard, having favored certain individuals who are endowed with the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) and possessed of distinguished merit, the Great Lord Ananta bestows upon them the status of a world-protector (bhuvanapati).
As it has been said: "The Great Lord, having favored certain others, grants them the status of world-protectors."
The *sakala* [individual] is also of two kinds, distinguished as those whose impurities are ripened (*pakva-kaluṣa*) and those whose impurities are unripened (*apakva-kaluṣa*).

Among these, the Supreme Lord leads the former to the status of the one hundred and eighteen Mantreśvaras, such as Maṇḍalin and others, through the process of ripening that [impurity] by means of a descent of power (*śaktipāta*) corresponding to it. As it has been said: "At the time of the dawn of the day, the remaining ones become *sakala*s due to their connection with the *kalās* and so forth."
He himself performs one hundred and eighteen of those [offerings] for the lords of mantras.
Therein, there are eight Maṇḍalins beginning with Krodha, as well as Vīreśa who is equal to them;
Śrīkaṇṭha and the hundred Śatarudras—thus [there are] one hundred and eighteen.
