In accordance with the degree of their maturation, the Supreme Lord, assuming the form of the Teacher (ācārya), bestows liberation by withdrawing his [limited] power and performing initiation. This too has been stated: "Abiding in the form of the Teacher, he unites those whose impurities are fully matured with the supreme reality through initiation, by means of the descent of power (śaktipāta) which is the cause of their eradication."
In the venerable Mṛgendra-tantra as well: "It removes the net of bonds for the individual soul (aṇu) that was previously cast into confusion."
And it has been explained by Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha;
all of that should be understood from that very source.
However, we do not introduce it here for fear of prolixity.
The Supreme Lord, by virtue of karma, ordains that some souls are unripened and impure, while others are bound, subtle, and partaking of experience.
As it has been said: "He employs the remaining bound souls for the sake of experiencing enjoyment, due to the persistence of their karma. Thus are the individual souls (paśus) described.
Now, the category of *pāśa* (the bond) is explained.
The *pāśa* is fourfold, due to the distinction between *mala*, *karman*, *māyā*, and the power of obstruction (*rodhaśakti*).
But surely, in the Śaiva Āgamas, the primary triad is given in the sequence of *pati*, *paśu*, and *pāśa*.
In that system, Śiva is said to be the Lord (*pati*), the individual souls (*aṇu*) are the bound ones (*paśu*), and the five categories are the fetters (*pāśa*).
Thus, the fetter is described as being fivefold.

How, then, is it reckoned as fourfold? It is replied: although the *bindu*—which is of the nature of *māyā* and is to be known as the stage of the *śivatattva*—is a fetter with respect to the supreme liberation characterized by the attainment of the state of Śiva, its conjunction [with the soul] is not included as a fetter because it is a cause for attaining the status of a *Vidyeśvara* and so forth, which constitutes an inferior form of liberation; thus there is no contradiction.

For this very reason, it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "The bonds (pāśas) are of four kinds. Also, in the venerable *Mṛgendra*: "The net of bonds consists, in brief, of the fourfold effects of Māyā—namely, obscuration (prāvaraṇa), lordship (aiśvarya), strength (bala), and karma; these properties are designated by their very names."

The meaning of this is as follows: *prāvṛtti* is the impure *mala* (taint), so called because it "covers" (*prāvṛṇoti*), that is, it thoroughly obscures the innate powers of perception and action belonging to the self. And that [taint] "rules" (*īṣṭe*) by its own autonomy, thus it is the *īśa*.
As it has been said: "For there is one *mala* which possesses manifold powers and is the obscurer of the perception and action of the person."
It should be understood as being like the husk surrounding a grain of rice, or like the black coating adhering to copper.
"Power" (*bala*) refers to the power of obstruction (*rodha-śakti*).
Because this power of Śiva causes the concealment of the individual soul (*puruṣa*) by presiding over the fetters (*pāśa*), it is metaphorically designated as a "fetter."
As it has been said: "Among them, I am the supreme power (*śakti*), the auspicious one (*śivā*) who bestows grace upon all;

it is only because she follows [the laws of] *dharma* that she is metaphorically designated as 'bond' (*pāśa*). That which is performed by those seeking fruits is *karman*, consisting of *dharma* and *adharma*; like the seed and the sprout, it exists in the form of a beginningless stream. (2)
As it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*: "Just as his impurity (*mala*) is beginningless, so too is his karma beginningless.

If that which is beginningless were not established [as such], by what cause would there be this diversity? (3) It is called *māyā* because in the state of dissolution (*pralaya*), the entire universe is absorbed within it in the form of power (*śakti*), and at the time of creation, it attains manifestation.
As it is said in the venerable *Saurabheya*: "At the great dissolution, all effects are merged within it in the form of power."
In its transformation, it manifests through its effects, such as the *kalās* and other constituents.
(4) Although there is much more that could be said on this matter, I shall desist for fear of excessive prolixity.
Thus, the three categories of Pati, Paśu, and Pāśa have been shown;
likewise, Vidya, Avidya, Paśu, and Pāśa constitute the causal framework.
When that [ignorance] ceases, the six categories have thus been briefly explained.
Other methods such as these are well known in works like the *Jñānaratnāvalī*;
everything should be understood from those very sources, and thus all is consistent.
Now, the philosophy of recognition (pratyabhijñā). ||8||

There, others—dissatisfied with the view that the causality of insentient things devoid of dependence is untenable, seeking an alternative doctrine, and proclaiming that the creation of the universe proceeds solely by the will of the Supreme Lord—practice the Pratyabhijñā (Recognition) scripture as supreme Śaivas. They assert that the Supreme Lord, who possesses various distinctions and non-distinctions such as means of knowledge and objects of knowledge, who is established through scripture and confirmed by self-awareness and reasoning, and who possesses the sovereignty characterized by not looking to any other source, manifests all entities like reflections in the mirror of His own Self. Thus, they accept a novel and easily accessible means for attaining both higher and lower accomplishments (*siddhi*), consisting of mere recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) alone, which is free from the entire burden of hardships such as external and internal rituals, breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), and the like.
The extent of this [scripture] has also been delineated by investigators: the Sūtra, the Vṛtti, the Vivṛtti, and both the Laghvī and Bṛhatī Vimarsinīs;
together with the five Prakaraṇa-vivaraṇas, such is the Pratyabhijñā Śāstra.

In this regard, the first aphorism is as follows: "Having somehow attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara, and desiring to benefit even ordinary people, I shall establish that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) which is the cause for the attainment of all perfections."
"In some way" (kathaṃcit) means: by means of the propitiation of the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru, who is non-different from the Supreme Lord, and which is itself fashioned by the Supreme Lord.
"Having attained" (āsādya) means: having brought [the teaching] to complete perfection on all sides, and having rendered it an unrestrained object of enjoyment for one's own self.
By this, his qualification for composing a scripture for the sake of others is demonstrated through his state of having known that which is to be known.
Otherwise, it would result in nothing but deception.

Even Viṣṇu, Viriñca (Brahmā), and others, though they have transcended *māyā*, are presided over by the Great Māyā (*mahāmāyā*); they have become lords only through a mere fraction of His sovereignty. That Blessed One is Maheśvara, whose ultimate reality is uninterrupted light, bliss, and freedom.
[The goal is] His servitude (*dāsya*).

A *dāsa* is so called because everything desired is given to him by his master; the meaning is that he is a vessel for the sovereignty of the nature of the Supreme Lord. By the word *jana*, the absence of restriction regarding the scope of eligibility is demonstrated.
For whoever this description of the true nature [of reality] is given, for that person there arises a great fruit;
because it is precisely through wisdom (*prajñā*) that the ultimate fruit is attained.
Thus it was taught by the supreme gurus, the venerable Somānandanātha, in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*: "Even once, by means of valid cognition, from the scripture, or from the word of the guru..."
When the state of Śiva, which resides in all things, has been known through firm realization, [one attains liberation].
Once [the truth] is known, there is no further need for any instrument or even for meditative cultivation;
when gold has been recognized, one may abandon both the instruments and the mental states.

By the word "api" (also/even), which reveals His own identity as non-different from that [the Supreme Self], any possibility of another purpose within Himself— distinct from the fulfillment of the welfare of others— is excluded by virtue of His perfection. And yet, the welfare of others certainly remains His purpose,
for it possesses the defining characteristics of such a purpose.
For this is not a divine curse that "one's own interest alone is the purpose, and not the interest of others.
It is for this very reason that Akṣapāda stated: "That object aiming at which one acts is the purpose" (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.24).
The prefix *upa* signifies proximity.
Therefore, the sole fruit for people is merely being brought into the presence of the Supreme Lord.
For this very reason, he says "all" and so forth.
Indeed, upon the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord, all forms of prosperity are already attained as its natural outflow, just as the wealth of gems is attained upon reaching Mount Rohaṇa.

When the state of supreme lordship has been attained in this way, what else remains to be prayed for? As it was said by Utpalācārya: "For those enriched by the fortune of devotion, what else is there to be sought?
Or for those impoverished of it, what else is there not to be sought?"
Thus, the purpose has been indicated according to the view that this is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
Now, we shall establish it according to the view that it is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*).

That *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) is so described because it is the cause for the "perfect attainment" (*samyagavāpti*) of that perfection—the manifestation of the state of being—which consists of the eternal bliss and other qualities of the entire [reality], both external and internal.
The *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) of that Maheśvara is knowledge (*jñāna*) directed toward (*prati ābhimukhyena*) him.
For in the world, when an object has become present through a synthesis such as "this is that very Caitra," the resulting knowledge is conventionally termed *pratyabhijñā*.

Here too, while the Supreme Lord—whose perfect powers are known through well-known Purāṇas, established scriptures, inference, and so forth—is present within one's own self, there arises a knowledge through the synthesis of His powers: "Surely, I am that very Lord."
I shall establish this very recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

"Establishment" (*upapatti*) means possibility (*saṃbhava*). The meaning is: "I bring it about," that is, I accomplish it through an efficient operation (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*), by performing what is effective for its existence.

If it is asked, "If the self shines forth as the very nature of God, then what is the purpose of this effort to demonstrate its recognition (pratyabhijñā)?"—the resolution to this is as follows: Although the self is constantly manifesting by virtue of its own self-luminosity, it appears only partially due to the power of *māyā*. Therefore, recognition is demonstrated by the manifestation of its powers of knowledge (*dṛk*) and action (*kriyā*), in order to establish the manifestation of its fullness.
And thus the formal argument: "This self must be the Supreme Lord."
Because it possesses the powers of knowledge and action;
for whoever is a knower and an agent to whatever extent is a lord (īśvara) to that same extent, as is well known in the case of a [supreme] Lord or a king.
And the Self is the knower and the agent of the universe.
"Therefore, this is God.

This recourse to the five-membered syllogism is just like [the use of] *māyā*, because the Naiyāyika doctrine has been accepted. Thus it was said by the son of Udayākara: "In the Great Lord, who is the agent, the knower, one's own self, and established from the very beginning..."
Who, being a non-inert self, could perform either a negation or an establishment?
However, although this [Self] is seen, it is not perceived due to the power of delusion;
therefore, this recognition is demonstrated by manifesting its inherent capacity.
For thus it is: for all beings here, the foundation is the support of life;
knowledge and action are considered the life of living beings.
In that regard, knowledge is self-established, whereas action, being dependent upon its effects, may be perceived by others as well; thus it is called "knowledge of another."
And that intuitive flash (pratibhā) of theirs, which takes the form of the sequence of various objects,
is the Great Lord— the subject whose nature is consciousness, bliss, and timelessness.
And so it is said.
Somanandanātha also says: "One always knows through the self that is Śiva; one always knows through the self that is [the individual] *mada*," and so forth.
Even at the conclusion of the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*), he states: "Without identity with That, there is no worldly course for cognitions."
Due to the identity of illumination, there is oneness; the established position is that the knower is one.
He alone, by virtue of his determinate nature as reflective awareness, is Maheśvara;
for the pure power of knowledge and action belong solely to the God insofar as they consist of that very reflective awareness.

And this has been elucidated by the teacher Abhinavagupta: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.2.15). By this Śruti, it is accepted that the entire multitude of objects is made manifest through the majesty of the Light whose nature is Consciousness.

Consequently, the distinction between the manifestation of an object—such as the manifestation of blue or the manifestation of yellow—is due to the difference in the coloring provided by the respective objects.
In reality, however, because it is devoid of any limitation of space, time, or form, there is indeed non-duality.
That very light, whose nature is consciousness (*caitanya*), is called the subject (*pramātṛ*).
Thus it is stated in the *Śivasūtras*: "The Self is consciousness" (1.1).

Its nature as consciousness, its state of uninterrupted self-reflection (*vimarśa*), its non-orientation toward anything else, and its being a single mass of bliss—these are synonyms for *māheśvarya* (the Lordship).
For this very self-nature of existence, which is self-reflection, constitutes pure, ultimate knowledge and action.
Among these, the aspect of luminosity (*prakāśa*) is knowledge.
Action (*kriyā*) is the state of being the creator of the universe by one's own nature.
And that has been defined in the section on action (*kriyādhikāra*): "And he, because of his infinite power, manifests these entities in this way;
by virtue of his will, this manifestation of them is his action, which is his creative agency."
In the conclusion as well: "Thus, for Him who desires to abide in the form of the world consisting of jars, cloths, and so forth, His very will—produced by the agent—is the cause and the action."
Even that relationship of cause and effect, expressed as "this being present,
that exists," is not possible for insentient things that are devoid of mutual dependence.

According to this principle, since insentient matter possesses no causal power, nor does a sentient being who is not the Lord, therefore it is the very will (*icchā*) of the independent Lord Maheśvara—who desires to exist in the form of thousands of distinct actions and modifications of being such as the birth and maintenance of the world—that is called "universal agency" (*viśvakartṛtva*), as it is that will which, through its progressively swelling nature, constitutes action.
Regarding the creation of the world by mere will, an illustrative example is clearly pointed out: "Even for yogis, that which occurs by the force of will alone, even without clay or seeds..."
A jar or other such object arises as the performer of various stable states and actions.

If clay and the like were, in the ultimate sense, the sole cause of a jar and so forth, then how could the birth of a jar and such things occur through the mere will of a yogin? If it is argued that the jars and sprouts produced from clay and seeds are one thing, while those produced by the will of a yogin are quite another—then even in that case, it is well known to all people that a difference in effects arises from a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Furthermore, those who maintain that the production of a jar and the like does not occur without a material cause (*upādāna*), but that the yogin, by means of his will, sets the atoms into motion and joins them together, must also be addressed [with this same reasoning].

If a reversal of the observed relationship between cause and effect were not possible, then [in the production of] a jar, clay, a staff, a wheel, and so forth would have to be required; likewise, for the body, the union of male and female and so on would be required.
Consequently, the arising of jars, bodies, and the like immediately following the mere will of a yogi would be impossible to justify.

However, it is the conscious [Lord] alone who appears in such a manner; thus, in the view that the Blessed One, the illustrious Mahādeva, possesses an absolute sovereignty characterized by the dense capacity to both follow and transcend fixed necessity (*niyati*), there is no inconsistency whatsoever.

Therefore it has been said by the teacher Vasugupta: "Homage to that Śiva, the Lord of the digits (Kalānātha), who creates the variegated picture of the universe upon no wall and without any collection of material causes."

If it is asked, "How can there be a connection with transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) if the inner self (pratyagātman) is non-different from the Supreme Lord?"—it has been stated in the *Āgamādhikāra*: "This cognizer (pramātā), blinded by Māyā, is a transmigrator bound by karma;
when his sovereignty is made manifest through Vidyā and the other [means], he is called liberated, consisting of pure consciousness."

Now, if the object of cognition (*prameya*) is non-different from the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), what is the distinction between the bound and the liberated with respect to that object? To this, too, an answer has been stated in the *Tattvārthasaṃgraha*: "The liberated one perceives the object as non-different from his own self, just like Maheśvara; the bound one, however, perceives it as possessing absolute difference."
Now, if the state of the self as the Supreme Lord is innate, there is no purpose in the request for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
For a seed, when its auxiliary causes are complete, does not fail to produce a sprout even if it has not been recognized.
Therefore, if it is asked why such insistence is placed on the recognition of the self, it is said in reply: [The text continues: ...it is said.
Listen first to this secret:

for purposeful action (arthakriyā) is indeed twofold—namely, external, such as [producing] a sprout and so forth, and that which consists of the essence of the wonder of resting within the subject, taking the form of joy and so on.
Of these, the former does not require recognition (pratyabhijñāna).
The second [type of action], however, depends precisely upon that.

Here too, there must be required the recognition of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-pratyabhijñāna*), which consists in the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) characterized by the manifestation of the powers of the unity of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) with the Supreme Self—the very essence of the wonder (*camatkāra*) that "I am the Lord."

Now, it may be asked: where has it been observed that a purposeful activity (arthakriyā), whose essence is repose in the subject (pramātṛviśrānti), which was previously unperceived without recognition (pratyabhijñāna), is perceived therein? To this it is replied: a certain amorous woman, her passion intensified by hearing of the multitude of virtues of a hero, overwhelmed by love and unable to endure the pain of separation, composes messages to convey her condition by means of a love-letter.

Likewise, even as she wanders in haste toward his vicinity, although he is seen, that sight does not attain the state of being heart-touching if there is no reflection upon his virtues, for it would then become common to all people.
But when, through the words of a messenger, one reflects upon His qualities, at that very moment one attains the state of fullness (*pūrṇabhāva*).

Thus, although the Lord of the Universe shines within one's own self, that manifestation does not bring about the state of fullness at a time when there is an absence of reflection upon His qualities.

However, when through the words of a Guru or other means, a reflection arises upon the excellence of the Supreme Lord—characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth—at that very moment the attainment of the nature of the Full Self occurs.

As it has been stated in the fourth *Vimarśa*: "Just as a lover, though standing near her and having been entreated with various supplications, remains unrecognized by her as if he were an ordinary person and thus unable to enjoy her company;
even so, the Lord of the Universe, whose qualities are not perceived by the world, does not manifest his own majesty to the world. Therefore, this 'Recognition' (*pratyabhijñā*) has been proclaimed."

Although this subject has been elaborated upon by teachers such as Abhinavagupta and others, we have not expanded upon it here, as we are beginning with a summary and fear prolixity; may all be auspicious!
Now, the doctrine of the Lord of Mercury (Raseśvaradarśana). ||9||

Others, who are followers of Maheśvara and proponents of identity with the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-tādātmya-vādinaḥ), maintain that once the stability of the body (piṇḍasthairya) is achieved, liberation while living (jīvanmukti)—which is desired by all—will be attained; thus, they assert that the very means for the stability of the body is mercury (rasa), which is designated by terms such as pārada.
Mercury is called *pārada* because it is the cause for reaching the further shore (*para-pāra*) of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
As it has been said: "Because it grants the further shore of saṃsāra, it is known as *pārada*."
In the Rasārṇava it is also said: "Because it is employed for the supreme goal by the best of practitioners, mercury (pārada) has been so called.
O Goddess, while asleep, this [mercury] is equal to me; it is produced from my very limbs. Since it is the essence (rasa) of my body, it is therefore called 'rasa'."

If it is argued that this line of reasoning is not logical because liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) can be established through other means as well, we say no. For in all six philosophical systems (*ṣaddarśana*), liberation is stated to occur only after the fall of the body; since trust in such a liberation would be untenable, purposeful activity toward it would be impossible without doubt.
This too has been stated in that very same work: "Even in the six systems of philosophy, liberation is shown to occur upon the falling of the physical body (*piṇḍapātana*);
yet even that [liberation], though as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, is not perceived [in this life]."
Therefore, one should protect that physical body with elixirs and rejuvenating tonics.

Govinda Bhagavatpādācārya also said: "Considering wealth, body, and enjoyments to be always impermanent, one should always strive for liberation; that [liberation] comes from knowledge, that [knowledge] from practice, and that [practice] when the body is stable."

If it be asked, "How can the eternity of the body be determined when it is observed to be perishable?"—do not think thus. For although the body composed of the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika*) is impermanent, the eternity of that which is born from the creation of Hara and Gaurī—designated by the terms *rasa*, *abhraka*, and *pada*—is logically established. Thus it is said in the *Rasahṛdaya*: "And those who, without abandoning their bodies, have attained a body born from the creation of Hara and Gaurī—they are liberated as perfected adepts of mercury (*rasasiddha*). What can the host of mantras do for them?"
(1/7) Thus.

Therefore, a yogi desiring liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) must first prepare a divine body. Regarding the essence (*rasa*), its origin from the union of the creation of Hara and Gaurī is stated through its identity with them: mercury being born of Hara and mica (*abhraka*) being born of Gaurī. Thus it is said: "O Goddess, mica is your seed, while mercury is my seed;
the union of these two, O Goddess, destroys death and poverty."
This which has been said is too little.

It is heard in the *Rameśvara-siddhānta* that among gods, daityas, sages, humans, and others, many have resorted to divine bodies through the power of *rasa* and attained liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*): "Certain gods, such as Maheśa and others; daityas, headed by Śukra (Kāvya);
sages, such as the Bālakhilyas and others; and kings, such as Someśvara and others."
Govinda Bhagavatpādācārya, Govindanāyaka,
Carvaṭi, Kapila, Vyāli, Kāpāli, and Kandalāyana.
Indeed, these and many other perfected ones wander as those liberated while living,
having attained bodies composed of rasa and being skilled in discourse concerning that very essence.
This very meaning was elaborated by the Supreme Lord to the Supreme Goddess: "O Mistress of the Gods, the maintenance of the body is attained through the yoga of action (karmayoga).
This yoga of action is traditionally taught to be twofold: alchemy (rasa) and breath-control (pavana)."
O Bhairavī, mercury, when swooned, removes diseases; when dead, it restores life itself;
and when bound, it grants the power of moving through the sky, as does the vital air (vāyu).
The nature of the "mūrchita" (coagulated) state has been described: having abandoned its intense volatility, the mercury (sūta) becomes multicolored;
that in which such a characteristic is observed is indeed called "mūrchita."
One in whom moisture, density, radiance, weight,
and mobility are not observed— know him to be a dead embryo.
Elsewhere, the nature of the bound [mercury] has also been stated: "Unbroken, easily fusible, brilliant, pure, and heavy;
its bursting upon being returned [to the crucible] is the characteristic of bound mercury.

Now, one might ask: "Once the creation of Hara and Gaurī is accomplished, it is possible to establish the stability of the *piṇḍa* (the alchemical body); but how is that very accomplishment achieved? To this we say: No.
Because that [attainment] arises through the power of the eighteen purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*).

As it was said by the Teachers: "In the procedure for its accomplishment, the wise person must first diligently understand the eighteen purificatory rites, which are rendered stainless by each respective rite."
And those operations have been described: sweating, rubbing, fainting, fixing, falling, arresting, and restraining;
inflaming, moving, the measure of the morsel, then digesting, covering;
internal liquefaction, external liquefaction, fluxing, coloring, and purifying.
Transference, piercing, and consumption—thus the alchemical work on mercury consists of eighteen types.

The detailed elaboration of this [topic] has been set forth by ancient teachers such as the venerable teacher Govinda Bhagavatpāda and the lord Sarvajña Rāmeśvara Bhaṭṭāraka; therefore, it is omitted here for fear of excessive length.

Nor should it be thought that the science of mercury (rasa-śāstra) is intended solely for the purpose of alchemy (dhātu-vāda), since its supreme purpose is liberation itself, achieved through the transmutation of the body (deha-vedha).
As it is said in the Rasārṇava: "O Lord, you have described to me the piercing of metals;
now explain that piercing of the body by which the state of a sky-walker (khecarī) may be attained."
Just as it is with metal, so should the elixir (sūtaka) be applied to the body by the virtuous;
O Goddess, it produces an identical conviction regarding both the body and the metal.
First one should test it on iron, and afterwards one should apply it to the body.

If it is objected: "Since liberation is established simply through the manifestation of the Supreme Reality whose nature is *sat*, *cit*, and *ānanda*, what is the use of this effort to produce a divine body?"—this is a mere trifle. For as long as an undecaying body is not obtained, that [liberation] cannot be realized. As it is said in the *Rasahṛdaya*: "Cidānanda, in whom all manifold conceptual constructions have dissolved and who is intended throughout all the paths..."
What can it do for the multitude of living beings whose bodies are insentient, even though it is manifest?
(Ra-hṛ 1.20) Thus it is said:
that which is worn out by old age, clearly afflicted by the sufferings of cough, asthma, and the like,
and unfit for meditative absorption because the activity of the intellect and the senses is obstructed.
Thus [ends the verse] (Ra0 Hṛ0 1.29).
How can a mortal man— first a youth of sixteen years, addicted to relishing the flavors of sense-objects,
and later an old man whose discernment has departed— attain liberation?

If it be objected: "Is it not the case that 'jīvatva' (the state of being a living soul) means being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), while 'muktatva' (the state of liberation) is its opposite? And thus, how can it be logically possible for these two mutually contradictory states to have a single substratum?"—this objection is untenable.
Because conceptual construction is untenable.
Liberation is indeed accepted by all the founders of philosophical systems;
does it, then, fall within the category of the knowable or not?
In the latter case, it would be like the horn of a hare;
in the former case, life cannot be discarded,
because consciousness is impossible for one who is not alive.

Thus it is stated in the *Raseśvarasiddhānta*: "The liberation of the individual soul is declared [to occur] through the path measured by the six metals; otherwise, it does not occur, especially among those who rely on various logical arguments within the doctrines of other systems of authority."
Know that this knower and the knowable are accepted in all tantras;
one who does not live will not know the knowable, and therefore life itself truly exists.
Nor should it be thought that this is something never before seen;

for according to the followers of Viṣṇusvāmin, the eternity of the body of Nṛpañcāsya is established. As it is said in the *Sākārasiddhi*: "The singular form which is being, consciousness, eternal, innate, inconceivable, perfect bliss..."
I salute Nṛpañcāsya, who is esteemed by Śrī Viṣṇusvāmin.

"Now, this [being] which appears as having parts and possessing form—this body of the Man-Lion—is not consistent with being real," and so forth; preceded by such objections, there is the direct perception of Sanaka and others, as well as the Śruti text, "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 3.14), and: "That wonderful child, lotus-eyed, four-armed, bearing weapons such as the conch and mace..."

"By the three means of valid cognition established through the characteristics of the Purāṇas, such as *Bhāgavata* 10.3.9, how could the body of the lion-faced [Lord] be non-existent? Thus have the qualifiers beginning with "existent" (*sat*) been propounded by Śrīkāntamiśra and others, whose inner hearts were transformed by the feet of Viṣṇusvāmin.
Therefore, the eternality of the body desired by us is not something entirely unseen; this must be accepted by persons who desire the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
For this very reason it has been said: "It is the abode of sciences and the root of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation."
What other supreme good is there than this alone: leaving behind the body, which is subject to decay and death?
And it is the Lord of Mercury alone that possesses the power to render one free from old age and death;
thus it is said: "This unique King of Mercury makes the body free from old age and death."
How can the majesty of rasa be described?
Even by seeing, touching, and so forth, a great fruit is obtained.
As it is said in the Rasārṇava: "From seeing, from touching, from eating, and even from remembering it..."
Through worship and the gift of mercury, a sixfold fruit is seen.
"Whatever signs there may be on earth, such as the Lingas made of wood and so forth—by seeing those, whatever merit is obtained, that same merit is obtained from seeing the Rasa-Linga," and so on.
Elsewhere also: "Through the worship of the Rasa-Linga, Śiva [is attained] more than through all the Lingas of Kāśī and other places."
That by which it is attained is the Liṅga, which bestows enjoyment, health, and immortality.

The sin resulting from the disparagement of the tongue has also been shown: "If, through negligence, a wise person should hear this disparagement of the tongue, he should immediately abandon the slanderer, who is filled with inauspiciousness by that very act of calumny."

Therefore, by the method we have described, having attained a divine body through the power of yoga practice, the supreme goal of human existence is achieved when the ultimate reality (paratattva) is perceived. At that time: "That light consisting of consciousness, which shines upon the world like fire, lightning, and the sun, situated between the two eyebrows, unfolds for those of meritorious vision."
The object of knowledge is the supreme light, whose nature is non-conceptual and whose sole essence is ultimate bliss;
it is peaceful, free from all afflictions, and to be realized by oneself.
Fixing the mind upon that [Self], beholding the entire world as radiant and consisting of consciousness,
one whose bonds of karma are destroyed attains the state of Brahman even here on earth.
And the Śruti says: "He is indeed rasa; for only by attaining rasa does one become blissful" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7.1).
Thus, it is established that rasa alone is the means for crossing over the burden of the misery of worldly wretchedness.

And thus, there is a verse establishing the similarity of rasa with the Supreme Brahman: "He who is attainable by those whose minds are intent on not casting off their outer covering, yet who, once endowed with that very [covering], sports with it while the supreme Vaiśvānara remains awake."
If known, it does not cause further experience; it shines by itself from itself.
May that mercury protect you from the fear of the miserable cycle of worldly existence, for it is like Brahman.
Now, the Aulūkya system. ||10||

In this world, indeed, every discerning person, desiring to abandon suffering— which is established by the self-awareness of all beings as being inherently disagreeable— and seeking the means to abandon it, recognizes the direct realization of the Supreme Lord as that means:
"When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather,
only then will there be an end to suffering without knowing Śiva."
This is because of the authority of such a collection of scriptural statements.

Furthermore, the direct realization of the Supreme Lord is to be cultivated through hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). As it has been said: "By means of scripture, by inference, and by the power of the practice of meditation..."
By conceptualizing wisdom in three ways, one attains the supreme yoga.
In this context, reflection (manana) is dependent upon inference (anumāna);
inference is dependent upon the knowledge of pervasion (vyāpti);
and the knowledge of pervasion is dependent upon the discrimination of categories (padārtha-viveka).
Therefore, the six categories were established by the venerable Kaṇabhakṣa in the *Daśalakṣaṇī* beginning with "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma" (*Kaṇāda-sūtra* 1.1.1).

Among those, in the first chapter—which consists of two daily lessons—the exposition of all the categories as they are inherent [in reality] was carried out. Even there, in the first daily lesson, the definition of that which possesses a genus (*jāti*) was provided.
In the second daily lesson (āhnika), there is the definition of the specific universal (jāti-viśeṣa).
In the second chapter, which consists of two daily lessons, there is the definition of substance (dravya).
Therein, the first daily lesson contains the definition of the specific elements (bhūta-viśeṣa).
In the second [chapter], there is the exposition of space and time.
In the third, which consists of two daily lessons (āhnika), there is the definition of the self (ātman) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
therein, the definition of the self occurs in the first [lesson].
In the second [chapter], the definition of the internal organ is given.
In the fourth [chapter], which consists of two daily lessons (āhnika), there is an analysis of the body and its requirements;
therein, in the first [lesson], the analysis of those requirements is presented.

In the second [book], there is the analysis of the body; in the fifth [book], which consists of two daily lessons (āhnika), there is the exposition of action (karma). Even therein, in the first [lesson], there is the consideration of action related to the body, and in the second, the consideration of mental action.
In the sixth [chapter], which consists of two daily lessons (āhnika), there is an exposition of the Vedic duties (śrauta-dharma).
Therein, in the first [lesson], there is a discernment of the rules regarding giving and receiving;
in the second, there is an exposition of the duties appropriate for the four stages of life (cāturāśramya).
In that seventh [chapter], there is the exposition of the inherence of qualities;
therein, in the first [section], there is the exposition of qualities independent of cognition,
and in the second, the exposition of qualities dependent upon it, as well as the exposition of inherence.
In the eighth [chapter], there is an investigation of non-conceptual and conceptual perception as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
In the ninth, there is the exposition of specific types of intellect (*buddhi*). In the tenth, there is the exposition of the divisions of inference (*anumāna*).
"In this regard, the operation of this treatise is threefold: enumeration (*uddeśa*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), and critical examination (*parīkṣā*)" (Vātsyāyana 1.1.1).
Now, if it is asked, "Since there are four types when considering the divisions, why has it been stated that there are only three?", do not think so.
Since a specific definition (*viśeṣa*) consists in the form of a brief enumeration (*uddeśa*), it is included within that very enumeration itself.
In this regard, "substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—these are the six categories" constitutes the enumeration.
What is the reason for the fixed order here? It is said: substance is enumerated first because it is the primary [category], being the locus of all other categories.

Immediately after that, [the category of] quality (guṇa), which resides in all substances by virtue of the limiting condition (upādhi) of being a quality; following that, action (karman), due to its similarity in possessing a universal (sāmānyavatva);
and finally, the universal (sāmānya), which resides in those three.
Immediately after that comes the particularity (*viśeṣa*), which is the substratum of inherence;
and at the end remains inherence (*samavāya*).
Now, if it is asked, "How can it be said that there are only six categories, since non-existence (*abhāva*) also exists?", do not speak thus.

Because it is intended that there are exactly six [categories], since they are objects of a cognition that does not delineate the meaning of a negative particle (*nañ*) and because they are positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*).
Even so, how is the restriction "exactly six" justified? Because no alternative is possible:
is the object to be excluded by the restriction already known through valid cognition (*pramita*), or not?
If it is already established as a category, how can it be denied? If it is not established, how much less so? For no discerning person would strive to deny the existence of a mouse's horn.
Therefore, since this is logically untenable, there can be no such restrictive rule—if you say this, do not speak thus.

For we observe the denial of "existence" in darkness and the like when they are cognized as the seventh category, and the denial of "being the seventh category" in power (*śakti*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), and the like when they are cognized as existing entities. Thus, enough of this prolixity.
In that context, the definition of the triad beginning with substance (dravya) is their respective universals (jāti), such as substanceness (dravyatva).
Substancesness is defined as a universal that is co-inherent in ether and a lotus, while being eternal and not co-inherent in odor.

Qualitiesness (guṇatva) is defined as a universal directly pervaded by existence (sattā) which is co-inherent in something distinct from both non-inherent causes and that which is not co-inherent in an inherent cause.
Action-ness (*karmatva*) is a genus directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*), accompanied by the property of not being eternally inherent.
A universal (*sāmānya*), however, is that which is devoid of being the counter-positive of destruction and is inherent in many.
A particular (*viśeṣa*), on the other hand, is that which is inherent and devoid of any universal that is opposed to mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Inherence, moreover, is a relation devoid of inherence; thus the definitions of the six categories are established.
Substance is of nine kinds: earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind.
Among these, the definition of the four beginning with earth is the genus "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva) and so forth.

Earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is the genus directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) and co-inherent with color produced by baking (*pākajarūpa*). Water-ness (*aptva*) is the generality (*sāmānya*) that is inherent in rivers and oceans while not being inherent in fire. Fire-ness (*tejastva*) is the generality that is inherent in the moon and gold while not being inherent in water.
The nature of air (*vāyutva*) is a genus directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) and inherent in the sense organ of touch (*tvagindriya*).

Since ether (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), and space (*diś*) each possess only oneness, there is no subordinate genus (*aparajāti*) in them; therefore, they have three technical designations (*paribhāṣikī-saṃjñā*): ether, time, and space.
Ether is the substratum of particularity (*viśeṣa*) which coexists with a produced specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that is not produced by conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Time is that which, being all-pervasive, is the substratum of the non-inherent cause of "priority" (paratva) that does not reside in space.
Space is that which, while not being time, possesses no specific qualities and is all-pervasive.
Selfhood and mindness belong respectively to the self and the internal organ.

Selfhood (*ātmatva*) is a subordinate genus of substance (*dravyatvāparajāti*) inherent in that which is incorporeal (*amūrta*). Mindness (*manastva*) is a subordinate genus of substance inherent in atoms (*aṇu*) that lack the nature of being an inherent cause of a substance. The qualities are twenty-four in number: seventeen explicitly mentioned—color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort—and seven implied by the word "and" (*ca*), namely heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and sound. Thus, there are twenty-four qualities.
In this context, the definition for everything from "form" (rūpa) up to "sound" (śabda) is their respective universals (jāti), such as "form-ness" (rūpatva).

That which is called "form-ness" is a universal subordinate to "quality-ness" (guṇatva) that inheres in blue [and other colors]. Following this same method, the definitions of the remaining [categories] are to be understood.
Action is of five kinds,
distinguished as throwing upward, throwing downward, contraction, expansion, and locomotion. Whirling, evacuation, and so forth are included within locomotion itself.
The definition of throwing upwards (*utkṣepaṇa*) and the other [motions] is their respective universals (*jāti*), such as "throwing-upward-ness" (*utkṣepaṇatva*).
Among these, "throwing-upward-ness" is a subordinate universal (*apara-jāti*) residing in a motion that inheres in the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of conjunction with an upward location.
In the same manner, the definitions of "throwing-downward-ness" (*apakṣepaṇatva*) and the others should be formulated.
Generality is of two kinds: the higher and the lower. The higher is existence (*sattā*), which inheres in substances, qualities, and actions. The lower is substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
The definition of that [separation] has already been stated.
Because particulars are infinite and inherence is unitary, separation is not possible. And its definition has already been explained.
Those whose intellect does not falter regarding duality, the production of qualities from heating, and disjunction produced by disjunction— they indeed know him as a Vaiśeṣika.
Because of the existence of this traditional saying, the manner in which duality and so forth arise is demonstrated.
In that process, first there is the contact between the sense organ and the object (1).
From that arises the cognition of the generality of oneness (2).
Then there is the enumerative cognition (3). Then follows the production of duality (4).
Then follows the cognition of the generality "duality-ness" (5).
From that arises the cognition of the quality of duality (6).
From that arises the cognition "two substances" (7).
From that arises a mental impression (saṃskāra) (8).

Regarding this, it is said: First, through the operation of sense-object contact, there arises a cognition of the universal "oneness" which has oneness as its object; from that, the cognition of both [substances] as possessing oneness arises, and from that, duality is produced.

Subsequently, there is the cognition of the nature of duality (dvitvatva); after that cognition of duality, the cognition "two substances" arises. This is declared to be the process of the emergence of duality.

What is the proof for the fact that duality and so forth are produced by enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)? On this point, the Teachers say: Enumerative cognition must be the producer of duality and so forth, because it follows the variations of those qualities when no other manifestation is possible, just as conjunction [is the cause] with respect to sound.

We, however, say: duality and so forth are not manifested by an eternal cognition whose object is a pair of unities, because they are qualities residing in multiple substrata, like separateness (*pṛthaktva*) and other such qualities.

The sequence of their cessation is now described: the cessation of the cognition of the generality of unity occurs simultaneously with the production of duality, following from the cognition of dependence (*apekṣābuddhi*).
The cessation of the cognition of dependence occurs at the same time as the cognition of the quality of duality, following from the cognition of the generality of duality (*dvitvatva*).

The destruction of duality occurs simultaneously with the cessation of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). The destruction of the cognition of the quality occurs simultaneously with the production of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) following the cognition of the substance. The destruction of the cognition of the substance follows immediately after that, by means of the mental impression.
And thus there are summary verses: "In the beginning, the cognition of the universal 'oneness' is destroyed by the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*);
subsequently, it [the universal] is destroyed along with the arising of duality by the cognition of that universal."
Then, at the time of the cognition of the quality called duality,
that duality ceases due to the destruction of the relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), occurring simultaneously with the arising of the cognition of the substance.
"The cognition of quality [is destroyed] by the cognition of substance from the time of the arising of the latent impression (saṃskāra);
and the cognition of substance [is destroyed] by the latent impression—this is considered the sequence of destruction.

Regarding the proof for the fact that one cognition is destroyed by a subsequent cognition and that it is also destroyed by the latent impression: "The cognitions under dispute are destroyed by each successive effect, because they are momentary, pervasive, and specific qualities, like sound."

In some cases, the cessation of duality occurs precisely through the cessation of its substratum, which happens simultaneously with the action that produces the disjunction opposing the conjunction that initiates the substance; this is due to the consideration of the generality of oneness (*ekatva-sāmānya*).

In other cases, it is due to both [the cessation of the substratum and the cessation of the cause], because the consideration of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) occurs simultaneously with the action. This is the summary.
It should be understood that "relative cognition" refers to a cognition that is the counter-positive of the destruction that destroys [duality].

Now, in response to the inquiry as to how many moments it takes for another dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) to arise and possess color and other qualities following the destruction of a [previous] dyad, the process of production is described: the destruction of the dyad occurs through a sequence beginning with impulsion (*nodana*).
When the dyad has been destroyed, the cessation of blackness and other qualities occurs in the atom due to its conjunction with fire.
Once blackness and the others have ceased, the production of redness and other qualities occurs again in that same atom due to a further conjunction with fire.
When passion and other qualities have arisen, due to the conjunction of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) with the self, motion arises in the atom for the purpose of initiating a substance;
likewise, there is disjunction from the previous location. Through that disjunction, the conjunction with the previous location ceases.
When that [destruction] has occurred, a conjunction arises with another atom;
from the two conjoined atoms, a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is produced;
and once the dyad has been produced, the qualities of the effect, such as color and so forth, arise from the qualities of the cause and other factors—thus, in due order, there are nine moments.
Other modes, such as the ten-moment theory (*daśakṣaṇa*) and so forth, are not elaborated here for fear of prolixity.
Thus, the process of baking in the grain (*pīlupāka*) and the process of baking in the pot (*piṭharapāka*) are the two theories accepted by the intellect of the Naiyāyikas.
Disjunction produced by disjunction (*vibhāgajavibhāga*) is of two kinds: that produced by the disjunction of the cause alone, and that produced by the disjunction of the cause and the non-cause.

Regarding this, the first [point] is stated: when an action arises in a cause that is pervaded by its effect, it brings about disjunction from another constituent part, but not disjunction from a location such as space.
However, when there is disjunction from a location such as space, there is no disjunction from another constituent part; such is the established rule.

This is because an action’s non-production of disjunction from space is never observed to deviate—just as smoke is never observed to deviate from the class of fires—since its production of disjunction is invariably concomitant with its opposition to the conjunction that initiates a substance.
Then, the action in the part produces disjunction only from another part, not from a location such as space.
From that disjunction follows the cessation of the conjunction that initiates the substance.
Then, by the principle that "in the absence of the cause, there is the absence of the effect," there occurs the cessation of the [composite] part.

When the whole has ceased to exist, the disjunction residing in its two constituent parts, depending on the time characterized by the destruction of the effect or on an independent part, initiates a disjunction of that very part possessing action from the point of space conjoined with the effect; it does not do so for a part devoid of action, because of the absence of a cause. However, the second [type of disjunction], namely the action produced in the hand, while effecting a disjunction from another part, initiates disjunctions from points of space such as the ether.

Those disjunctions resulting from causes and non-causes, depending upon the direction toward which the action is oriented for the commencement of an effect, initiate the distinction between what is produced and what is not produced.
For example, from the disjunction of the hand and space, there arises the disjunction of the body and space;
yet this latter is not the effect of the action of the body itself.
For at that time, it (the hand) is inactive;
nor can it be the effect of the action of the hand, because it is impossible for an action residing in a different substratum to be the agent of disjunction.
Therefore, by the method of exhaustion, one must accept that its cause is the disjunction between the cause and the non-cause.
As for the claim that "the existence [of darkness] and so forth is denied," that is inconsistent,
because a fourfold dispute arises in that regard. To explain:
The Bhāṭṭas and the Vedāntins declare that darkness is a substance (dravya).
Śrīdhara Ācārya says it is a superimposed blue color (nīlarūpa).
A certain faction of the Prābhākaras maintains that it is the absence of light and cognition (ālokajñānābhāva).
If it is argued that the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that darkness is the absence of light— that position is untenable regarding its being a substance (*dravya*),
because the conceptual alternatives do not hold.
For if this thing called "darkness" were a substance, it would have to be either one of the [nine] substances beginning with earth, or something else entirely.
Not the first,
because it would entail that [the substance] possesses as many qualities as there are qualities of that [quality] within which it is included.
Not the second.
Since that [darkness] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), it is impossible for it to possess substantiality (*dravyatva*), and consequently, its being a distinct substance is all the more impossible.
If it is objected: "How can darkness, which is perceived as dark as the *tamāla* tree, be devoid of qualities?"—that is without merit;
for blue color, which is pervaded by [the presence of] odor and other qualities, ceases when those [qualities] cease.

If it is asked, "What then is the status of the perception 'darkness is blue'?"—the answer is that it is merely an illusion, just like the notion that "the sky is blue. Enough of this burdening of the ancients with such arguments!
For this very reason, darkness is not a superimposed form, because a superimposition is impossible without the cognition of an underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Furthermore, the capacity of the eye to apprehend form is not observed when it is deprived of the assistance of external light;
nor is this cognition non-visual,
because its conformity to the visual organ is established as being otherwise inexplicable.
For this very reason, darkness is not the absence of light and knowledge;

for since it is a rule that an absence is perceived by the same sense organ that perceives its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), it would follow [absurdly] that it must be perceived by the mind (*mānasa*).
Therefore, darkness is simply the absence of light.
Nor is it correct to argue that non-existence (*abhāva*) cannot be established by being cognizable through an optative suffix (*vidhipratyaya*),
for this would lead to fallacious exceptions in cases such as dissolution (*pralaya*), destruction (*vināśa*), and the end (*avasāna*).
Furthermore, it is impossible to justify the superimposition of the attributes of an entity (*bhāvadharma*) onto non-existence.
For it is observed that pleasure is superimposed upon the absence of pain, and the notion of "separation" is attributed to the absence of conjunction.

Furthermore, one should not maintain that the absence of light—like the absence of a jar or other objects—is an absence of something possessing color (rūpavat), and thus must be an object of cognition produced by the eye depending on light.

According to the logical principle that "the eye depends on whatever [auxiliary] it requires for the apprehension of a positive entity, it depends on that same auxiliary even for the apprehension of the absence of that entity," there is no requirement for light in the apprehension of light itself; consequently, there is likewise no requirement for it in the apprehension of its absence.
Nor is there a necessity for the apprehension of a locus;
for we do not accept that the apprehension of a locus is necessarily required for the cognition of non-existence.
Otherwise, the destruction of sound in such cases as "the clamor has ceased" would not be perceptible—this being merely the unfounded assertion of another.
Intending all this, the Blessed Kaṇāda composed the aphorism: "Darkness is non-existence, because it differs from the production of substance, quality, and action" (Kaṇāda Sūtra 5.2.19).

Non-existence, which is cognized through the means of knowledge consisting of negation, is now described as the seventh category. And that [non-existence] is non-inherence, provided it is not itself inherence.

Briefly, it is of two kinds, distinguished as relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Relational non-existence is also threefold, distinguished as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), destructive non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Among these, antecedent non-existence is that which is impermanent and beginningless.
Destruction is that which possesses origination but lacks annihilation.
Absolute non-existence is a negation that has a counter-positive and a locus.
Mutual non-existence is a negation that is distinct from absolute non-existence and is without temporal limit.
If it is argued that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is indeed simply mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), alas, this is a delusion even on the royal highway!
For mutual non-existence is a negation whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is identity (*tādātmya*).
As in: "A jar is not identical with a cloth."
Absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) is a negation whose counter-correlative is a relation;
for example, "there is no connection with color in air.
Nor should it be suspected that this [non-existence] has no utility for human goals.
Because it has the nature of *niḥśreyasa*, which is another synonym for the absolute eradication of suffering, it constitutes the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
Now follows the system of Akṣapāda. 11.

It has been established even in the sister system (*samānatantre*) that the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), characterized by the absolute cessation of suffering, arises from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

Thus says the author of the Sūtras: "From the knowledge of reality—beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*)—there is the attainment of the supreme good.
This is the first sūtra of the Nyāya-śāstra.

The Nyāya-śāstra consists of five chapters (*adhyāyas*), each of which contains two daily lessons (*āhnikas*). In the first daily lesson of the first chapter, the venerable Gautama established the definitions of the nine categories (*padārthas*) beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); in the second, he provided the definitions for the seven categories beginning with formal debate (*vāda*).
In the first [section] of the second [book], there is an examination of doubt and the refutation of the suspicion that the four means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) lack authority.
In the second [section], there is a determination of the subsumption of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and so forth.
In the first [section] of the third [book], there is an examination of the self, the body, the sense organs, and their objects.
In the second [section], there is an examination of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*).

In the first part of the fourth [section], there is an examination of activity (*pravṛtti*), defects (*doṣa*), rebirth (*pretyabhāva*), fruit (*phala*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and liberation (*apavarga*).
In the second part, there is a determination of the causality of defects and an examination of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth.
In the first [section] of the fifth [chapter], there is the determination of the different types of *jāti* (futile rejoinders);
in the second, there is the determination of the different types of *nigrahasthāna* (points of defeat).

According to the principle that "the establishment of the object of knowledge (*meyasiddhi*) is dependent upon the means of knowledge (*māna*"), since the definition must be stated in accordance with the enumeration, the definition of *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition), which was enumerated first, is stated first: *Pramāṇa* is that which, while not being distinct from the locus of the proof (*sādhana*), is pervaded by valid cognition (*pramā*).
In this way, the authority of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), established as a tenet within our own specific system (*pratitantrasiddhānta*), is summarized.
As the author of the Sūtras stated: "And its authority is like the authority of the Mantras and Āyurveda, because of the authority of the reliable person (*āpta*)" (Gauḍapāda’s Nyāyasūtra 2.1.67).

Likewise, the teacher Udayana, whose fame is world-renowned and who has seen the further shore of the ocean of the Nyāya system, also states in the fourth chapter of the *Nyāyakusumāñjali*: "Valid cognition (*miti*) is correct apprehension; and the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtā*) is the possession of that [valid cognition]."
Therefore, in the system of Gautama, validity consists in the exclusion of non-connection [with the object].
(Nyāyakuṃjalatā 4/5). Thus:

[it is] a direct perception, eternally associated [with its object], existing independently of other means, an experience of a real object in which the entire sequence of things to be expressed is contained;
it is one from which the husks of doubt have fallen away due to the removal of defects caused by partial vision.
"What need have I for others who are stained by the opening and closing of their own doubts? Śiva alone is my authority. (Nyāyakuṃjalisaurabha 4.6).
That [means of valid cognition] is fourfold, distinguished as perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony. That which appears in valid cognition is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
And that is of twelve kinds, distinguished as: self, body, sense-faculties, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation.
Doubt is knowledge that is non-definitive in nature.

It is threefold, distinguished by its characteristics as arising from common attributes, uncommon attributes, and conflicting testimony. That with respect to which persons act is purpose (*prayojana*).
That [example] is of two kinds, based on the distinction between the perceived and the unperceived.
An example is the locus for the apprehension of pervasion;
it is of two kinds, based on the distinction between similarity and dissimilarity.

A tenet (*siddhānta*) is an object accepted as being authoritative. It is fourfold, distinguished as: universal (*sarvatantra*), specific (*pratitantra*), contextual (*adhikaraṇa*), and implied (*abhyupagama*).
A member (*avayava*) is a single part of the statement of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
It is fivefold, due to the distinction between the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāhara�aṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*).
Hypothetical reasoning (*tarka*) is the attribution of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) based on the attribution of the pervaded (*vyāpya*);
it is of eleven kinds.

[The types of invalidity] differ due to contradiction, self-dependence, mutual dependence, circularity, infinite regress, counteracting assumptions, parsimony of assumption, prolixity of assumption, general rule, exception, and difference of genus.
Valid cognition (*pramiti*), which is synonymous with experience of an object as it truly is, is a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*).
It is of four kinds.
[Knowledge] is divided into perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony. *Vāda* (debate) is a specific type of discussion whose fruit is the determination of truth.
*Jalpa* (wrangling) is a discussion between those seeking victory, wherein both parties employ means of proof.

Vitaṇḍā (cavil) is a specific type of debate that lacks the establishment of one's own position. Debate (*kathā*) is defined as the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis by the proponent and the opponent respectively.
A fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is that which is intended as a reason but is not actually a valid reason (*asādhaka*).
It is of five kinds, distinguished by the fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa) known as savyabhicāra, viruddha, prakaraṇasama, sādhyasama, and atītakāla.
Quibble (chala) is a refutation based on a perversion of the meaning of words;
it is of three types.
Based on the distinctions of primary denotation (*abhidhāna*), intention (*tātparya*), metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), and the transposition of functions (*vṛttivyatyaya*),
a rejoinder that contradicts itself is a *jāti*.
It is of twenty-four kinds.

It is divided into the following types: *sādharmyasama* (balancing the similarity), *vaidharmyasama* (balancing the dissimilarity), *utkarṣasama* (balancing the addition), *apakarṣasama* (balancing the subtraction), *varṇyasama* (balancing the subject of proof), *avarṇyasama* (balancing the non-subject of proof), *vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative), *sādhyasama* (balancing the probandum), *prāptisama* (balancing the attainment), *aprāptisama* (balancing the non-attainment), *prasangasama* (balancing the consequence), *pratidṛṣṭāntasama* (balancing the counter-example), *anutpattisama* (balancing the non-arising), *saṃśayasama* (balancing the doubt), *prakaraṇasama* (balancing the inquiry), *hetusama* (balancing the cause), *arthāpattisama* (balancing the implication), *aviśeṣasama* (balancing the lack of distinction), *upapattisama* (balancing the justification), *upalabdhisama* (balancing the perception), *anupalabdhisama* (balancing the non-perception), *nityasama* (balancing the eternal), *anityasama* (balancing the non-eternal), and *kāryasama* (balancing the effect).
A point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is a ground for failure;
it is of twenty-two kinds.

[The points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)] are divided into: abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*), shifting the proposition (*pratijñāntara*), contradiction of the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*), renouncing the proposition (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*), shifting the reason (*hetvantara*), shifting the subject matter (*arthāntara*), the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), the incoherent (*apārthaka*), the mistimed (*aprāptakāla*), the deficient (*nyūna*), the redundant (*adhika*), the repetitive (*punarukta*), failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), evasion (*vikṣepa*), admission of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*), neglecting to censure when one should (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), censuring when one should not (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), deviating from one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), and the various fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
Although the specific distinctions among all these sub-categories are clearly explained in that treatise, they are not presented here for fear of excessive prolixity.

[Objection: But if sixteen categories, beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are being expounded, how is this designated as "Nyāya-śāstra" (the Science of Logic)? [Response: True. Nevertheless, designations occur by way of what is unique [to a thing], according to the principle that "designations are based on what is distinctive. Since Nyāya—which is synonymous with *parārthānumāna* (inference for others)—is the most important because it favors all branches of knowledge and serves as the instrument for the performance of all ritual actions, such a designation is appropriate.
Thus it was stated by the Omniscient One: "This is the supreme Nyāya, because it provides instruction to a person who is in disagreement [with the truth]."

And likewise: "Because it is the cause of engagement" (*Gauṇasūtravārtika* 1.1.1). And by Pakṣilasvāmin: "This very science of *Ānvīkṣikī*, being divided into categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—[is] the lamp of all sciences, the means for all actions, and the foundation of all duties; thus it has been examined in the enumeration of sciences."
(Nyāyasūtra-bhāṣya 1.1.1).
Now, it has been stated that "from the knowledge of reality, the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) arises.
In this regard, is the supreme good accomplished immediately after the knowledge of reality? No, it is said.

However, from the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), upon the successive disappearance of false knowledge (mithyājñāna), defects (doṣa), activity (pravṛtti), birth (janma), and suffering (duḥkha), there follows the disappearance of each preceding member, resulting in liberation (apavarga).
In this context, false knowledge is the notion of a self with regard to what is not the self, such as the body and so forth;
it is attachment toward that which is favorable to such [notions].
Aversion arises toward things that are contrary to that [desire].
In reality, however, there exists no object whatsoever that is truly either contrary to or favorable to the self.

Furthermore, because passion and the other afflictions are mutually interconnected, the deluded person becomes passionate; being passionate, he becomes deluded; being deluded, he becomes angry; and being angry, he becomes deluded.
Then, impelled by those defects, a living being commits with the body prohibited acts such as violence and theft;
with speech, falsehood and so forth;
and with the mind, malice toward others and so forth.
This engagement in the form of evil is unrighteousness (adharma).
By means of the body, there are praiseworthy acts such as giving, protecting others, and so forth;
by means of speech, there are beneficial and truthful words, and so forth.
The desire to kill and so forth by means of the mind—
this is activity in the form of merit, which is dharma.
This is the twofold activity.
From that [birth] follows a new manifestation of the body and so forth, which is either praiseworthy or censurable according to its own nature.
When that exists, there arises suffering, which consists of affliction because it is experienced as disagreeable.
For no one experiences suffering unless they have first engaged in activity.

These factors beginning with false knowledge and ending with suffering, proceeding without interruption, constitute the meaning of the term *saṃsāra* and continue endlessly like the wheel of a water-pot.

When a certain preeminent person, through the ripening of previously performed merit and by means of a teacher’s instruction, perceives all this as a locus of suffering and as connected with suffering, he then understands it all as something to be abandoned.
Thereupon, he desires to remove its cause, namely ignorance and the rest.
And the means for its cessation is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
For one who meditates upon the objects of knowledge divided into four categories, there arises the knowledge of reality, which is designated by the term "right vision" (*samyagdarśana*).
From the knowledge of reality, false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) departs.
Upon the disappearance of false knowledge, the defects disappear; upon the disappearance of the defects, activity ceases; upon the cessation of activity, birth ceases.
When birth ceases, suffering is absolutely eliminated.
This absolute cessation of suffering is liberation (apavarga).
The absoluteness of this cessation means that nothing of the same class as that which has been ceased ever arises there again.

And likewise, there is the aphorism of the Great Sage: "Upon the successive removal of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the removal of each subsequent one, resulting in liberation" (Gautama Sūtra 1.1.2).
Now, if it is objected: "The claim that liberation is the absolute cessation of suffering remains as elusive as trying to lick honey from the back of one's elbow;
how then can it be treated as an established fact?"—do not say so.

Since the principle that for all proponents of liberation there is an absolute cessation of suffering at the stage of final emancipation (*apavarga*) is established as a tenet common to all systems (*sarvatantra-siddhānta*), it constitutes the royal road (*ghaṇṭāpatha*). To illustrate: in the Madhyamaka school’s doctrine that liberation is the annihilation of the self (*ātmoccheda*), it is at least beyond dispute that there is an annihilation of suffering.
Now, if you should think that the self, like the body and so forth, must be annihilated because it is a cause of suffering—that is not tenable.
Because conceptual construction is untenable:
is the self intended as the continuum of cognition, or as something distinct from it? In the first case, there is no dispute;
for who indeed would act favorably or act unfavorably toward that? In the second case, if it were eternal, its cessation could not possibly be established.
If [the self] were impermanent, activity would be untenable;
furthermore, the impossibility of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is an additional refutation.
Indeed, no discerning person would strive for the total destruction of the self, which is dearer than everything else, on the grounds that "everything becomes dear for the sake of the self."
Indeed, every living being, while there exists a substratum (*dharmin*), conventionally designates it as "liberated.

However, in the doctrine of the Vijñānavādins, where they claim that the arising of stainless knowledge constitutes the "Great Awakening" upon the cessation of the substratum, there is both an absence of causal conditions and an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
For they maintain that the fourfold meditative cultivation (*bhāvanācatuṣṭaya*) is the intended cause [of that awakening].

Furthermore, under the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), since a single stable substratum is impossible, [the practice of meditation]—like the practice of jumping and so forth—is unable to produce clear supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāna*) because it has not attained excellence.

Moreover, if the stream of consciousness (*jñānasaṃtāna*) accompanied by afflictions (*sopaplava*) is the state of bondage and the one free from afflictions (*nirupaplava*) is liberation, then the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the statement "he who was bound is the very same one who is liberated" would not be tenable.
Even the path favored by the Jaina people—that liberation is the removal of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*)—is not inherently free from logical constraints.
My dear sir, being asked, please explain: what is the obscuration?
If you say it is dharma, adharma, and delusion—that is indeed acceptable.
Or, if you say the body itself is the obscuration—
And if it is argued that liberation is the soul’s perpetual upward movement upon the cessation of those [bonds], like a parrot released from its cage—then this must be asked:

Is this soul material (*mūrta*) or immaterial (*amūrta*)? In the first case, is it partless (*niravayava*) or with parts (*sāvayava*)? If it is partless, then being a material thing without parts, it would fall under the definition of an atom (*paramāṇu*); consequently, as a result of possessing the properties of an atom, the properties of the soul would necessarily be beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyatva*).

If [the self] were to possess parts, then by the force of the logical connection that "whatever possesses parts is impermanent," its impermanence would follow; consequently, the loss of what has been done (*kṛtapraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) would prevail without restraint. Furthermore, motion is impossible if it is formless (*amūrta*), because action, which consists of movement, is necessarily connected with having form (*mūrtatva*).
In the Cārvāka position as well—that dependence is bondage and independence is liberation—if independence consists in the cessation of suffering, there is no dispute.
If it consists in sovereignty, that is not desired by the discerning, because it is subject to degrees of excellence and is comparable to others.

Even in the Sāṃkhya doctrine, which states that liberation is the abiding of the self in its own nature upon the cessation of *prakṛti* through the realization of the distinction between *prakṛti* and the self, the destruction of suffering certainly exists.
It remains to be determined whether discriminative knowledge (vivekajñāna) has the person (puruṣa) as its locus or nature (prakṛti) as its locus.
In this regard, it cannot be said to have the person as its locus,
because that would result in the cessation of the person's state of immutable stability (kauṭasthya).
Nor can it have *prakṛti* as its substratum, because that [prakṛti] is insentient.
Furthermore, is *prakṛti* by nature active or by nature inactive? In the first case, there would be no liberation.
Because intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is indestructible;
in the second case, saṃsāra would cease at this very moment.
Even according to the views of Bhaṭṭa Sarvajña and others, who maintain that liberation is the manifestation of eternal, unsurpassed bliss, the cessation of suffering is nonetheless intended.
However, eternal happiness does not fall within the scope of the methods of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that scripture (*śruti*) is the authority for this, we say no;
for there is no room for such [scriptural claims] when [the object] is sublated by the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that such a state [of liberation] would apply even to a hollow space or a floating stone.
