If you object: "By abandoning the position that liberation is the manifestation of pleasure (sukha), and accepting instead that liberation is merely the cessation of pain (duḥkha-nivṛtti), you are like one who, afflicted by a loss of appetite for milk, develops a craving for fermented gruel (sauvīra)"—we disregard this statement of yours as falling into the camp of the dramatic art (nāṭaka). This is because pleasure, due to its being subject to degrees of excellence (sātiśayatva), its impermanence (sadṛkṣatva), its being beset by many adversaries, and its being exhausted by the pursuit of its means, is inseparable from pain; thus, like honey mixed with poison, it is relegated to the side of pain.

If you argue that this position is undesirable because, according to the maxim that "while one seeks to secure one thing, another falls away," pleasure must likewise be destroyed along with suffering, do not think so.

For in the pursuit of pleasure, there is an inevitable attachment to a multitude of means for suffering, which results in a state comparable to one who proceeds toward a red-hot iron ball thinking it to be gold.
To illustrate: among objects acquired through righteous means, how few are the fireflies of pleasure compared to how many are the storm-clouds of suffering!
But as for that which pertains to wealth acquired through unjust means, it is impossible even to contemplate what will happen;
may you, the best among the wise, understand this while remaining true to your own experience.

Therefore, by process of elimination, it is beyond reproach that the absolute cessation of suffering—the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—belongs to that preeminent person who, through the grace of the Supreme Lord, has realized the truth of the Self via the sequence beginning with hearing (*śravaṇa*).

Now, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the existence of God— is it perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*)? Perception does not apply here, because [God],
being devoid of form and other such qualities, is beyond the reach of the senses.
Nor is there inference,
because of the absence of a pervaded mark (liṅga). Nor is there scripture (āgama).
Because it cannot withstand critical analysis:
does [the means of knowledge] convey [an object] as eternal or as non-eternal? In the first case, there would be the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets;
in the second case, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence.
If it is argued that [proofs] such as analogy and the rest cannot be suspected [of error] because they have restricted objects,
and therefore God is like the horn of a hare— this does not produce any wonder in the minds of the wise.
The subject of dispute, such as the serpent-king Nāga, the ocean, and so forth, possesses a creator because it is an effect, like a pot. Nor is this reason unestablished,
for its establishment is easily achieved through the fact of its possessing constituent parts.
Now, what is this "having parts"? Is it the state of being conjoined with parts, or the state of inhering in parts? Not the first, because it would deviate in the case of space and so forth.
Not the second, because it would be inconclusive due to [the presence of] thread-ness and the like.
If you argue that this is therefore untenable, do not speak thus;

for it can be stated that "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*) is defined as "being a substance inhering [in others]," or because it is easy to infer its being an effect (*kāryatva*) by means of its intermediate magnitude (*avāntaramahattva*).
Nor is the reason contradictory,
because there is no pervasion by the opposite of the probandum;
nor is it inconclusive.
Nor is it "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), because no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) is perceived, since its occurrence is not observed anywhere other than in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Nor is there a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), because no such opposing argument is observed.
If it is argued: "The earth and so forth are without a creator, because they are not produced by a body, like the ether (*gagana*)," this is seen to be incapable of withstanding scrutiny.
For a young fawn cannot be a rival to a lion with a formidable throat;
since the mere fact of being unproduced (*ajanyatva*) is sufficient for the purpose, the qualification "of the body" (*śarīra-viśeṣaṇa*) is redundant.
If it is argued that "unproducedness alone is the probans"—no.
Because [the reason] is unestablished;
nor can the sprout of the suspicion that it is vitiated by an extraneous condition (upādhi) possibly arise,
because there exists a favorable logical argument (anukūlatarka).

If this [universe] were without an agent, there would be no effect either. It is beyond dispute that in this world there is no such thing as an effect that could come into being while disregarding the entire cycle of causal factors; and all such effects are delimited by a specific agent.

Agency (*kartṛtva*) is the state of being the substratum of knowledge, desire to act, and effort, characterized by being the instigator of all other causal factors while itself not being instigated by them.

Thus, the gross error [of yours] is that if agency were excluded, all the causal factors subsumed under it would also be excluded, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the production of an effect without a cause. This has been firmly established by the servant of Śaṅkara: "When the means of proof is accompanied by a favorable logical argument..."
Because the pervasion of the probandum is destroyed, there is no possibility of a limiting condition (upādhi) in the subject (pakṣa).

If it is argued that a host of counter-arguments (pratikūlatarka) such as "if God were the creator, He would have to possess a body" remains active, [we reply]: there is a contradiction (vyāghāta) between the proof and the non-proof of God.
This was stated by Udayana: "If scripture and the like are valid means of knowledge, there is no negation because of sublation;
but if they are fallacious, then that very same formidable 'unestablished locus' (āśrayāsiddhi) would arise."
(Nyāyakusumāñjali 3.5). Nor can a contradiction with specific particulars be suspected, because such a position is refuted by the dilemma of whether [the object] is known or unknown.
This might be the case:

for what purpose is the Supreme Lord’s engagement in the creation of the world—is it for his own sake or for the sake of others? Regarding the first alternative, is it for the attainment of something desired or for the avoidance of something undesired? It cannot be the first, because that is impossible for one who has already attained all desires.
For this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable;
in the case of the second, activity would be impossible.

Indeed, who could call one who exerts effort for the sake of another a "discerning person" (*prekṣāvān*)? If someone were to claim that activity is possible due to compassion (*karuṇā*), one would refute him as follows:
In that case, God would have created all living beings as happy alone,
and not as mired in suffering,
because that would contradict His compassion.
Compassion is indeed the desire to eliminate the suffering of others without regard for one's own interest.
Therefore, the creation of the world by God is not tenable.
As it has been said by Bhaṭṭācārya: "Not even a fool acts without aiming at some purpose."
For him who creates the universe, what indeed would not be accomplished?
To this it is replied:
O crest-jewel of nihilists, close your eyes—which have been stained by the impurity of envy—and reflect upon this:
activity indeed arises from compassion.
Nor does it follow that the creation would naturally consist of nothing but happiness;
for diversity is established by the specific ripening of the good and evil deeds performed by the living beings who are the objects of creation.
Furthermore, one should not suspect a violation of [the Lord's] sovereignty.
On the contrary, by the maxim that "one's own limb does not obstruct itself," that very [scripture] establishes [the point];
the scripture beginning with "Rudra is one alone, a second did not exist" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.8.6) is the authority therein.
If you say, "If this is so, then provide a remedy for the affliction of mutual dependence and contradiction," we reply: because such a charge does not arise.
Is a mutual dependence (parasparāśraya) suspected regarding their origination or regarding their cognition?
Not the first;
for although the origin of the scripture depends upon Īśvara, the Supreme Lord is eternal, and thus his origination is impossible.
Nor is it [the case] regarding its cognition;
for although the Supreme Lord's cognition is dependent upon scripture, that [scripture] is understood from other sources.
Nor is it [the case] regarding the cognition of His impermanence.
Because the impermanence of scripture is easily understood through its possession of qualities such as intensity and so forth.

Therefore, when the grace of the Lord is accomplished by virtue of the performance of those duties that bring about cessation, the desired goal is attained; thus all is clear. Now begins the system of Jaimini. 12.
Now, you have proclaimed that the accomplishment of one’s desired dharma occurs through the performance of dharma.
If it is asked, "What is the definition of dharma, and what is its means of valid cognition?"—it is said:
listen with attention; the answer to this question was demonstrated by the sage Jaimini in the earlier Mīmāṃsā.
That Mīmāṃsā consists of twelve chapters (dvādaśalakṣaṇī).

In the first chapter, there is the establishment of the authority of the collection of words—comprising injunctions (vidhi), explanatory passages (arthavāda), mantras, traditional law (smṛti), and names (nāmadheya).

In the second, the subject matter consists of introductory matters (upoddhāta), the differentiation of rituals (karmabheda), the refutation of [erroneous] authorities (pramāṇāpavāda), and the differentiation of performance (prayogabheda).

In the third [book], there is an investigation of contradictions involving *śruti*, *liṅga*, *vākya*, and so forth; of the acts of comprehension (*pratipatti-karma*); of those taught as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*); of the many principal acts that assist [the sacrifice] such as the *prayāja*s; and of the duties pertaining to the sacrificer (*yājamāna*).

In the fourth [book], there is an investigation of whether the principal act is the motivator (*prayojaka*) or not; of the fruit of the wooden ladle being made of *parṇa*-wood (*juhū-parṇatā*) and so forth; and of the inferior auxiliary elements (*jaghanyāṅga*) within the *Rājasūya*, such as gambling with dice (*akṣadyūta*) and so forth.

In the fifth [book], there is an investigation of the order established by *śruti* and other means, its specific variations, increase and decrease [of elements], and their relative strength and weakness.

In the sixth [section], there is an investigation into the qualified person (*adhikārī*), his duties (*taddharma*), substitutes for materials (*dravyapratinidhi*), the omission of purpose (*arthalopa*), expiation (*prāyaścitta*), the *sattra* sacrifice, what is to be given (*deya*), and the sacred fires (*vahni*).

In the seventh, there is an investigation into the extension of application (*atideśa*) based on direct scriptural statement (*vacana*), as well as the extension of application based on name (*nāma*) and indicative mark (*liṅga*).
In the eighth, there is an investigation into the extension of application and its exceptions (*apavāda*) based on clear and obscure, yet powerful, indicative marks (*liṅga*).

In the ninth [book], there is the commencement of the investigation into modification (*ūha*), the modification of *sāman* chants, the modification of mantras, and incidental discussions related thereto.

In the tenth, there is the investigation into sublation (*bādha*)—including its causes, the loss of the means (*dvāralopa*), detailed treatment, the reasons for sublation, the unity of purpose (*kāryaikatva*), combination (*samuccaya*), and miscellaneous matters concerning the *graha* vessels and *sāman* chants.

In the eleventh, there is the consideration of the introduction to the *tantra* (the common application), the *tantrāvāpa* (the insertion of the common), the expansion of the *tantra*, and the expansion of the *āvāpa*.
In the twelfth [chapter], there is an investigation into the application (*prasaṅga*), the determination of the *tantra*, and the consideration of *samuccaya* and *vikalpa*.

Among these, the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), "Now, therefore, the inquiry into Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*; Jaiminisūtra 1.1.1), is intended to establish the commencement of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā. And investigators declare that a section consists of five members (*pañcāvayava*).
And those five members consist of the subject (*viṣaya*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), established conclusion (*siddhānta*), and connection (*saṅgati*).
Among these, the topic (*adhikaraṇa*) is defined according to the opinion of the Teacher (Jaimini):
the sentence "One's own Veda is to be studied" is the subject.

Beginning with "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.1.2) and ending with "And because it is seen in the case of the *Anvāhārya* [fee]" (Jaimini Sūtra 12.4.47), there arises the doubt as to whether Jaimini’s treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*) is not to be commenced or is indeed to be commenced.
This depends on whether the injunction for study has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) or a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*).
On this point, the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that it is not to be commenced.
This is because it is untenable for the injunction to study (*adhyayanavidhi*) to have the comprehension of meaning as its visible fruit (*dṛṣṭaphala*).

One who argues that the injunction to study is for the sake of comprehending the meaning must be questioned: "Is the study, which was absolutely unestablished, being enjoined, or is it being restricted—like the threshing of grain—to a specific occasion when it might otherwise be optional? It cannot be the first case, because the study of the Veda under dispute is already established independently of the injunction by means of the following inference: "The study of the Veda is a cause for the comprehension of meaning, because it is a form of study, like the study of the *Mahābhārata*."

"Let it be, then, the second [alternative]: just as threshing is restricted by an injunction because it must necessarily be performed—since the production of rice grains is possible through means such as splitting them with the fingernails—so too, since the knowledge of the meaning is possible through written recitation, study is restricted by an injunction as a contingent possibility. This is not tenable, because of the disparity between the example and the case to which it is applied.

For it is only when rice grains are produced by means of threshing that they, through the mediation of the intermediate *apūrva*, bring about the ultimate *apūrva* of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) via the preparation of flour-cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth; it cannot be otherwise.
Therefore, the unseen potency (*apūrva*) is the cause for the restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding threshing.

In the present case, since the performance of the sacrifice is accomplished through the comprehension of the meaning—whether that comprehension arises from the written text or from oral study—there is no restrictive rule for study itself.
Consequently, the study of the science of inquiry (*vicāraśāstra*), which is the cause for the comprehension of meaning, does not possess a mandatory scriptural injunction (*vaidhatva*).

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the fate of the injunction that is actually heard?"—then may you be satisfied with the view that it is an injunction for the mere acquisition of syllables, having heaven as its fruit;
for even though heaven is not explicitly mentioned, it can be postulated according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice.

Just as in the case of the Viśvajit, where it is established by reasoning that heaven is the fruit—a qualification of the eligible agent—even though it was not heard in the text, on the grounds that "heaven belongs to all equally" (Jaiminisūtra 4.3.13), so too let it be the case here with regard to Vedic study.
As it has been said: "Since the visible result is obtained even without an injunction, the injunction does not have that [result] as its purpose;
rather, heaven must be postulated by the power of the injunction, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others.
This being so, the Smṛti rule, "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe," is upheld.
For here, the absence of any interval between the study of the Vedas and the formal graduation (samāvartana) is understood.
In your view, however, even after the Veda has been studied, one must remain at the teacher's house for the investigation of dharma;
if that were the case, the lack of an interval would be contradicted.

Therefore, since the treatise on inquiry lacks mandatory status (*vaidhatva*), and since heaven is attained through mere recitation [of the Veda] according to the rules for graduation (*samāvartana*), the treatise on the inquiry into Dharma need not be commenced; such is the summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
As for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): let it be that it is not an original injunction (*aprāptavidhi*) because it is already obtained from another source;
however, the position that it is a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) cannot be set aside even by the wielder of the thunderbolt (Indra).

For instance, in the injunction "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo'dhyetavyaḥ*), the suffix -tavya conveys the verbal productive energy (*abhidhā-bhāvanā*), which is synonymous with *preraṇā* (instigation) and has as its objective the objective productive energy (*artha-bhāvanā*) consisting of human activity. This objective productive energy, in turn, requires an objective (*bhāvya*).
It does not, however, embrace the act of study—though mentioned in the same word—as its objective.

For it is impossible for the meaning of the word *adhyayana*—namely, the mental and vocal activity consisting in the capacity for independent recitation, which involves effort—to be that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*).
Nor can the *svādhyāya* (one's own Vedic study) mentioned in the same sentence be so;

for since the meaning of the word *svādhyāya* is a collection of phonemes that is eternal and all-pervading, the four fruits of action, such as production (*utpatti*) and the rest, are impossible in its case.
Therefore, the comprehension attained through this capacity remains as that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*).

According to the maxim that "one who is desirous, capable, and learned is qualified," the injunctions for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) and others, requiring the comprehension of their own respective objects, employ the Veda (*svādhyāya*) for the purpose of bringing about the understanding of their own meaning.
Furthermore, the injunction for study indicates that the Veda is sanctified by the act of study, thereby excluding methods such as reading from a written manuscript.

And so, just as the supreme *apūrva* produced by the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices is the postulator of the intermediate *apūrva* produced by acts such as threshing (*avaghāta*), likewise the collection of *apūrvas* produced by the entire sacrifice will postulate the *apūrva* produced by the restrictive rule (*niyama*) of study, which is the means for the knowledge of the sacrifice.
If the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from the restriction were not admitted, the hearing of the injunction would result in futility.
Nor can the postulation of a fruit be justified here by the logic of the *viśvajit* sacrifice.
Since the visible result of the comprehension of the meaning is already perceived, it is improper to postulate another result.
As it has been said: "When a visible result is being obtained, there is no postulation of an invisible result;
however, because the injunction serves the purpose of restriction, it will not be rendered meaningless."

If it is argued that the science of inquiry is useless because, although a person who has studied the Veda with its auxiliary limbs (*sāṅga*) may achieve comprehension of the meaning even when one who studies the Veda alone does not, this is incorrect. For even if mere comprehension is possible, definitive certainty (*nirṇaya*) depends upon inquiry.

For example, regarding the injunction "He places the sugar-cubes smeared [with something]" (*aktāḥ śarkarā upadadhāti*), the determination that they are smeared with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) specifically, and not with oil or other substances, cannot be obtained through grammar, traditional exegesis (*nigama*), or etymology (*nirukta*).
However, through the science of inquiry (vicāra-śāstra), the determination of the meaning is obtained by means of the supplementary statement, "But indeed, ghee is fire.
Therefore, the mandatory nature of the science of inquiry is established.

Nor should it be thought that the scriptural injunction, "Having studied the Veda, one should perform the ritual bath (snāna)," which aims at the departure from the teacher's house and acts as an obstacle to any intervening period, would be contradicted.

Just as in the expression "having bathed, he eats," there is only the understanding of a sequence of actions and a common agent, but no understanding of immediate succession between the two; likewise, there is no understanding of an immediate sequence between the study [of the Veda] and the *samāvartana* ceremony.

Therefore, precisely because of its utility for the injunctions (*vidhi*), the treatise of Pūrva-mīmāṃsā, consisting of thousands of topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), must be commenced. And this first topical section is connected to the treatise as its introductory prolegomenon (*upoddhāta*).
Thus it is said: "They declare that an introductory discussion (upoddhāta) is for the purpose of establishing the nature of reflection."
This very point of contention is presented here following the opinion of the Guru (Prabhākara):
"One should initiate a Brahmin boy at eight years of age and teach him"—in this [injunction], teaching appears to be the object of the mandate (*niyoga*).
And a mandate requires a person to be mandated (*niyojya*).
If it is asked who is the person to be enjoined in this matter, it is simply one who desires the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*).
This is because, according to Pāṇini’s rule "saṃmānana-... (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.3.36), the Ātmanepada suffix is prescribed for the root *nī* when the state of being a teacher is implied.
Furthermore, the very person who is enjoined at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is the same person who is enjoined in the act of teaching.
Because the two have a single purpose;

for this very reason it was said by the sage Manu: "That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs and its secret portions (Upanishads), him they call an Ācārya."

Therefore, since teaching performed by the teacher cannot be accomplished without the act of studying performed by the student, the performance of study will be established solely through the impulsion of the injunction for teaching;
for the operation of the instigator cannot be brought to completion without the operation of the one being instigated.

If it is argued that, in that case, the injunction "it should be studied" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.15) does not establish its status as an injunction, let it not be so; what loss is there to us? For there is no purpose in accepting a separate injunction for study, since the injunctive sentence can be accounted for as a *nityānuvāda* (a permanent restatement).
Therefore, the prima facie and final positions previously set forth regarding the injunction for study should be demonstrated by another method.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the science of inquiry (*vicāraśāstra*) should not be commenced because it is not mandatory; the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*) is that it should be commenced because it is mandatory.

Regarding this, one who asserts its mandatory nature must state whether the injunction for teaching (*adhyāpanavidhi*) impels the student toward the comprehension of meaning as well, or merely toward the recitation of the text. It cannot be the former, because the act of teaching is accomplished even without the comprehension of meaning.
Not the second [alternative],
because in the case of a mere recitation, the subject matter (*viṣaya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*) of the inquiry are impossible.
An object that appears at first glance to be doubtful becomes the subject matter of the treatise on inquiry.

That being the case, where there is no comprehension of the meaning at all, what talk can there be of doubt? And as for the expectation of a conclusion, which is the fruit of inquiry—that is far off indeed. Thus, according to the maxim that "that which is free from doubt and devoid of purpose is not an object of investigation for a discerning person"—as in the case of a jar clearly situated in bright light and in contact with the senses when the mind is attentive—the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) position is that the treatise on inquiry should not be commenced, due to the impossibility of both a subject matter and a purpose.
Let it not be argued that the comprehension of meaning is not the purpose of the method of instruction;

nevertheless, for a person who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) and has grasped the connection between words and their meanings, the comprehension of meaning certainly arises from the sacred tradition (āmnāya) just as it does from human compositions.

But one might object: just as in the case of the statement "Eat poison," even though a meaning is perceived, it is not intended [as the primary sense], because the mother's intention lies in the prohibition of eating—namely, "Do not eat in this man's house."

If it is argued that, in the case of the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the meaning of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), the aforementioned defect of the absence of a subject matter (*viṣaya*) and so forth would arise—do not speak thus.
For a disparity exists between the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the thing illustrated (*dārṣṭāntika*).

In the case of the sentence regarding eating poison, since it was composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*), its primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) would be contradicted; therefore, the intention [to convey that primary meaning] is not accepted.
But why is the meaning perceived in the impersonal Veda not intended [by an author]?
And once the meaning of the Veda is intended, whatever doubt a person may have regarding it will all become the subject matter of the science of inquiry (mīmāṃsā),
and its definitive resolution will be its purpose.

Therefore, since the meaning understood through study—which is itself impelled by the injunction to teach—is worthy of investigation, the science of investigation must be commenced as something enjoined by scripture; this is the summary of the final conclusion (*rāddhānta*).
It might be argued:
how can the Veda be said to be authorless (*apauruṣeya*), given the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that?

Now, you might think: "The Vedas are not of human origin, because, while there has been no interruption in their tradition, no author is remembered, just like the Self. This argument is weak, because the qualifying condition (viśeṣaṇa) is unestablished.
This is because those who maintain that the Vedas are of human origin accept that the tradition was interrupted during the period of dissolution (*pralaya*).

Furthermore, what is this so-called "having no remembered author"? Does it mean having no author known through valid cognition, or having an author who is outside the scope of memory? It cannot be the first alternative, because the existence of the Supreme Lord as the author is admitted to be known through valid cognition.
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis.

For instance, is non-remembrance intended by one person or by all? It cannot be the first, because there is deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of detached verses such as, "He who is virtuous, who has conquered pride and anger," and so forth.
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because the non-remembrance of everything is difficult to ascertain for one who is not omniscient,
and because there exists proof for their being of human origin.
Vedic sentences are of human origin, because they are sentences, like the sentences of Kālidāsa and others.

The Vedic sentences were composed by a trustworthy person, because they are sentences and possess validity, like the sentences of Manu and others. Now, [an objection]: "All study of the Veda is preceded by the teacher's own study, because it is a general case of Vedic study, just like the study performed today."
If it is argued that this counter-inference (*pratisādhana*) is more forceful—
namely: "All study of the *Mahābhārata* is preceded by study under a teacher,
because it is the study of the *Mahābhārata*, just like the present study"— that too is unable to enter the ranks of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is because [the Mahābhārata] shares the same logical status as that appearance.
Now, it is recorded in tradition that Vyāsa was the author there:
"For who else but the lotus-eyed one could be the creator of the Mahābhārata?"
If you argue that this is so in such passages as:
"From Him the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born;
from Him the meters were born; from Him the Yajus was produced," [we reply: that is unsubstantial.
This is because the *Puruṣasūkta* establishes that the Veda has an author, as stated in *Taittirīya Āraṇyaka* 3.12.
Furthermore, sound is non-eternal, because, while possessing a universal (*sāmānya*), it is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves, like a jar.
If it is argued that this inference is refuted by the means of valid cognition known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—in the form "this is that very same letter *ga*"—that argument is extremely weak.
For, as in the case of a tree that has been cut down and grown again, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) concerns the universal (*sāmānya*) and thus lacks the power to subvert [the argument].

Now, if it is objected: "Since the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), being bodiless, lacks the locations such as the palate required for the utterance of phonemes (*varṇa*), how could the Veda be composed by Him?"—this is not a valid objection;
for although He is by nature bodiless, it is possible for Him to assume a playful body (*līlā-vigraha*) for the sake of bestowing grace upon His devotees.

If it is argued that, therefore, the expression "the Veda is not of human origin" (*apauruṣeya*) is not tenable, the following response is stated: What is this "human origin" (*pauruṣeyatva*) that you seek to establish? Is it merely being produced by a person—as in the case of the Veda as it is recited day after day by people like us—or is it being composed for the purpose of revealing an object after having apprehended that object through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as in the case of a literary work being composed by people like us? There is no dispute regarding the first [definition]. Regarding the second, is its proof based on the force of inference (*anumāna*) or the force of scripture (*āgama*)? It cannot be the first.

Because [the definition] would be over-extensive (*savyabhicāra*) in the case of sentences such as those in the *Mālatīmādhava* and other [secular works]. If it is argued that the definition is qualified by the condition "while being valid" (*prāmāṇye sati*), even that does not achieve clarity in the mind of the wise.
For a Vedic sentence is precisely that which conveys a meaning that is not within the scope of other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that [the Veda] establishes objects that fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this leads to a contradiction— like saying "my mother is barren. Furthermore,
even if one accepts that the Supreme Lord assumes a body for his divine play (*līlā-vigraha*), his perception of supersensible objects (*atīndriya-artha*) would still not be possible,
because he lacks the means to grasp objects remote in space, time, or nature.

Nor should it be thought that the eye and other such organs themselves are capable of producing such a cognition; for conceptual construction must be based strictly upon what is observed. As it was said by the Guru at the time of refuting the omniscient being: "Even where an excellence is observed, it does not transcend its own proper object."
In the perception of distant or subtle objects and so forth, there would be no functioning of the auditory faculty with respect to visible form.
For this very reason, its proof does not proceed from the force of scripture (*āgama*).

Just as in the grammatical rule of Pāṇini, "That by which it was spoken" (Pāṇini 4.3.101), even though the rule is present, designations such as *Kāṭhaka*, *Kālāpa*, and *Taittirīya* are justified as referring to the originators of the tradition of study; so too here, it is likewise justified as referring to the originators of the tradition.
Nor is the non-eternality of the Word established through the force of inference.
Because it would contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
Nor is it correct to claim that even in the absence of identity, that [recognition] is based on a universal (*sāmānya*),

for whether one posits its being based on a universal due to the onset of a powerful subverting argument (*bādhaka*), or because of the observation of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in some cases, [it remains untenable].

In that regard, when a deviation is observed somewhere and one suspects it [to be present elsewhere], those who maintain that validity is intrinsic have said: "For he who, out of delusion, suspects an invalidation even where none exists, perishes as one whose soul is filled with doubt regarding all worldly transactions."
If it is argued that this recognition has as its object the universals such as *gatva* and so on, and not the individual instances such as the letter *ga*,
because those individuals are perceived to differ from person to person—
and otherwise, there would be no distinction such as "Somaśarman studied"— that too does not deserve consideration.
Since there is no evidence for a difference between individual instances of the letter *ga* and the like, there is likewise no evidence for the postulation of universals such as *gatva*.

Just as one who does not recognize the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) perceives a single [cow] as if it were in different locations, of different sizes, and of different shapes—due to the influence of various individual instances (*vyakti*) characterized by distinct locations, dimensions, and configurations—so too, for one who does not recognize the individual instance of the letter *ga*, even though it is one, it appears as if associated with those various properties due to the difference in its manifestors (*vyañjaka*).
By this, the argument that "difference is established through the superimposition of contradictory properties" is refuted.

In this regard, is it an intrinsic superimposition of contradictory properties that is intended as the proof for difference, or is it a perceived one? In the first case, there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*). Otherwise, if an intrinsic difference were admitted, the cognition would be "Caitra uttered ten *ga*-sounds," rather than "the *ga*-sound ten times.
In the second case, however, an intrinsic difference is not established.
For the natural unity is not destroyed by a difference consisting of extrinsic adjuncts (upādhi);
otherwise, there would be no natural difference even in the case of space due to the difference of adjuncts such as jars. In that regard, the conventional usage of distinction has its cause in words.
As it has been said by the Teachers:
"Whatever purpose is served by the genus (jāti) will be obtained from the phoneme (varṇa) itself;
but that which is obtainable from the individual (vyakti) is obtained from the articulated sounds (nāda). Therefore, the cognition of [entities such as] *g*-ness and so forth is useless."
And so it is said: "When recognition of sound awakens unimpeded, it alone subverts all inferences of impermanence."

By this, the following argument advanced by Vāgīśvara in the *Mānamanohara* is refuted: "Sound is non-eternal, because it is a specific quality perceptible by a sense organ, like the color of the eye.

This is because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) for one who maintains that sound is a substance, and because it would constitute proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) with respect to the portion consisting of the audible sounds (*dhvani*).
Furthermore, [the argument] is sublated by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "not being audible.

Udayana, however, having established at great length that non-existence (*abhāva*) is perceptible even when its locus is not perceptible, cited the empirical usage—"the clamor has ceased," "the sound has arisen"—as the basis for perception as a proof for the non-eternality of sound.
That too is like a blood-smeared Vetāla ghost already slain by the very logic used to demonstrate that the association of contradictory properties is merely conditional (*aupādhika*).

Indeed, that argument regarding the consequence of constant perception or non-perception if [sound] were eternal, as stated by the author of the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, is also refuted by the admission that it is perceived when refined by *dhvani*.

As for the inference that there is an absence of a relationship between a specific refiner and a specific object to be refined due to simultaneous connection with the sense organs—that is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in the case of the self (*ātman*). Enough, then, of this excessive dispute.

Consequently, it is well established that the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-siddha-prāmāṇya*) regarding *dharma*, since its lack of human authorship has eliminated every sprout of the stain of doubt.
It might be argued as follows:
"The Sāṃkhyas rely on both validity and invalidity being intrinsic;
the Naiyāyikas [hold them] to be extrinsic; and the Buddhists hold the latter to be intrinsic."
The proponents of the Vedas state that validity is extrinsic (parataḥ),
while they maintain that invalidity is both intrinsic (svataḥ) and extrinsic (parataḥ).

Since such disputes among theorists are observed, how can it be accepted as an established fact that validity (*prāmāṇya*) exists intrinsically (*svataḥ*) with respect to Dharma? Furthermore, what is this so-called intrinsic validity? Is it (1) the birth of validity from itself alone; or (2) being produced by the cognition which is its own substratum; or (3) being produced by the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of the cognition which is its own substratum; or (4) residing in a particular cognition produced by the general causal complex of cognition; or (5) residing in a particular cognition produced solely by the general causal complex of cognition? Among these, the first [position] is flawed.
This is because the relation of cause and effect cannot exist within a single entity if it involves both difference and co-occurrence in the same locus.

Nor is the second alternative possible; for if knowledge already exists as a quality, its being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of its own validity would entail that it is a substance (*dravyatva*).
Nor is the third [alternative] tenable;
for whether validity (*prāmāṇya*) is considered an *upādhi* (accidental property) or a *jāti* (universal), its production would be impossible.
The absolute absence of sublation (*bādhātyantābhāva*) in a cognition that does not possess the nature of recollection (*smṛtitva*) is the *upādhi* of validity.
Furthermore, its production is impossible,
because absolute non-existence is admitted to be eternal.
For this very reason, it is not logical for even a universal (jāti) to possess a universal.
Nor is the fourth [alternative] tenable; for valid cognition (*apramā*) is indeed a specific kind of knowledge (*jñānaviśeṣa*).

And when there is a causal complex for a particular, the causal complex for the general is necessarily included within it, just as the causal complex for a *śiṃśapā* tree is included within the causal complex for a tree.
Otherwise, it would follow that its [invalidity] is accidental.
Therefore, if invalidity—accepted as being extrinsic (parataḥ)—were dependent on what is produced by the general causal complex of cognition, an over-extension (ativyāpti) would result.
We now consider the fifth alternative.

Does "being produced by the causal complex of cognition alone" mean being produced by the causal complex of cognition accompanied by the absence of defects, or does it mean being produced by the causal complex of cognition unaccompanied by the absence of defects? It cannot be the first, because those who maintain that validity is extrinsic (parataḥ-prāmāṇya-vādins) accept that validity is produced by the causal complex of cognition accompanied by the absence of defects.
Nor can it be the second.

Since it is established that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is accompanied by the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*), and since the causality of the absence of defects is as firm as a diamond coating (*vajralepa*)—being proven through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that cannot be otherwise accounted for—if it is argued that "absence cannot be a cause at all," then it must be asked: does absence possess the nature of an effect (*kāryatva*) or not? If it does not, then because the destruction of a jar would never arise, it follows as an absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the jar is eternal. If, on the other hand, it does possess the nature of an effect, then what harm has been done by its being a cause? Thus, this is a rope that binds one from both ends.

Regarding this, it has been stated by Udayana: "Just as existence (*bhāva*) is [independent], so too non-existence (*abhāva*) is considered to have a cause, like its effect" (*Nyāyakusumāñjali* 1.10).

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The validity under dispute (*vimataṃ prāmāṇyam*) depends upon a cause other than the cause of the cognition itself, because, while being an effect, it is dependent upon a specific quality of that [cognition], just like invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
Validity is known extrinsically (*parataḥ*), because in the state of non-habituation it is subject to doubt, just like invalidity."

If it is argued that, because there is evidence for the extrinsic nature (*paratastva*) of both the production and the cognition of validity, the claim that "validity is established intrinsically" (*svataḥ-siddha*) is like a rotten gourd, we reply: this is like striking at empty space with one's fist.

For the definition of intrinsic validity is possible as follows: validity is the state of being produced by the causal complex of cognition itself, while not being produced by any cause over and above that.
And there is an inference for this point: [Inference: Validity is intrinsic, because, while being produced by the causal complex of cognition, it is not produced by any cause other than that.
The cognition under dispute is not produced by anything other than the causal complex that produces valid cognition, while being produced by that very complex;
because it does not possess the locus of invalidity,
just like the valid cognition of a jar or similar objects.

Nor should it be suspected that the inference regarding origination (*audayana-anumāna*) does not establish extrinsic validity (*paratastva*). This is because such an inference is seized by the "grasping" of a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*): "Valid cognition is not produced by anything other than the causes of cognition—excluding defects of error—because it possesses the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*), like invalid cognition.

Furthermore, since the production of valid cognition is possible from the causal complex of cognition alone, there would result the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (*kalpanā-gaurava*) if one were to postulate an additional cause, whether it be a "quality" (*guṇa*) or the "absence of defects" (*doṣābhāva*).

[Objection: But surely, since a defect (*doṣa*) is the cause of invalid cognition (*apramā*), it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the absence of such a defect must be the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*).
[Reply: No; because the absence of a defect is otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*) as being merely the preventer of invalid cognition.
Therefore, from the excellences (*guṇas*) comes the absence of defects, and from that absence...
Because the two kinds of invalidity do not exist, the general rule remains unrefuted.
Likewise, the designation of valid cognition (*pramā*) also arises solely from the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of both the cognition and its indicator;
nor is it correct to argue that the undesirable consequence of the non-arising of doubt (*saṃśaya*) serves as a subverting objection,
for such [non-arising] is possible even when the abundant causes for appearance are present, due to the coincidence of obstructing defects (*doṣa*) and the like.

Furthermore, is your inference intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*) or not? In the first case, there is the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatā*). In the second case, its validity must likewise depend on something else, and for that too something else, leading to an untenable infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Regarding this, Udayana, in his *Kusumāñjali*, has stated that the immediate and frequent occurrence of activity does not depend upon the ascertainment of validity.
For activity depends upon desire;
the abundance of that [activity] depends upon the abundance of desire;
and desire is the cognition of something as a means to a desired end.
[The cognition] consists in the experience of a mark (*liṅga*) characterized by being of the same class as that [object];
that [experience], in turn, consists in the contact between the sense organ and the object.
However, the apprehension of validity (*prāmāṇya*) is of no use anywhere.
Even that [knowledge] appears to a thief like the exposure of all one's limbs while carrying gold in one's armpit.

For it is only when the knowledge of a means as being conducive to a desired end is apprehended as valid that it generates desire; thus, the utility of grasping validity is evident precisely in this regard.
Furthermore, if unhesitating activity were to arise from doubt in some instances, then, because such a possibility would exist everywhere, the ascertainment of validity would be useless.
Thus it has been said: "For that which is not ascertained, even existence is difficult to establish.
If existence were easily established, then validity would be as good as consigned to the waters of oblivion; enough, then, with this prolixity.
For it has been stated: "Therefore, the validity of cognition is attained by virtue of its making known what is existent."
It is set aside by the cognition of a defect arising from a cause that results in a change in the object's nature.

Therefore, since the Dharma possesses an intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-siddha-pramāṇabhāva*), the established doctrine of the venerable Bhaṭṭa—the proponents of the theory of "the connection of what has been expressed" (*abhihitānvayavāda*)—who accept that linguistic usage is established with respect to things already accomplished, is as follows: in the Veda, which consists of injunctions, explanatory passages, mantras, and names, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," the suffix *-ta* in the word *yajeta* denotes a productive activity (*bhāvanā*) colored by the meaning of its stem.

On the other hand, the established doctrine of the teacher Prabhākara—the proponents of the theory of "the expression of the connected" (*anvitābhidhānavāda*)—who follow the view that linguistic usage pertains to what is to be done (*kārya*), namely a mandate (*niyoga*) concerning the sacrifice, is as follows. Thus, everything is clear.
Now follows the philosophy of Pāṇini. ||13||

If it is asked, "How is this division into base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) understood?"—this objection does not cause surprise for those who have drunk the waters of Patañjali. For it is well known that the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) is devoted to demonstrating the division between bases and suffixes.
Indeed, this is the opening statement of the venerable Patañjali, the author of the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Now begins the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*).
The meaning of this is as follows: the word "atha" (now/then) is employed here in the sense of an introduction (*adhikāra*). An introduction means a commencement; that is to say, a beginning.

By the term "instruction of words" (*śabdānuśāsana*), the science of grammar composed by Pāṇini is intended. If only the expression "instruction of words" were stated, a doubt might arise as to whether the instruction of words is being commenced or not.
Thinking, "Let there not be such an unwarranted extension [of meaning]," he employed the word *atha*.
For, by the power of employing the word *atha*, through the exclusion of other meanings, it is indicated that what follows is being introduced.

Indeed, by this [work], Vedic words such as "May the divine waters be auspicious for our well-being" (*śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaye*), as well as worldly words that assist them—such as "cow," "horse," "man," "elephant," and "bird"—are taught; having been derived and refined, they are made understood through the analysis of stems and suffixes. Thus, it is the "Instruction on Words" (*śabdānuśāsana*).

On this point, some raise an objection: since the act of instruction (*anuśāsikriyā*) requires an object, when both the word (*śabda*), which serves as the object, and the teacher (*ācārya*), who serves as the agent, are present, this genitive case must be prescribed for the object by the force of the rule "when both [agent and object] are possible, [the genitive is used] for the object" (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.3.66).

Consequently, because the prohibition of compounding in the rule "and [in the presence of] an object" (Pāṇini Sūtra 2.2.14) would apply, the compound *śabdānuśāsana* does not enter the path of valid proof.

In this regard, the following rule of interpretation (*samādhi*) is stated: when there is the possibility of applying the genitive case to both the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) upon the occurrence of a *kṛt* suffix, it is restricted by the force of understanding it as a *bahuvrīhi* compound that the genitive case occurs only for the object and not for the agent.
For example: "The milking of cows is wonderful by an untrained cowherd.

However, in the case of the expression "instruction of words" (*śabdānuśāsanam*), since the intended meaning—that it is the instruction of words and not of meanings—is easily understood even without the mention of the teacher as the agent, the mention of the teacher is superfluous.

Therefore, because there is no occurrence of both [agent and object] simultaneously, this genitive case does not apply by the rule "the genitive is used when both [agent and object] are attained" (*ubhayaprāptau karmaṇi*).

Rather, according to the rule "the genitive is used for the agent and the object when a *kṛt* suffix is employed" (*kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, Pāṇini 2.3.65), the genitive case occurs for the agent and the object in connection with a *kṛt* suffix; thus, the genitive will be characterized by its connection with a *kṛt* suffix.
In that case, a compound will occur, as in the examples *edhma-pravraścana* ("wood-cutter") and *palāśa-śātana* ("leaf-shatterer").
Some say that the genitive case also occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Kāśikāvṛtti*: "Some desire the option (*vibhāṣā*) without distinction, [saying] 'the instruction of words by the Teacher' or 'of the Teacher'.
Alternatively, this genitive is characterized as being "residual" (*śeṣa*).
In that regard, no objection whatsoever arises.

If this is so, then since a genitive case based on residual indication (*śeṣalakṣaṇā*) could easily be stated everywhere, it would follow that the sūtras prohibiting genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) would become purposeless. To this we reply: True;
however, their utility in the consideration of accent (*svara*) was demonstrated by Bhartṛhari in the *Vākyapadīya*.
Regarding this, the Great Teacher Vardhamāna said: "In worldly affairs, let people act as they please;
however, regarding the Vedic paths, let specific instruction prevail."
Since he [Patañjali] states that Pāṇini’s sūtras possess meaningfulness by saying "of the agent of birth" (janikartuḥ) and also "its instigator" (tatprayojakaḥ).

Thus, the meaning of the sentence results in this: it should be understood that the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*), which has "Instruction in Words" (*śabdānuśāsana*) as its other name, has been commenced.

To ensure the immediate comprehension of that meaning, one might simply say "Now, grammar" (*atha vyākaraṇam*). Therefore, the phrase "Now, the instruction in words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) is stated unnecessarily, being composed of superfluous syllables.
Not so;

for by employing the etymologically significant designation "instruction in words" (śabdānuśāsana), the statement of the purpose—which establishes its status as an auxiliary of the Veda—is accomplished.
Otherwise, if the purpose were not stated, the engagement of students in the study of grammar would not even occur.

If it is argued that activity will indeed be established simply by the injunction to study—namely, "The Veda, together with its six limbs, should be studied as a duty without [further] motive"—it is not so.
Even if such an injunction exists, activity on the part of those [students] would be untenable if the purpose for which each of those limbs serves the Veda were not stated.
To illustrate: in former times, it is said, students who had finished their Vedic studies were prone to speak in haste.
"Vedic words are established from the Vedas, and worldly words from common usage;
therefore, grammar is useless.
Thinking thus that it was merely an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda, they did not apply themselves to its study.
Consequently, even the engagement of contemporary people in that [study] would not be established.
To prevent this contingency, the purpose (prayojana) demonstrating its status as an auxiliary to the Veda must indeed be explained.
Even if the purpose were explained, if they still did not engage, then—being devoid of knowledge regarding the refinement of worldly words—they would incur sin (pratyavāya) in the sacrificial rite.
They would fall away from the Dharma.

For this very reason, the ritualists (yājñika) recite: "Having employed an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should perform the expiatory *Sārasvata* sacrifice.

Therefore, it is stated as "Now, the instruction of words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*) for the purpose of explaining its utility as a limb (*aṅga*) of that [Veda], and not as "Now, grammar" (*atha vyākaraṇam*).
Furthermore, the refinement of words (*śabda-saṃskāra*) is the purpose of the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*).
Therefore, the instruction of words, which is understood by the term "refinement," is the purpose of the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*).
[Objection: Even so, the intended purpose is not attained, because there is no means for it.

Now, if you should think that the recitation of each individual word (*pratipadapāṭha*) is the means [to linguistic knowledge], then that indeed would not be a means for the comprehension of words, because words are infinite due to the distinction between correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*). For it is thus recorded in tradition: "Bṛhaspati taught Indra the complete mastery of words (*śabdapārāyaṇa*) consisting of words prescribed by the *pratipadapāṭha* for a thousand celestial years, yet he did not reach the end."
Bṛhaspati was the teacher, Indra was the student, and the period of study lasted for a thousand divine years;
yet even then, mastery was not attained.
How much more so today, when he who lives long lives but a hundred years?
Knowledge becomes fully utilized through four means: study (*adhīti*), comprehension (*bodha*), practice (*ācaraṇa*), and propagation (*pracāraṇa*).
In that case, one's entire lifespan would be consumed merely by the time spent on study.

Therefore, if it is argued that the purpose [of grammar] would not be established because the recitation of every single word (*pratipadapāṭha*) is not a viable means for the understanding of words—do not say so, for we do not maintain that the understanding of words is accomplished solely through the recitation of every single word.

Furthermore, because in the case of linguistic targets (*lakṣya*) that involve conceptualizations such as the division into *prakṛti* (base) and so forth, we observe the instruction of many words through the application of definitions (*lakṣaṇa*)—consisting of both general and specific forms—just once, like a rain-cloud. To illustrate:

by means of the single general definition "the suffix *aṇ* occurs after a verbal root when *karman* [as an object] is the upapada" (*Pāṇini Sūtra* 3.2.1), when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to any verbal root with *karman* as its attendant word, the instruction of many words such as *kumbhakāraḥ* ("potter") and *kāṇḍalāvaḥ* ("reaper of stalks") is obtained.

Thus, by means of a single specific rule, "āto 'nupasarge kaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.2.3), when the suffix *ka* is applied to a verbal root ending in the vowel *ā*, the grammatical instruction for numerous words such as *dhānyadaḥ* and *dhanadaḥ* is obtained.

The statement that Bṛhaspati [could not teach] to Indra refers to the impossibility of reciting every word individually (*pratipadapāṭha*), and is therefore an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Now, one might ask: since there are other auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) as well, why is this one alone esteemed? It is said in reply: among the six auxiliary sciences, grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is the most important.
And effort exerted toward the primary element becomes fruitful.
As it has been said: "The Brahmin who is near [to that goal] possesses the highest of all austerities;
the wise declare that grammar is the first limb of the Vedas."

(Vākyapadīya 1.11). Therefore, the direct purpose of the science of grammar (*vyākaraṇa-śāstra*) is the instruction of words (*śabdānuśāsana*); its indirect purposes, however, include the preservation of the Vedas and so forth.
For this very reason, it was stated by the venerable author of the Bhāṣya: "Preservation, modification, addition, facility, and removal of doubt are the purposes [of grammar]" (Pāṇini-mahābhāṣya).
Furthermore, through the employment of correct words, spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya*) also arises.

And thus it has been stated by Kātyāyana: "In the application [of words] preceded by the knowledge of the treatises (śāstra), there is prosperity; that is equal to the word of the Veda. Others have also said: "A single word, correctly understood and well-employed, becomes a cow of plenty (kāmadhuk) in the heavenly world. Likewise: "They go to heaven, which is a place of desired happiness, by means of chariots bound together with well-employed speech."
Then those who walk on their heels go forth, speaking with stuttering speech.

If it be asked, "How can such power be possible for sound, which is insentient?"—do not think thus; for its identity with the Great God (Mahādeva) is heard in scripture. Thus says the Śruti: "It has four horns, three feet, two heads, and seven hands."
Bound in three ways, the bull bellows; the great god has entered into mortals.
Thus [it is said in] *Māṇḍūkya-nirukta* 10.1.
And the Commentator explained: "The four horns are the four classes of words—nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles.
Its three feet are the three temporal domains—the past, future, and present—pertaining to the *laṭ* and other verbal suffixes."

There are two heads, two natures of sound: the eternal and the produced, distinguished as the manifested and the manifestor. He has seven hands: the seven case endings (sub-vibhaktis) together with the verbal suffixes (tiṅ).
"Bound in three ways" means bound at three places: on the chest, the throat, and the head.
The metaphor of "the bull" is employed because of his well-known nature as a bull, due to his power of raining down [blessings].
And "showering" (varṣaṇam) means the bestowing of fruit through performance preceded by knowledge.
"He roars" (roravīti) means he makes a sound;
the root *ru* has the sense of making sound.

Here, by the word "sound" (śabda), the phenomenal world (prapañca) is intended. "The great god has entered into mortals": the great god is sound; "mortals" refers to humans whose nature is subject to death; [the meaning is] that he has entered into them.

"Equality with the Great God, the Supreme Brahman, has been stated [in the Mahābhāṣya, p. 3]. Thus, in the *Brahmakāṇḍa*, Hari declared that the cause of the world—the partless and eternal word called *sphoṭa*—is indeed Brahman: "Brahman, which is without beginning or end, is the essence of speech; it is the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*)."
From which the process of the world evolves in the form of objective entities.
(Vākyapadīya 1.1).

If it is asked: "Since words are perceived to be of two kinds through the distinction between nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*), how can their fourfold nature have been stated?"—do not say so; for another classification is well-known.
As it is stated in the *Prakīrṇaka*: "Some divide the word into two parts, others into four or even five, having extracted them from sentences just like stems, suffixes, and so forth."
Helārāja has explained that there are five types of words, including the *karmapravacanīya* as the fifth.

However, it should be discerned that since *karmapravacanīyas* are causes for delimiting a relationship produced by a specific action (*kriyā*), they are included within *upasargas* because they indicate a specific action by way of illuminating a specific relationship; thus, it is appropriate that the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated there are only four types of words.
Now, you have asserted that the word is eternal and consists of the *sphoṭa*.
Some say: "We do not accept that, because there is a lack of evidence for it. To this it is replied:
"In this case, perception itself is the evidence."
Since it is universally recognized by all people that "gaurī" is a single word, distinct from its various constituent phonemes,

the experience of a word cannot be said to be false in the absence of a subverting factor. Furthermore, the *sphoṭa* must be accepted even on the grounds that the cognition of word-meanings would otherwise be inexplicable.

Furthermore, the claim that the cognition of the object arises from the phonemes alone is not able to withstand scrutiny, because it cannot bear logical analysis. Do the phonemes produce the cognition of the object collectively or individually? Not the first, because a collection of momentary phonemes is impossible.
Not the latter, because the comprehension of meaning is impossible from individual phonemes taken separately;
nor is there any other mode besides these two—separately or collectively.
Therefore, since it is untenable for phonemes to be the expressive agents, that by whose power the comprehension of meaning occurs is the sphoṭa.
Those who know [the truth] say that *sphoṭa* is the eternal word, which is distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), manifested by the phonemes, and the conveyor of meaning.

For this very reason, they explain the meaning of the word *sphoṭa* in two ways: it is called *sphoṭa* because it is "burst forth" or manifested by the phonemes (*sphuṭyate vyajyate varṇaiḥ*), thus being manifested by the phonemes; and it is called *sphoṭa* because the meaning "bursts forth" or becomes manifest from it (*sphuṭati sphuṭībhavaty asmād arthaḥ*), thus being the conveyor of meaning.

And so it was stated by the venerable Patañjali in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Now, in the case of the word 'cow' (*gauḥ*), what is the word? That which, when uttered, brings about the cognition of the dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns—that is the word" (*Mahābhāṣya*, p.
1). And this was explained by Kaiyaṭa: "The grammarians maintain that the word, as distinct from the individual phonemes (*varṇa*), is the expressive agent."

This has been established at length in the *Vākyapadīya* by the passage beginning with, "Because if the phonemes were the denoters [of meaning], it would follow that the utterance of the second and subsequent phonemes would be purposeless," and ending with, "therefore, the *sphoṭa*, distinct from those [phonemes] and manifested by sound (*nāda*), is the denoter.
Now, one might object: even for the *sphoṭa*, the capacity to convey meaning is not tenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpa*).

Does the *sphoṭa* convey meaning when it is manifested or when it is unmanifested? It cannot be the latter, because that would entail the production of the effect characterized by the comprehension of all meanings at all times. This is because, given the acceptance of the eternity of the *sphoṭa*, the cause—being independent—would exist constantly, and thus a delay in the arising of the effect would be impossible.

Now, if it is accepted that the *sphoṭa* manifests and conveys the meaning in order to avoid this fault, even then, do the phonemes (*varṇas*) manifest it individually or collectively? In either case, those very same faults that you have stated against the position that the phonemes themselves are the signifiers must be avoided here as well regarding the position that they manifest the *sphoṭa*.

As the Bhaṭṭācārya has stated in the *Mīmāṃsā-śloka-vārttika*: "He for whom the partless *sphoṭa* is manifested by the cognitions of the phonemes—he too cannot escape from even a single one of these objections."

Since Pāṇini has prescribed the technical term *pada* for phonemes ending in an inflectional suffix (*sup*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) in the rule "That which ends in *sup* or *tiṅ* is a *pada*" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.4.14), and Gautama has likewise done so for those ending in an inflectional suffix in the rule "Those [phonemes] ending in an inflectional suffix are a *pada*" (Nyāya Sūtra 2.2.60), the cognition of a word will arise with respect to the phonemes themselves, by virtue of being assisted by the apprehension of the convention.

If this were so, then however many phonemes there are in the word *sara*, there would be exactly that many in *rasa* as well. Likewise, in cases such as *vanaṃ navaṃ*, *nadī dīnā*, *rāmo māro*, and *rājā jārā*, there would be no perception of a difference in meaning. If this objection is raised, we say: no.
Because a difference [in meaning] arises from a difference in sequence.

As it has been stated by the Tautātitas: "However many letters there are, of whatever kind they may be, and whatever their capacity for the comprehension of a particular meaning may be known to be, they convey that meaning in exactly that way."

If it is argued that—according to the maxim that "one should not level a criticism against one party when the same fault applies to both"—the theory of the phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves being the denoters is logically consistent, and thus the postulation of an additional *sphoṭa* is untenable—this is merely a futile grasp at a straw, for the alternatives are untenable. Is it the individual phonemes alone that are the basis for the cognition of a word, or is it the collection of phonemes? Not the first; for in a series of mutually distinct phonemes, there can be no single, undifferentiated cause (without which the cognition "this is one word" would be impossible), just as there can be no cognition of a "garland" among flowers without a string. Thus, the understanding that "this is one word" would be inexplicable.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for it is impossible for letters that perish as soon as they are uttered to constitute a collection (*samūha*).

Indeed, the designation "collection" applies to those objects which are experienced as many existing together in a single location—for example, the designation "collection" applied to dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees when they are experienced as existing together in one place, or as in the case of elephants, men, horses, and so forth.
Furthermore, those phonemes are not experienced in that manner, because they perish as soon as they arise.
Even on the view that they are manifested, manifestation occurs only sequentially, since a simultaneous collection is impossible.
Nor can a conceptual aggregate be postulated among the phonemes.
This leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayaprasaṅga*):

the establishment of letters as conveying a single meaning depends on the cognition of "wordhood" (*padatva*) in those letters by means of that very [single meaning], and the establishment of that [wordhood] depends on the establishment of their conveying a single meaning.
Therefore, since it is impossible for letters to be the expressive agents (*vācaka*), the *sphoṭa* must be accepted.

If it is argued that even under the view that the *sphoṭa* is manifested by sounds, the same array of dilemmas mentioned previously applies—rendering the situation like "the dawn at the thief's hut"—this is merely a manifestation of wishful thinking, for there is a fundamental difference between the two cases.
To explain: even the first sound, acting as a manifestor, manifests the *sphoṭa* indistinctly.
Through a sequence of progressively more manifesting [expressions], it becomes clear, clearer, and clearest.
Just as a recitation, when read only once, is not fully grasped,
but through repeated practice there arises a clear comprehension.
Or, for example, the nature of silver does not shine forth clearly in the initial cognition;
it is manifested correctly only in the final consciousness,
together with the last sound that has deposited its seed in the mental continuum through the preceding sounds.
When the intellect has reached maturity through repeated practice, the word is firmly grasped.
As it has been stated by the authoritative [Vākyapadīya 1.84]:

"Therefore, because of the linguistic convention 'we understand the meaning from this word,' it is untenable for individual phonemes to be the expressers of meaning. Since this was declared by the venerable Bhartṛhari in the First Book (Prakīrṇaka-kāṇḍa), one must accept the reality of speech known as *sphoṭa*—which is partless and the conveyor of meaning.

All of this has been established in the *Jātisamuddeśa*, which is devoted to demonstrating that the meaning of all words is simply the universal (*jāti*) of existence (*sattā*), characterized by ultimate consciousness (*paramārthasaṃvit*).
[Objection: If existence alone is the meaning of all words, then all words would be synonyms.
Consequently, the simultaneous employment of three or four words in a single instance would be improper; such is the great cleverness of your honor!
As it has been said: "The simultaneous employment of synonyms is not desired;
for they express the object only in succession, not when combined."
If it is argued that this position cannot withstand scrutiny, we reply: that argument is as futile as chewing on the hair of the sky.

For just as a crystal gem appears different according to the various coloring substances—such as blue, red, or yellow—that reflect upon it, so too, due to the difference in its correlates, the universal *sattā* (Being) is established as being perceived through its own diverse forms. Consequently, the distinction in linguistic usage based on the differences between "cow-ness" (*gotva*) and other such forms of "cowness" (*gosattā*) is logically justified.
Thus, an authoritative scripture states: "Just as a pure substance, the crystal, is joined with various [colors] individually..."
It is perceived as having those colors, such as blue, red, yellow, and so forth.

Likewise, it has been stated by Hari: "Existence itself, being differentiated among cows and other things due to the difference in its correlates, is called a 'universal' (jāti). All words are established in that [existence].
They declare that to be the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) and the meaning of the verbal root (dhātu)."
She is eternal; she is the Great Self (Mahātman); of her they say the suffixes -tva and -tal, and so forth.

Being (*sattā*) itself—the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*)—is the genus (*jāti*), its apparent distinctions being constructed by the related substrates that differentiate it, as in the case of "cow," "horse," and so forth.

Lower universals (*aparasāmānya*) such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like do not, in the ultimate sense, differ from that [Great Universal]. Cowness is simply the being of a cow; no other recurring entity appears in cognition.
In the same way, it should be stated that "horse-ness" is the existence of a horse, and so forth.
And thus, all words such as "cow" and others are established as denotators with respect to that very universal *sattā* (existence), which is differentiated by the distinctions of "cow" and so on.
Furthermore, it is well known that the meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is *sattā*.

In the view that "a root (dhātu) denotes an action" (*bhāva*), since action is simply existence (*sattā*), it follows that the meaning of the root is indeed existence. Even in the view that "a root denotes an activity" (*kriyā*), since it is established in the *Kriyāsamuddeśa* that "others say that action is a universal (*jāti*) residing in multiple individuals," the meaning of the root is indeed existence.
Since the suffixes *tv* and *tal* are prescribed in the sense of "being" (*bhāva*) by the rule *tasya bhāvastvatalau* (Pāṇini 5.1.119), it is logical that [this Being] denotes existence.
Furthermore, because it is devoid of arising and passing away, that existence is eternal.

Since the entire phenomenal world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of it, and thus lacks limitation in terms of space, time, and substance, that existence is designated as the "Great Self" (*mahān ātmā*). This is the meaning of the two verses.

Even in the system of those who maintain that the category of reality consists of substances (*dravyapadārthavāda*), it has been established in the *Sambandhasamuddeśa* that the very essence characterized by consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the referent of all words: "The real entity is determined by its unreal forms;
the real alone is denoted by words which possess unreal limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)."
Just as Devadatta’s house, though apprehended by means of an unstable indicator,
is denoted by the word "house" as being purely [the house itself].

The Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), while explaining the Vārttika passage "the relationship between word and meaning being established," has also determined—in the text beginning with "for substance (*dravya*) is eternal"—that the reality of Brahman, delimited by unreal adjuncts (*upādhi*), is denoted by the word "substance" and constitutes the referent of all words.
According to the view of Vājapyāyana, who maintains that the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, words such as "cow" and the like denote the universal inherent in distinct substances;
when that universal is apprehended, the substance is understood through its connection to it.

Words such as "white" and the like denote the universal (jāti) inherent in a quality; there is no cognition of that [universal] in the quality itself due to the absence of its connection [with another substrate],
but in the substance [it is cognized] through the connection with that which is connected [to the quality].

Based on the force of the non-differentiating cognition that "this is that very same person," despite the differences in states such as infancy, childhood, and youth, one must accept the existence of a genus such as "Devadatta-hood" (devadattatva), which persists from the arising until the destruction of names and sounds.
A genus is also perceived in actions;
it is precisely this [genus] that is expressed by the verbal root (dhātu).

Because a recurring suffix appears in expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), in the system of Vyāḍi—who maintains that the individual substance (*vyakti*) is the referent of a word—the individual alone appears as the denotation; the universal (*jāti*), however, serves merely as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus, there is no room for defects such as infinite regress (*anantyadoṣa*).
Both [theories] are accepted by the teacher Pāṇini;
for, having accepted the universal (*jāti*) as the word-meaning, he employs such usage as "In the case of a single entity denoting a genus, the plural may optionally be used" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.58);
and having accepted the individual substance (*dravya*) as the word-meaning, he employs such rules as "Of similar forms, only one remains when followed by the same case-ending" (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.64).
Since grammar is intended for all audiences, there is no contradiction in accepting both views.
Therefore, it is established that the non-dual reality, the supreme Brahman-tattva, is the referent of all words.
As it has been said: "Therefore, through the division of its powers, everything is real and consists of Being."
A single object, when expressed by words, appears in many forms.

The true nature of reality has also been stated by Hari in the *Sambandhasamuddeśa*: "Those who know the Vedanta declare that the truth belongs to that very object where the seer, the seen, and the seeing are non-conceptualized."

In the *Dravyasaṃuddeśa* it is also said: "Just as gold remains true even when its modification has ceased, that in which there is the cessation of modification is called the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*)."

In order to sustain the accepted doctrine of non-duality, the non-distinction between the signified and the signifier has been demonstrated: "She is the signified of all words, and she is not separate from the word;
even though they are non-separate, there is a relationship between them, like that between the individual soul and the Self."

Because the profusion of distinctions is imagined through various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and because conventional usage is constructed solely by ignorance (*avidyā*), the reality of Brahman—whose nature is qualified by specific forms—is the object of all words.

And while non-duality is the ultimate truth, due to the power of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), the manifold world (*prapañca*) unfolds during the state of worldly transaction like a dream; such is the meaning of the verse.
