Thus say those skilled in the Vedānta doctrine: "Just as this dream-world is manifested by me through illusion (*māyā*)."
In this same way, the waking world-phenomenon as well is a manifestation of Māyā within me.

Thus, when the supreme Brahman—which is immutable, of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and non-different from the inner self—is realized, primordial ignorance is removed, and the highest beatitude (*niḥśreyasa*), characterized by abiding as that very Brahman-self, will be attained.

As the learned say: "One who is proficient in the *Śabdabrahman* attains the Supreme Brahman" (*Mahābhārata*, Śāntiparvan, Chapter 270). Consequently, it is established that the science of grammatical instruction is a means to the highest beatitude.
As it has been said: "It is the gateway to liberation, the remedy for the impurities of speech;
they declare it to be the purifier of all sciences, the science that transcends all."
(Vākyapadīya 1.14).
Likewise: "This is the primary station for those standing on the rungs of the ladder to perfection;
this is that straight royal road for those seeking liberation."
(Vākya 1.16).
Therefore, it is established that the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa-śāstra) should be studied as a means for attaining the supreme goal of human life. Now begins the Sāṃkhya philosophy. 14.

Now, when the theory of transformation (pariṇāmavāda), which is maintained by the Sāṃkhyas, stands as a vigilant adversary, how could the theory of illusory manifestation (vivartavāda) be worthy of acceptance?
For this is their proclamation:
in brief, four types [of causality] are possible according to the Sāṃkhya treatise.
Some entity is a primal nature (*prakṛti*) alone; some is both a modification (*vikṛti*) and a primal nature; some is a modification alone; and some is neither.
Among these, that which is a primal nature alone is to be understood by the term *pradhāna*, the root-primal-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).
It is not a modification of anything else.
By the etymological derivation *prakṛti* from the sense of "that which acts" (*prakaroti*), it denotes the state of equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇas*) of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
As it has been said: "Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification" (*Sāṃkhyakārikā* 3).
It is the root (*mūla*) and it is nature (*prakṛti*); thus, it is "root-nature" (*mūlaprakṛti*).

This [Prakṛti] is the root of the entire collection of effects beginning with the Mahat; however, there is no other root for this Pradhāna, because that would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā). Nor should it be argued that the fault of infinite regress does not apply here as it does in the case of the seed and the sprout, for the sense is that there is a lack of valid evidence (pramāṇa) for such a claim.
The evolutes and the primal natures are the Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi).
This has also been stated: "The seven, beginning with the Great Principle, are both primal natures and evolutes" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3).
This is its meaning.
Those which are both primal natures (*prakṛti*) and modifications (*vikṛti*) are the seven principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*);
among them, the principle of the Great One— which is designated by such terms as "internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— is the primal nature of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*),
but it is a modification of the root-primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*).
Thus, the principle of *ahaṃkāra* (ego), also known by the name *abhimāna*, is a modification (*vikṛti*) of *mahat*.
That same principle of *ahaṃkāra*, being characterized by *tamas*, is the subtle source (*prakṛti*) of the five *tanmātras*;

and that same [principle], being characterized by *sattva*, is the source (*prakṛti*) of the eleven organs: the five sense organs called eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin; the five organs of action called speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; and the mind (*manas*), which partakes of the nature of both.
However, since *rajas* possesses causality in both cases by way of producing activity, it is not purposeless.
This was stated by Īśvarakṛṣṇa: "From that [the *tamas*-dominated *ahaṃkāra*] proceeds the ego-sense (*abhimāna*), from which a twofold creation issues forth:
the group of eleven organs and the pentad of subtle elements (*tanmātra*)."
The group of eleven [senses] proceeds from the *vaikṛta* (modified) ego;
the subtle elements proceed from the *bhūtādi* (elemental-origin) ego, which is *tāmasa*; and from the *taijasa* (fiery) ego, both arise.
The organs of cognition are called the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin;
they say that speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ are the organs of action.
In this context, the mind possesses the nature of both; it is the faculty of volition and an organ of sense because of its common characteristics [with the others].
Thus [ends the commentary on] Sāṃkhyakārikā 24–27.
And this has been explained by the teacher Vācaspati in the *Tattvakaumudī*:
"The modification alone consists of the five great elements beginning with space and the eleven sense organs.
As it has been said: "The group of sixteen, however, is the modification (*vikāra*)."
(Sāṃkhya Kārikā 3). The meaning is that the group delimited by the number sixteen—the "sixteenfold"—is only a transformation (*vikāra*) and not a primal nature (*prakṛti*).

Although earth and the other elements are the material causes (*prakṛti*) of cows, jars, and so forth, they are nonetheless not primal natures because they do not constitute a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*) from earth and the others.
In this context, "being the material cause" (prakṛtitva) is intended to mean being the material cause of another principle (tattvāntara).
Since cows, pots, and so forth share the common characteristics of grossness and perceptibility by the senses, they do not constitute distinct principles.

In that regard, from the subtle elements (tanmātras) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—each accompanied by its respective preceding subtle element—the five great elements (mahābhūtas), beginning with space, arise in succession, possessing one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively.

The creation of the sense organs has already been explained. As it has been said: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements arise."
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 22).
Thus, the *puruṣa* is of neither nature.
As it has been said: "The *puruṣa* is neither primordial matter (*prakṛti*) nor a transformation (*vikṛti*)" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3).
The Puruṣa, however, is immutably eternal and unchanging; the meaning is that he is neither the material cause (prakṛti) of anything, nor is he the modification (vikṛti) of anything.
To establish these twenty-five principles, three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are accepted.
As it has been said: "Perception, inference, and authoritative testimony [are the means], because all objects of knowledge are established through these means of valid cognition."
Threefold is the means of valid cognition accepted, for the establishment of the objects of cognition proceeds from the means of valid cognition.
Thus [it is said in] Sāṅkhyakārikā 4.
Here, regarding the relationship between cause and effect, four types of misconceptions prevail.
The followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) maintain that "the existent is born from the non-existent."
The Naiyāyikas and others hold that the non-existent arises from the existent;
the Vedāntins hold that the collection of effects is an illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of the existent and not a real entity;
the Sāṃkhyas, however, maintain that the existent arises from the existent.

In this regard, the position that "the non-existent arises from the existent" is not supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is impossible for the non-existent—which is indefinable like the horn of a hare—to function as a cause, and because it is impossible for identity to exist between the void and the non-void.

Nor does "the existent arise from the non-existent," because it is impossible for that which is non-existent prior to the operation of causal factors to undergo origination characterized by a connection with existence, just like the horn of a hare.
Indeed, even by the most skillful person, blue cannot be made yellow.
If it is argued that existence and non-existence are both properties (*dharma*) of the pot, that is not tenable;
for since the designation "a property of that" is untenable when the substratum (*dharmin*) is non-existent, it would follow that the substratum must itself exist.
Therefore, even prior to the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*), the effect is indeed existent.
Furthermore, manifestation is possible for that which already exists, just as oil [is manifested] from sesame seeds by pressing, or milk from cows by milking.
No example whatsoever is seen for the production of that which is non-existent. Moreover, is the cause related to the effect when it produces it, or unrelated?
In the first case, the existence of the effect would follow, because of the rule that a relation exists only between two things that already exist.
In the latter case, the entire range of effects would arise from everything, since there would be no distinction in their lack of connection.
This was stated by the Sāṃkhya teachers: "Because of non-existence, there is no connection with causes that are associated with existence."
Furthermore, for one who desires the arising of that which is unconnected, there can be no established order.
Now, if it should be argued that even an unrelated thing produces a particular effect insofar as it is capable of doing so,
and that this capacity is to be inferred from the observation of the effect—
that is not tenable.

Regarding the statement that "the power to produce oil exists in sesame seeds," since the oil is non-existent [at that time], it is impossible to define that power through the dilemma of whether it is related or unrelated [to the seeds].
Furthermore, because cause and effect are non-different, the effect does not exist separately from the cause.
A cloth is not different from its threads, because it possesses their properties.
That which is not thus is not thus, just as a cow is not a horse; and the cloth possesses those properties. Therefore, it is not a different entity.

If it is argued that, in that case, those very [threads] individually would perform the function of covering, we say no; for it is logical that they perform the purposeful action of covering once the state of being a cloth has manifested through a particular configuration (*saṃsthāna*).

Just as the limbs of a tortoise, when entering its body, become hidden, and when emerging, become manifest, so too the specific modifications such as cloth emerge from their cause—the threads—and becoming manifest, are said to "arise"; while entering [the cause] and becoming hidden, they are said to "perish.
It is not, however, that non-existent things arise, nor that existent things perish.
As it is stated in the Bhagavadgītā: "The non-existent has no being; the existent has no non-being" (Gītā 2.16).
Therefore, the existence of that Pradhāna is established through inference from its effects.

As it has been said: "Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is the grasping of a material cause, because everything is not possible [from everything], because the efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and because the effect exists within the cause, the effect pre-exists in the cause."
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 9).

Nor is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the existent reality of Brahman, because no sublation (*bādhā*) is perceived; furthermore, since there is an absence of similarity (*sārūpya*) between the substratum and the superimposed object—namely, between consciousness and insentience, like gold and mother-of-pearl—an illusory attribution is impossible.
Therefore, a cause of like nature must be determined for this phenomenal world, which consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion.
And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The collection of existing things under dispute has pleasure, pain, and delusion as its cause, because it is permeated by them.
Whatever is permeated by something has that as its cause; for example, a necklace and the like, being permeated by gold, have gold as their cause.
And this [collection of things] is likewise; therefore, it is so.

In that regard, regarding the cause of the world: that which consists of the nature of pleasure is *sattva*, that which consists of the nature of pain is *rajas*, and that which consists of the nature of delusion is *tamas*. Thus, the existence of a cause composed of the three *guṇas* is established.
For indeed, every entity is experienced as possessing these three *guṇas*.
Just as happiness manifests for Maitra toward Satyavatī, the wife of Maitra,
due to the emergence of the quality of goodness (sattva) directed toward her,
there is suffering for her co-wives.
This is because of the manifestation of the quality of passion (rajas) toward them;
and for Caitra, who does not obtain them, delusion arises,
because of the emergence of the quality of darkness (tamas) toward him.
In the same way, other things such as a jar, when obtained, produce pleasure;
when seized by others, they produce pain;
and when one is indifferent, they present themselves as objects of equanimity.
Being an object of equanimity is indeed delusion (*moha*),
because the word *moha* is derived from the verbal root *muha*,
meaning "to be bewildered," since no mental activity arises toward things that are to be treated with equanimity.
Therefore, it is understood that the entire collection of existing things consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and has as its cause the Pradhāna composed of the three *guṇas*.
And so it is heard in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad:
"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form."
For one unborn, indeed, lies by her while enjoying her; another unborn leaves her once her enjoyments have been experienced.
Thus [it is said in Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 4.5].

In this context, the terms "red," "white," and "black" are intended to demonstrate the three qualities (*guṇas*)—rajas, sattva, and tamas—by virtue of their common characteristics of coloring, illuminating, and veiling, respectively.
Now, one might object: the insentient *pradhāna*, being unpresided over by a conscious principle, cannot engage in the production of effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest;
therefore, there must be some conscious presiding agent.
If it is argued that, in that case, a Supreme Lord who perceives all objects must be accepted, that is incorrect;

for the activity of even the insentient *pradhāna* is possible by virtue of its purpose. Moreover, it is observed that even the insentient proceeds toward the goal of the person (*puruṣārtha*) without being presided over by a conscious being.

Just as insentient milk flows for the sake of the growth of the calf, and just as insentient water flows for the benefit of the world, so too will insentient *prakṛti* proceed toward the liberation of the *puruṣa*. As it has been said: "Just as the flow of insentient milk occurs for the purpose of the calf's growth, so does the activity of the *pradhāna* occur for the purpose of the *puruṣa*'s liberation."
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 57).
As for that drum-beating proclamation of those who maintain the existence of a Supreme Lord— that the Supreme Lord acts out of compassion— that has miscarried,
because the logical alternatives do not hold up.

Does it (compassion) operate prior to creation or after the time of creation? In the first case, since there is an absence of bodies and so forth, suffering does not arise; thus, the desire of living beings to abandon suffering would be impossible.
In the second case, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence: creation results from compassion, and compassion results from creation.

Therefore, even though the *pradhāna* is insentient and not presided over by a conscious being, its transformation into the form of the *mahat* and so on is impelled by the purpose of the *puruṣa* and has as its cause the conjunction of the *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa*.

Just as iron undergoes activity through the proximity of a magnet, even though the magnet itself is devoid of activity, so too the activity of *pradhāna* is possible through the proximity of the *puruṣa*, who is himself devoid of activity.
Furthermore, the relationship between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is based on mutual dependence, like that of a lame man and a blind man;
for *prakṛti*, as the object of enjoyment, depends upon the *puruṣa* as the enjoyer.

The Puruṣa also, because it fails to grasp the distinction [between itself and Prakṛti], undergoes the reflection of the intellect (buddhi) and, seeking to ward off the threefold suffering residing therein, desires isolation (kaivalya).
Since that [isolation] is based on the discrimination between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and since it is not possible without that [discrimination], the Puruṣa requires Pradhāna for the sake of isolation.

Just as, for example, two people—one lame and one blind—travelling along a road with a caravan might, due to a calamity sent by fate, be separated from the caravan and wander slowly here and there in great fear, until by the power of destiny they come together.
In that case, the blind man has placed the lame man upon his shoulders;
then, by the path shown by the lame man, the blind man reaches the desired destination, and the lame man as well, mounted upon the shoulders, arrives there.
In the same way, creation is based on the mutual dependence of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.

As it has been said: "For the purpose of the Puruṣa's perception, and likewise for the purpose of the Pradhāna's isolation (kaivalya), there is a union of both like that of the lame and the blind; from this [union] proceeds creation."
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 21).
Now, one might ask: "Granted that the activity of *prakṛti* is motivated by the purpose of the *puruṣa*, how is its cessation to be accounted for? To this it is replied:

Just as an unchaste woman who has been seen through her faults by her husband does not return to him, or as a dancer desists once her purpose is accomplished, so too does primordial nature (prakṛti). As it has been said: "Just as a dancer desists from her dance after having shown herself to the audience, so does primordial nature desist after having manifested herself to the Spirit (puruṣa)."
(Sāṃkhyakārikā 59).
This is the view presented by those who follow the doctrine of Kapila and others, the founders of the atheistic Sāṃkhya system.
Thus ends the Sāṃkhya philosophy in the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Mādhava, son of Sāyaṇa.
Now begins the Pātañjala-darśana (the Yoga system of Patañjali). ||15||
Now, the doctrine of those who follow the views of sages such as Patañjali, the founder of the Sāṃkhya with God (Seśvara-sāṃkhya), is presented.
In this regard, the Yoga-śāstra composed by Patañjali—also known by the name Sāṃkhya-pravacana—consists of four chapters (pādas).

In that regard, in the first *pāda*, having established the promise to begin the *Yogaśāstra* with "Now, the instruction on Yoga" (*atha yogānuśāsanam*, Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.1), and having stated the definition of Yoga with "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*yogaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ*, Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.2), the venerable Patañjali explained *samādhi* in detail.

In the second [chapter], he taught the *kriyāyoga* for one whose mind is in a state of worldly emergence, beginning with "Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute *kriyāyoga*" (*tapaḥsvādhyāyeśvarapraṇidhānāni kriyāyogaḥ*, Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.1), as well as the five external means of practice, such as the *yamas*.

In the third [chapter], by the aphorism "Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to a single place" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 3.1) and so forth, the triad of concentration, meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*)—which constitutes the internal limb (*antaraṅga*) denoted by the term *saṃyama*—and the collection of supernatural powers (*vibhūti*) which are its intermediate fruits, are presented.

In the fourth [chapter], by the aphorism "Perfections (*siddhi*) arise from birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and absorption" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 4.1) and so forth, the ultimate goal, *kaivalya*, is set forth following an elaboration of the five types of perfections. The twenty-five principles (*tattva*), beginning with *pradhāna*, are accepted exactly as they were formulated by the ancient [Sāṃkhya] authorities.

The twenty-sixth principle, however, is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), the Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, or latent dispositions. By His own will, having presided over a manifested body (nirmāṇakāya), He is the initiator of both worldly and Vedic traditions and the benefactor of living beings who are tormented by the coals of saṃsāra. If it be asked: "How is it possible for that [Lord], who—like a lotus leaf—is untainted, to undergo suffering, such that the Supreme Lord must be accepted as a benefactor?"—it is replied: [The text continues: ...It is said: "Just as a person who has mastered the art of archery, though himself free from desire, acts for the sake of others by means of his arrows; or just as a physician, though himself free from disease, administers medicine to those who are ill; so too the Supreme Lord, though Himself eternally liberated and free from all suffering, manifests through His power of māyā for the sake of bestowing grace upon those bound by karma. This is the view of the venerable Gauḍapāda and others. Thus, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, since the Lord is omniscient and omnipotent, His capacity to act for the benefit of others is not impossible. Therefore, the Supreme Lord exists as the benefactor of the world. This concludes the section on the twenty-sixth principle. Now begins the consideration of the twenty-seventh principle. The twenty-seventh principle is the one who is eternally liberated (nityamukta). This is because he is eternally free from the bondage of karma and its fruits. He is the one who, having realized the truth, remains forever in the state of liberation. This is the twenty-seventh principle. Now begins the consideration of the twenty-eighth principle. The twenty-eighth principle is the one who is eternally bound (nityabaddha). This is because he is eternally subject to the cycle of birth and death due to the persistence of ignorance and the accumulation of karma. He is the one who, being devoid of discriminative knowledge, wanders perpetually in saṃsāra. This is the twenty-eighth principle. Thus, these three—the eternally liberated, the Supreme Lord, and the eternally bound—are established as the three distinct categories of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the twenty-eighth principle. Now begins the consideration of the twenty-ninth principle. The twenty-ninth principle is the one who is potentially liberated (mumukṣu). This is because he possesses the desire for liberation and is engaged in the practice of yoga. He is the one who, having turned away from worldly objects, seeks the means to attain the ultimate goal. This is the twenty-ninth principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirtieth principle. The thirtieth principle is the one who is potentially bound (baddhamumukṣu). This is because he is bound by strong attachments and lacks the inclination toward liberation. He is the one who, being immersed in worldly pleasures, does not seek the path to freedom. This is the thirtieth principle. Thus, these five—the eternally liberated, the Supreme Lord, the eternally bound, the potentially liberated, and the potentially bound—constitute the fivefold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirtieth principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-first principle. The thirty-first principle is the one who is potentially bound again (punarbaddha). This is because, even after attaining temporary liberation, he falls back into bondage due to a lapse in his spiritual discipline. He is the one who, having once reached the heights of realization, returns to the mire of saṃsāra. This is the thirty-first principle. Thus, these six—the previously mentioned five plus the potentially bound again—constitute the sixfold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-first principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-second principle. The thirty-second principle is the one who is potentially liberated again (punarmumukṣu). This is because, even after falling back into bondage, he again develops the desire for liberation. He is the one who, having experienced the bitterness of worldly existence, strives once more for the attainment of peace. This is the thirty-second principle. Thus, these seven—the previously mentioned six plus the potentially liberated again—constitute the sevenfold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-second principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-third principle. The thirty-third principle is the one who is potentially bound again and again (punarbhūyo baddha). This is because he is subject to repeated cycles of bondage and rebirth due to the persistence of deep-seated ignorance. He is the one who, despite occasional glimpses of truth, remains trapped in the wheel of transmigration. This is the thirty-third principle. Thus, these eight—the previously mentioned seven plus the potentially bound again and again—constitute the eightfold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-third principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-fourth principle. The thirty-fourth principle is the one who is potentially liberated again and again (punarbhūyo mumukṣu). This is because, despite repeated falls into bondage, he repeatedly seeks the path to liberation. He is the one who, through the grace of a teacher or the ripening of past merit, turns his mind toward the ultimate truth. This is the thirty-fourth principle. Thus, these nine—the previously mentioned eight plus the potentially liberated again and again—constitute the ninefold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-fourth principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-fifth principle. The thirty-fifth principle is the one who is potentially bound and potentially liberated simultaneously (baddhamumukṣu). This is because he is in a state of flux, sometimes bound by worldly desires and sometimes seeking liberation. He is the one whose mind is unstable, oscillating between attachment and renunciation. This is the thirty-fifth principle. Thus, these ten—the previously mentioned nine plus the potentially bound and potentially liberated simultaneously—constitute the tenfold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-fifth principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-sixth principle. The thirty-sixth principle is the one who is potentially liberated and potentially bound simultaneously (mumukṣubaddha). This is because he is in a state of conflict, desiring liberation yet still entangled in the snares of karma. He is the one who, though yearning for freedom, remains unable to sever the bonds of worldly existence. This is the thirty-sixth principle. Thus, these eleven—the previously mentioned ten plus the potentially liberated and potentially bound simultaneously—constitute the elevenfold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-sixth principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-seventh principle. The thirty-seventh principle is the one who is potentially bound, potentially liberated, and potentially bound and liberated simultaneously (baddhamumukṣubaddhamumukṣu). This is because he experiences all three states in rapid succession due to the complexity of his mental condition. He is the one who is tossed about by the winds of various thoughts and dispositions. This is the thirty-seventh principle. Thus, these twelve—the previously mentioned eleven plus the potentially bound, potentially liberated, and potentially bound and liberated simultaneously—constitute the twelvefold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-seventh principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-eighth principle. The thirty-eighth principle is the one who is potentially liberated, potentially bound, and potentially liberated and bound simultaneously (mumukṣubaddhamumukṣubaddha). This is because he is characterized by a profound inner turmoil, seeking liberation while simultaneously being bound and yearning for further liberation. He is the one who is caught in a web of contradictory impulses. This is the thirty-eighth principle. Thus, these thirteen—the previously mentioned twelve plus the potentially liberated, potentially bound, and potentially liberated and bound simultaneously—constitute the thirteenfold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-eighth principle. Now begins the consideration of the thirty-ninth principle. The thirty-ninth principle is the one who is potentially bound, potentially liberated, potentially bound and liberated, potentially liberated and bound, and potentially bound, liberated, and bound simultaneously (baddhamumukṣubaddhamumukṣubaddhamumukṣubaddhabaddhamumukṣu). This is because he represents the most complex state of existence, encompassing all the preceding variations in a single individual. He is the one who is the very embodiment of the struggle between bondage and liberation. This is the thirty-ninth principle. Thus, these fourteen—the previously mentioned thirteen plus the potentially bound, potentially liberated, potentially bound and liberated, potentially liberated and bound, and potentially bound, liberated, and bound simultaneously—constitute the fourteenfold classification of Puruṣas. This concludes the section on the thirty-ninth principle. Now begins the consideration of the fortieth principle. The fortieth principle is the one who is potentially liberated, potentially bound, potentially bound and liberated, potentially liberated and bound, potentially bound, liberated, and bound

The *sattva* alone—which has been transformed into the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*)—is that which is heated by the heating *rajas*. When the *sattva* is being heated, the *puruṣa*, through the force of superimposition upon it, is said to be heated as well because he apprehends no difference from it. As the Teacher [Vācaspati Miśra] has stated: "The *sattva* exists in the form of the intellect and is that which is heated; those states which are characterized by *rajas* are the heaters.
The *puruṣa* is said to be 'heated' with respect to that tamasic state of cognition which apprehends no difference from that which is heated."
Pañcaśikha also said: "The power of the enjoyer is indeed unchanging and non-transmigratory; yet, as if transmigrated into the changing object, it follows its modifications.
By "the power of the enjoyer," the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is meant, and that is the Self itself.

The meaning is this: although the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is reflected as if transferred or mirrored into the transforming principle of the intellect (buddhitattva), it follows its modifications; thus, by falling into the shadow of the intellect, that power of consciousness appears in the intellect as if it were imitating the intellectual modifications.
Likewise, even though the Puruṣa is pure, he perceives the cognition belonging to the intellect; perceiving that, although not identical with it, he appears as if he were of its very nature.

Thus, for the person who practices in this manner, through the performance of the eight-limbed yoga—consisting of *yama*, *niyama*, and so forth—which is characterized by devotion, continuity, and long duration, and through dedication to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-praṇidhāna*), when the unobstructed discriminative discernment (*sattva-puruṣānyatā-khyāti*) arises, the five afflictions (*kleśa*) beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) are eradicated along with their very roots.
Furthermore, the latent deposits of karma (*karmāśaya*), whether wholesome or unwholesome, are destroyed root and branch.
Consequently, the state of the untainted person abiding in isolation (*kaivalya*) is established as *kaivalya*.

In this context, by the first aphorism, "Now, the instruction on yoga" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.1), the fourfold preliminary requirements—the subject matter, the purpose, the relationship, and the qualified student—which constitute the prerequisites for the engagement of a discerning person, are set forth.
Here, the word "atha" (now) is accepted as signifying the commencement of a new topic.

If it is possible for the word *atha* to have multiple meanings, how can there be a partiality toward the view that it signifies "commencement"? If it is argued: "The word *atha* has multiple meanings such as auspiciousness and so forth, as taught in the *Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana*: 'The words *atho* and *atha* [are used] in the senses of auspiciousness, sequence, commencement, inquiry, and totality' (*Amarakośa* 3.3.246). Since, although the senses of inquiry and totality are impossible here, the four meanings—sequence, auspiciousness, dependence on what was previously mentioned, and commencement—are possible, it is untenable to claim that it signifies commencement alone"—do not think thus, for [this argument] cannot withstand scrutiny.

Regarding the position that the meaning of the word *atha* is "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), it must refer either to immediacy following something or other, or to immediacy following a specific preceding cause such as tranquility (*śama*) and so forth.
It cannot be the first [alternative],
for no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action.

According to the reasoning in *Gītā* 3.5, "every living being necessarily does something after having already done something," it follows that [the commencement of yoga] is already established even without its explicit mention; thus, there would be the contingency of the word *atha* being useless for that purpose.

Nor is the latter [alternative] correct, because although yoga proceeds immediately after tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, since those are presented as the necessary conditions for the commencement of the instruction (*anuśāsana*), they lack primacy in terms of verbal expression.

Nor should it be argued that, from the perspective of the word itself, why the meaning of the word *atha* could not be the immediate succession of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth to the "instruction" (*anuśāsana*), which is the primary subject;

for by "instruction" (*anuśāsana*) one refers to the scripture (*śāstra*). This is because of the etymological derivation: that by which yoga—along with its characteristics, divisions, means, and fruits—is taught (*anuśiṣyate*) and explained (*vyākhyāyate*) is "instruction" (*anuśāsana*).

Furthermore, since the desire to communicate the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānacikhyāpayiṣā*) follows immediately after the instruction (*anuśāsana*), there is no rule that it must be preceded by tranquility, self-control, and so forth.

However, the sequence of inquiry (*jijñāsā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) being preceded by tranquility and the rest is indeed enjoined in scripture: "Therefore, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one should see the Self alone in the self" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.23), and so on.
Nor is the meaning of the word *atha* the immediate succession to the desire to communicate the knowledge of reality.
Even if that [author] were to exist, he would not be the subject matter [of this work], because he is of no use for the listener’s comprehension or engagement.
Furthermore, for you as well, is the instruction on yoga (yogānuśāsana) established as a means to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa), or not?
In the first case, it would have to be accepted even in the absence of such an author.
In the second case, even though that [nature] exists, it would be subject to abandonment;
yet its status as the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is established by valid cognition, according to the Śruti:

"Having known the God through the attainment of the yoga of the self, the wise man leaves behind joy and sorrow" (Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad 2.12), and the Smṛti: "When the intellect becomes unshakable in samādhi, then you shall attain Yoga" (Bhagavad Gītā 2.53).
For this very reason, the immediate succession [of the inquiry] following the student’s question, the practice of austerities, the use of elixirs (*rasāyana*), and so forth, has been rejected.

However, regarding the aphorism "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*, Brahma-sūtra 1.1.1), Śaṅkarācārya determined that since the desire to know Brahman cannot itself be the subject of an injunction, the word *atha* abandons its sense of "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*) as a marker of qualification; rather, it signifies the immediate succession of the tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*) prescribed in the relevant scriptural passages, for the purpose of presenting the qualified aspirant who possesses the fourfold equipment (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*).
Now, let it be granted that the word *atha* does not signify immediate succession.
Why should it not have the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*)? It could not, because auspiciousness lacks coherence with the meaning of the sentence.
Auspiciousness is the attainment of what is desired without being censured. And "desired" means that which is sought after in the form of the attainment of happiness and the avoidance of suffering.
Furthermore, since the instruction on yoga (*yogānuśāsana*) is neither pleasure nor the cessation of pain, it does not possess the quality of being auspicious (*maṅgalatā*).

Consequently, it does not follow that "the instruction on yoga is auspicious. Moreover, because the hearing of the word *atha*—like the sound of a drum—is itself an effect, it is impossible for auspiciousness to be either its denoted meaning (*vācya*) or its indicated meaning (*lakṣya*). Just as a secondary purpose (*arthikārtha*) does not enter into the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), so too an effect (*kārya*) would not enter into it.
Because there is no difference in their not being word-meanings (*padārtha*). For it is only a word-meaning that is integrated into the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
Otherwise, for those who hold verbal testimony to be a valid means of knowledge, the established principle that "verbal expectancy is fulfilled by words alone" would be violated.

Now, at the commencement of a treatise, one ought to perform an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) in order to pacify the multitude of obstacles that hinder the completion of the work one has begun, and to maintain the tradition of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). For it has been said by the authoritative masters: "Treatises that begin with an auspicious word, have an auspicious word in the middle, and end with an auspicious word, flourish; they become possessed of long-lived authors and possessed of heroic authors" (*Pātañjala-mahābhāṣya* 1.3.1).
Furthermore, the word *atha* possesses the sense of auspiciousness: "The syllable *Oṃ* and the word *atha*—these two were formerly [uttered] by Brahmā..."

"Having pierced the throat, they both emerged; therefore, both are auspicious"—since such a tradition exists in the Smṛti, one might argue that, like the words *vṛddhi* and others in the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1), the word *atha* must have the sense of auspiciousness. Do not speak thus! For even when the word *atha* is employed to express another meaning, its status as having the fruit of auspiciousness through mere hearing—like the sound of a lute or a flute—is established.

If it is asked: "How can the word *atha*, which has as its fruit the cognition of the meaning of a sentence that initiates a different subject matter (*arthāntarārambha*), have a different fruit [such as auspiciousness]?"—we say no, because such a possibility exists, just like the perception of a water-jar being carried for another purpose. Nor does this contradict the traditional Smṛti.
The word *atha* is used here with the intention of expressing that it serves as an auspicious invocation (*maṅgalaprayojana*), because such usage is established for that purpose.

Nor does the word *atha* depend upon what was previously mentioned, for even if it were so, it would result in no difference from mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and thus the previously stated objections would still apply.

In the deliberative statement, "Is this word *atha* intended for the purpose of introduction (*adhikāra*), or is it intended for the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*)? and so forth, although other alternatives may be proposed, they are impossible in the present context. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the specific point is stated: the word *atha* signifies the commencement of that which is to be understood as the subject matter (*adhikāra*).

Just as in the passage, "Now this is the Jyotis, now this is the Viśvajyotis," the word *atha* is accepted as signifying the commencement of a particular sacrifice, and just as in the passage, "Now begins the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*), the word *atha* signifies the introduction of the science of grammar, so it is here as well.

Regarding that, in the *Vyāsabhāṣya*, which is devoted to the exposition of the *Yogasūtras*, it is stated: "The word *atha* is employed here in the sense of an introduction (*adhikāra*). Vācaspati explained this as follows: "In the view that this word *atha* signifies an introduction, because the yoga about to be presented by the treatise is brought forward, the student’s engagement with the text occurs through an easy comprehension achieved by explaining the intended meaning of the entire scripture; thus, the status of the word *atha* as signifying an introduction is established."

If it is asked, "But how can Patañjali be the teacher of Yoga, given the Yājñavalkya-smṛti which states: 'Hiraṇyagarbha is the ancient speaker of Yoga, and no other'?"—it is true. For this very reason, the Lord who is an ocean of compassion, the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa), perceiving that Yoga was scattered here and there in the Purāṇas and elsewhere and its meaning difficult to grasp, commenced this instruction with the desire to collect its essence; he did not, however, act as its original author.
When this word *atha* has the sense of "commencement" (*adhikāra*), then the meaning of the sentence becomes as follows: "The treatise on the instruction of yoga is to be understood as commenced.
Therefore, it is established that this word *atha* indicates commencement and serves the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).
In that treatise, yoga—along with its means and its results—is the subject matter (*viṣaya*) because it is what is to be explained.
The intermediate fruit is the thorough understanding of that [yoga].
The ultimate purpose of the yoga thus understood is liberation (*kaivalya*).
The relationship between the treatise and yoga is characterized by the nature of the object to be explained and the means of explanation.
The relationship between yoga and liberation (kaivalya) is characterized by that of the means and the end.
Furthermore, I have already stated previously that this is well-established through scripture and other authorities.
It follows as a matter of course that those who aspire for liberation alone are the qualified practitioners (adhikārin).
Nor should one suspect that the qualification of the seeker is established only by implication in passages such as "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.1).

For in that case, since the qualification is already established through the word *atha*, which—by way of denoting immediate succession—serves to provide the qualified person, there is no possibility of it being merely implied.
Precisely for this reason it has been said: "When [a requirement] is obtained from direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), there is no room for context (*prakaraṇa*) and the other [means of proof]."

The meaning of this is as follows: for it is only where the meaning is not obtained through direct statement (*śruti*) that context (*prakaraṇa*) and the other means provide the meaning, not elsewhere.
However, where the meaning is apprehended from the word itself, there no other means can apply;

because once the application has been made known by the directly expressive *śruti*, which brings about immediate understanding, the other means find no scope due to the resulting lack of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*).

Furthermore, when an object has been made known by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), does the context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth present an object that contradicts it, or one that is not contradictory? Not the first, because that which conveys a contradictory meaning would be sublated.
Not the latter, because it would be redundant.

Thus it is said: "In the case of a conflict between direct scriptural statement, indicative mark, syntactical connection, context, position, and name, each subsequent one is weaker than the preceding due to the remoteness of the meaning" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.3.14).
And it is said: "The direct Vedic statement (śruti) is always sublated, while the designation (samākhyā) is always sublated;
but for those in between, there is both sublation and sublation-by-relation.

Therefore, it is established that the instruction on yoga (yogānuśāsana) is a treatise that ought to be commenced, because it possesses a subject matter and other such requirements, just like the treatise concerning the inquiry into Brahman.
If it is argued that it is indeed *yoga* alone that is introduced here as the subject to be explained, and not the treatise (*śāstra*), that is true;
however, *yoga* is introduced primarily as the object to be expounded.
And since that [yoga] is expounded by means of the treatise which has it as its subject matter, the treatise is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for its exposition.
Furthermore, the operation of an agent does not function within the domain of the object; rather, it functions within the domain of the instrument.
For example, the action of the cutter Devadatta—consisting of raising, lowering, and so forth—is directed toward the instrument, the axe, and not toward the object, such as the tree.
Likewise, with respect to the act of teaching by the speaker Patañjali, the Yoga subject matter is the domain of the instrument, which is the treatise (śāstra).
However, with regard to the function of denotation, the distinction is that it belongs to yoga alone.
Consequently, the undertaking of the Yoga-śāstra is rendered plausible.
And here, the yoga to be taught is stated to be the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (citta-vṛtti-nirodha).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the word *yoga*, derived from the root *yuj* which is listed as having the meaning "joining" (*saṃyoga*), must denote only conjunction and not cessation (*nirodha*)?

For this very reason, Yājñavalkya stated: "The union of the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) is called *yoga*. [Reply: This is merely a superficial argument, because the cause for a conjunction between the individual and the supreme selves—such as the action of one or the other—is impossible; furthermore, an eternal conjunction (*ajasaṃyoga*) has been rejected by Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, and others.

Even if that [yoga] were accepted according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, it would result in the futility of the scripture because that which is eternally established lacks the quality of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, since verbal roots have multiple meanings, it is logical for the root *yuj* to signify "concentration" (*samādhi*).
As it has been said: "Particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and verbal roots (*dhātu*)—these three..."
"All words are remembered as having multiple meanings; their recitation is merely an illustration.
For this very reason, some also read the root *yuj* in the sense of "concentration" (*samādhi*), stating: "*yuj* in concentration.
Nor is there any contradiction with the statement of Yājñavalkya.
For even when the word "yoga" refers to that state, it has the meaning of "samādhi," as it has been stated by that very same author:
"Samādhi is the state of equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
that which is the abiding of the inner self (pratyagātman) in Brahman alone is samādhi."
This was stated by the venerable Vyāsa: "Yoga is samādhi" (Yogabhāṣya 1.1).

Now, an objection may be raised: if this is so, then it has been stated by Patañjali that among the eight limbs of yoga, the final limb is samādhi (Pātañjala Yogasūtra 2.29): "Restraint, observance, posture, breath-control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and samādhi are the eight limbs of yoga.

Furthermore, a constituent part cannot itself become the whole, for the relationship between the beneficiary and the benefactor—as seen in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the Prayāja offerings—is one of absolute distinction due to their having different bases.

If it is argued that, for this reason, even *samādhi* cannot logically be the meaning of the word "yoga," we reply: that is not tenable. For, while the term *samādhi*—which denotes the final limb [of yoga]—was defined as "that very [state] in which only the object appears and which is, as it were, devoid of its own form" (*Pātañjala Yogasūtra* 3.3), it is appropriate to employ it as a designation for the whole (*yoga*) by intending to express its non-difference from the parts.
Furthermore, a word does not function everywhere solely on the basis of its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*).
If that were the case, since the word "cow" (*go*) is derived from the sense of "going" (*gacchati*), a cow standing still would not be a cow.
And Devadatta, while walking, would become a cow;
for the ground for the application [of the term] has already been stated as "the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*cittavṛttinirodha*).
Thus it is said: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind" (*yogaścittavṛttinirodhaḥ*, Pātañjala Yogasūtra 1.2).

Now, if yoga is intended to be the cessation of the mental modifications (vṛtti), then since those modifications are of the nature of cognition and reside in the self, their cessation—designated by the term "destruction" (pradhvaṃsa)—would also have that [self] as its locus; for there is a rule that antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and destruction must share the same locus as their counter-positive (pratiyogin).

And if it is argued that, according to the principle that "a property undergoing appearance and disappearance indeed modifies the substratum," the immutability (*kauṭasthya*) of the Self would be destroyed—that too is untenable. For we accept that the mental modifications (*vṛtti*), which are the counter-correlates of cessation and consist of valid cognition, error, conceptualization, sleep, and memory, are properties of the *citta*—which is synonymous with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth.
The immutable, eternal power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), being unchanging, cannot possibly be the locus of the properties of cognition.

Nor should it be thought that the unchangeability of the power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) is unproven; for the power of consciousness is unchanging because it is eternally the knower, as can be established by such inference as: "Whatever is not thus [eternally a knower] is not thus [unchanging], like the mind and so forth.
Likewise, if this *puruṣa* were subject to change, then because change occurs only occasionally, the eternal cognition of those mental modifications (*citta-vṛtti*) would be untenable.

Since the pure *sattva*, which is the internal organ (*antaraṅga*) of the conscious Puruṣa who always exists as the presiding witness, also exists eternally, the Puruṣa’s state of non-attachment is possible because whatever object it becomes colored by is always capable of being manifested through the falling of the shadow of consciousness (*cicchāyāpatti*).
Consequently, his status as the eternal knower is established, and thus no suspicion of transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) ever arises.

Furthermore, that object by which the mind becomes colored (uparakta) is known, while that by which it is not colored remains unknown. Since the mind possesses the property of being colored or uncolored—which serves as the cause for the knowledge or ignorance of an object that is like a magnet—it is said to be subject to transformation (pariṇāmī).

Now, an objection might be raised: since the mind and the senses, which are derived from ego-consciousness (ahaṃkārika), are all-pervading (sarvagata), they must always be in contact with all objects.

If it is argued that, in that case, knowledge would result for everyone, at all times, and regarding everything—[we reply: no, because even though [the mind] is all-pervading, knowledge arises for this [mind] only with respect to those objects which are connected to that body in which the mind possesses its function (vṛtti), and not with respect to others; thus there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For this very reason, it has been said that objects, which are like magnets, color the mind—which possesses properties similar to iron—by connecting with it through the channel of the senses.
Therefore, the modifications (vṛttis) are attributes of the mind, not of the Self.

And thus says the Śruti: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intellect, and fear—all these are indeed the mind alone" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.3).
The unchangeability of the power of consciousness was declared by the teacher Pañcaśikha: "The power of the enjoyer is unchanging.
Patañjali also stated: "The fluctuations of the mind are always known to its master, the Puruṣa, because of his unchangeability" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 4.18).
An inference regarding the mutability of the mind is stated: the mind is mutable because its objects are both known and unknown, like the sense of hearing and so forth.
Furthermore, mutation is well known to be threefold, distinguished by the differences of *dharma*, *lakṣaṇa*, and *avasthā*.
The perception of blue and other objects by the mind, which is the substratum (*dharmin*), is the *dharma*-mutation, just as bracelets, crowns, and armlets are mutations of gold.
The modification of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*) consists of the presentness and so forth of a dharma;
the modification of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) consists of the clarity and so forth of the perception of blue and other objects;
and the modification of state consists of the newness and antiquity of a bracelet and the like.
In this same way, the threefold transformation should be inferred elsewhere as well, according to what is possible.
And thus, since the modifications such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are properties of the mind, their cessation also has that very [mind] as its locus; therefore, nothing is untenable.

Now, if one accepts that "yoga is the cessation of modifications," then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that states such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth would constitute yoga, because the cessation of the modifications of the mind—such as those that are distracted (*kṣipta*) or stupefied (*mūḍha*)—is possible therein.

And this is not tenable, because in states such as the "distracted" (kṣipta), the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth is impossible, and because they are obstacles to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). To explain: that which is called "distracted" is the unstable mind being tossed about among various objects.
That which is submerged in the ocean of darkness, permeated by the state of sleep, is proclaimed as "deluded" (*mūḍha*).

A mind that is superior to the "scattered" (kṣipta) state is called "distracted" (vikṣipta). This distinction refers to the stability—though only occasional—that arises in even an unstable mind when it encounters an object, according to the principle stated in the Gītā: "The mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate" (6.34). This instability may be either innate or produced by the persistence of diseases and other such afflictions.

Thus it is said: "Illness, languor, doubt, negligence, laziness, lack of renunciation, erroneous perception, failure to attain a stage, and instability—these are the distractions of the mind; they are the obstacles" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.30).
Among these, illness (*vyādhi*) refers to fever and the like, caused by an imbalance of the three humors (*doṣa*).
Languor (*styāna*) is the mind's lack of serviceability (*akarmaṇyatva*).
Doubt is a cognition that penetrates two contradictory alternatives.
Negligence is the failure to cultivate the means for achieving meditative concentration.
Laziness is the lack of application due to heaviness of body, speech, and mind.

Non-abstinence is the longing for sense objects. Delusion is the perception of something as what it is not. Not having attained a stage [of meditative concentration] is the failure to acquire a stage of samādhi due to some cause.
Even when that [one-pointedness] is attained, the mind’s lack of stability is its non-abiding; this is the meaning.

Therefore, if it is argued that the cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti-nirodha*) does not deserve to be included within the category of Yoga—do not speak thus. For although the cessation of fluctuations cannot constitute Yoga during the three undesirable states such as the "distracted" (*kṣipta*) and so forth, it can indeed constitute Yoga during the two desirable states of "one-pointedness" (*ekāgra*) and "restricted" (*niruddha*). A mind that is focused on a single object is called one-pointed.
The mind, in which all fluctuations have ceased and only the latent impressions (saṃskāra) remain, is said to be "ceased.
And that samādhi is of two kinds,
distinguished as cognitive (saṃprajñāta) and non-cognitive (asaṃprajñāta).

In that state, when the mind is one-pointed, the cessation of the fluctuations such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which have external objects is *samprajñāta* samādhi. This is because of the etymological derivation: "that in which the object of meditation is correctly known (*samyak-prajñāyate*) through its distinction from primordial nature (*prakṛti*). It is of four kinds, according to the divisions beginning with *savitarka*. Samādhi is indeed cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

And that [meditation] consists in the repeated placement of the mind upon the object of meditation by means of avoiding other objects. The object of meditation is twofold: the Lord and the principles (tattvas).
These, too, are twofold, based on the distinction between the insentient and the sentient.

The twenty-four principles beginning with *prakṛti*, *mahat*, and *ahaṃkāra* are insentient (*jaḍa*), while the *puruṣa* is sentient (*ajaḍa*). Among these, when contemplation (*bhāvanā*) proceeds by taking gross objects such as earth and so forth as its objects, through the synthesis of preceding and succeeding moments and through the blending of the mental reflection on words and their meanings, that is *samādhi* with deliberation (*savitarka*).

When cultivation proceeds by taking as its object a subtle entity characterized by the subtle elements (tanmātra) and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), delimited by space and so forth, then it is "with deliberation" (savicāra).
When the mind is cultivated while permeated by even slight traces of rajas and tamas, then, due to the predominance of sattva—which consists of bliss and luminosity—it is "with joy" (sānanda).

When cultivation proceeds by taking as its object pure sattva that is not overwhelmed by even slight traces of rajas and tamas, then, because of the subsiding of sattva and the predominance of the power of consciousness (citiśakti), that samādhi is "with the sense of self" (sāsmita), as it remains as pure existence alone.
As it was stated by Patañjali: "Cognitive [samādhi] arises from being accompanied by vitarka, vicāra, ānanda, and asmitā" (Pātañjala Yogasūtra 1.17).

However, when all fluctuations [of the mind] are suppressed, that is asamprajñāta samādhi. If it is objected: "If yoga is defined as the suppression of all fluctuations, then there would be no pervasion (vyāpti) in the case of cognitive samādhi, because the fluctuation characterized by the discriminative discernment of the difference between the sattva and the puruṣa—which is dominated by sattva—is not suppressed therein"—this objection is invalid. For we accept that yoga is the suppression of those mental fluctuations which stand in opposition to the afflictions (kleśa), karma, its fruition (vipāka), and their latent impressions (āśaya).
Furthermore, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are established as being fivefold: "Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the afflictions" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.3).

Now, in the term *avidyā* (ignorance), what is relied upon? Is it the predominance of the first member of the compound, as in the case of *amakṣikaṃ vartate* ("there is no fly")? Or is it the predominance of the second member, as in *rājapuruṣaḥ* ("the king's man")? Or is it the predominance of a meaning distinct from both members, as in *amakṣiko deśaḥ* ("a place where there are no flies")?

In this regard, the first [alternative] is not tenable; for if the meaning of the prior member were predominant, it would follow that *avidyā* is a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), which makes its status as a producer of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth impossible, and it would also result in the word *avidyā* lacking feminine gender. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable; for knowledge (*vidyā*) qualified by the absence of something cannot logically be the seed of those [afflictions], since it stands in opposition to them.

The third [alternative] is not tenable; for according to the statement of the author of the *Vṛtti*, "A *bahuvrīhi* compound may be formed with words meaning 'existent' after the word 'nañ', or there may be elision of the final member," the compound *avidyā* would mean "that intellect (*buddhi*) which has no knowledge (*vidyā*)," and it is illogical for such an intellect to be the seed of afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth. Furthermore, it would follow that even the intellect endowed with the cessation of all mental fluctuations preceded by discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) would be of that nature [i.e., a seed of afflictions]. Moreover, it has been stated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the source of the afflictions such as egoism (*asmitā*) and the rest: "Ignorance is the field for these [afflictions], whether they are dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active" (*Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra* 2.4).
Dormancy is non-manifestation due to the absence of the auxiliary conditions for awakening.
Thinning is the loosening [of the afflictions] through the cultivation of their opposites.
Interruption is the suppression by a more powerful affliction.
Magnanimity (*udāratva*) is the capacity to produce an effect due to the proximity of auxiliary factors.

This was stated by Vācaspatimiśra in his commentary on the Vyāsa-bhāṣya: "The afflictions are dormant in those [who have realized] the principles, attenuated in yogis, and manifest in their gross form in those attached to sense objects."

Since two independent word-meanings are not understood as being like those in a *dvandva* compound, the possibility that both word-meanings are primary has not been raised. Therefore, [one might argue] that in all three positions, the well-established fact that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root cause of afflictions and so forth would be lost. Even this does not appear sound, because the elders accept that by relying on the power of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the word "ignorance" denotes a cognition contrary to knowledge (*vidyā*), namely, erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*). As it is said: "But when joined with a noun or a verbal root, the negative particle (*nañ*) is certainly not a negator."

"It speaks of non-Brahminhood and unrighteousness as being opposed to anything other than [the specific individuals]. And: "For us, the meaning of every word is to be understood through the usage of the elders;
therefore, that which has been employed in a particular instance is not to be removed from it."
Vācaspatimiśra has also stated: "The relationship between a word and its meaning is determined by worldly usage.

And in the world, it is observed that even the negative particle (*nañ*), though subordinate to the following word, functions in various instances by negating the meaning of that following word because it is its opposite; therefore, here too, it operates toward what is contrary to it.

With this very point in mind, it was said: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self" (Pātañjala Sūtra 2.5).
Thus, it is said that "error" (viparyaya) is the cognition of something as being what it is not.
For example: the conceit of permanence regarding impermanent things such as a jar;
and the notion of purity regarding the impure body and so forth.
Because of its place of origin, its seed, its support, its discharge, and its end,
as well as because it requires purification, the wise indeed know the body to be impure.

"According to the principle stated in the *Pātañjala-yoga-sūtra* (2.15), 'To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the guṇas,' there is the superimposition of happiness upon things such as garlands, sandalwood, and women which are actually suffering.
Likewise, there is the notion of a self with regard to what is not the self, such as the body and so forth.
As it has been said: 'The embodied beings possess the notion of a self with regard to the body and other things that are not the self.'"
Ignorance, the bondage caused by it, and its destruction are called liberation.
Thus, this ignorance consists of four parts.

Now, one might ask: must not some common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that runs through these specific types of ignorance be described, otherwise the specific [instances] would not be established?
As it has been said by the Bhaṭṭācāryas: "Without a general definition, the definition of the specific alone [is impossible]."
It is not possible to state it as something absolute; therefore, even for this [reason], it is not expressible.
That too should not be asserted,
because it has already been answered by the definition of the universal characteristic as "the cognition of that in what is not that.
Asmitā is the conceit of oneness between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, [in the form] "I am."
That too has been stated: "Asmitā is the identity, as it were, of the powers of the seer and the seeing" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.6).
Attachment (*rāga*) is the greed in the form of thirst for the means of pleasure, preceded by the recollection of pleasure by one who has experienced pleasure.
Aversion (*dveṣa*) is the turning away from the means of pain, preceded by the recollection of that [pain] by one who has experienced pain.

As it has been said: "Attachment is that which lies latent in pleasure" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.7), and "Aversion is that which lies latent in pain" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.8). In this context, regarding the word *anuśayin*, is the suffix *ṇini* intended in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*), or is the possessive suffix *ini* intended? It cannot be the first, because in the rule *supyajātau ṇinistācchīlye* (Pāṇini 3.2.78), since the term *supi* is already present, the repetition of *sub* is for the purpose of excluding verbal prefixes; consequently, the suffix *ṇini* cannot arise after a verbal root that is accompanied by a prefix.

Even if one were to somehow accept that [the suffix *ini* is applied], since the rule "aco ñṇiti" (Pāṇini 7.2.115) would entail the application of *vṛddhi*, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of using the word *anuśāyin* just as one uses words such as *atiśāyin*. Nor is the second alternative [correct], because its prohibition is stated in the rule: "The two [suffixes *ini* and *ṭhan*] are not prescribed after a monosyllable, after a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, after a genus name, or when a locative case follows"; and here, the word *anuśaya* ends in the vowel *a* and is thus a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix. Therefore, if you argue that the word *anuśayin* cannot be properly formed—this is not sound, because it shows a lack of understanding of the matter.
This statement is intended to express a general rule (*prāyika*).
For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* stated: "The particle *iti* is used for the sake of specifying the intended meaning and is connected everywhere.
Consequently, in some instances, the forms *kāryī*, *kāryikaḥ*, *taṇḍulī*, and *taṇḍulikaḥ* occur.
Thus, it is established that the prohibition [of the suffix -in] after a word ending in a *kṛt* affix and after a genus-term (*jāti*) is merely general.

Since the word *anuśaya* ends in a *kṛt* affix, its derivation from the root *śī* with the prefix *anu* is justified. The fifth affliction (*kleśa*) is *abhiniveśa*, which is the nature of fear arising—without any external cause—every day in every living being, from the lowest worm up to the wise man, due to the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from experiencing the pain of death in previous births. It manifests as the thought, "May my separation from the body, objects, and so forth not occur. This is proven by the individual experience of each person in the form of the prayer, "May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist."
Thus it is said: "The instinctive clinging (*abhiniveśa*), which flows spontaneously, is rooted even in the wise" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.9).
These five, beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), are well known as the "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because they afflict the person by being the cause for the presentation of various worldly sufferings.
Actions (*karman*) consist of prescribed and prohibited forms, such as the *jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and the killing of a Brahmin, respectively.
The ripenings (*vipāka*) are the fruits of karma, namely birth, lifespan, and enjoyments.
The latent dispositions (*āśaya*) are the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of merit and demerit, so called because they lie within the ground of the mind until the ripening of their fruit.
Yoga is the cessation of the mental fluctuations that obstruct those [dispositions].
Cessation (*nirodha*) is not intended as mere non-existence, because, being a void, it lacks the capacity to produce the direct realization of the nature of existence.

Rather, it is a specific state of the mind (*citta*) which serves as the substratum for that [realization]—designated as *madhumatī*, *madhupratīkā*, *viśokā*, and *asaṃskāraśeṣa*—since the etymological derivation "in this [state], the mental fluctuations such as valid cognition and the rest are ceased" is thus justified. As it is said: "The cessation of fluctuations occurs through practice and dispassion."
In that regard, "effort toward stability is practice" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.13).
Stability is a specific transformation of the mind— free from fluctuations— which consists in abiding in its own nature and taking the form of a tranquil flow.
Taking that as the objective, the repeated application of the mind toward its true nature is practice (*abhyāsa*).
It is stated that this locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of the "objective" (*nimitta*), as in the expression "one kills the leopard for its skin.
"Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 1.15).

Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is said to be the discernment of one who is free from desire for objects pertaining to this world or the next, having seen their defects, thinking: "These objects are under my control; I am not under their control.

First, a yogi must be intent on the practice of *kriyā-yoga* (action yoga) in order to attenuate the afflictions (*kleśa*) that obstruct *samādhi* and to attain *samādhi*, because it is through the accomplishment of *kriyā-yoga* that both practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion become possible. As the Blessed One has said: "For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means."
"For one who has ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the cause" (Bhagavad Gītā 6.3).

And the yoga of action (*kriyāyoga*) was taught by Patañjali: "Austerity (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) constitute the yoga of action" (Pātañjala Yoga Sūtra 2.1).
The nature of austerity was defined by Yājñavalkya: "By means of the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances, according to the path prescribed by rule..."
"They say that the emaciation of the body is the highest austerity among all austerities.
The study of mantras such as the *praṇava* and the *gāyatrī* is *svādhyāya*.
These mantras are of two kinds: Vedic and Tantric.
The Vedic [texts] are of two kinds: those that are set to melody (*pragīta*) and those that are not set to melody (*apragīta*).
Among these, those set to melody are the *Sāmans*.
Those not set to melody are of two kinds: those composed in metrical form (*chandobaddha*) and those that differ from that.
Among those, the first are the *ṛc*s and the second are the *yajus* formulas.
This has been stated by Jaimini: "The *ṛk* is that where there is a division into quarters (*pāda*) according to the sense;
the designation *sāman* applies to the melodies."
"The term *yajuḥ* applies to the remainder" (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.33–35).
Among the *tantras*, those described in the *Āgamas* such as the *Kāmika*, *Kāraṇa*, and *Prapañca* are the *tāntrika* [mantras].
Furthermore, these mantras are of three kinds, distinguished as female, male, and neuter.
Thus it is said: "The classes of mantras are threefold according to whether they are feminine, masculine, or neuter.
Feminine mantras end with the wife of fire (svāhā), while those that end with 'namas' are neuter."

"The remaining males are praised as perfected (siddha) for rites such as subjugation (vaśya) and so forth. Even in the absence of sacraments (saṃskāra) from birth onwards, they possess the status of being "perfected" because they are the cause of success due to having all defects eliminated. And those ten types of sacraments are described in the *Śāradātilaka*: "Ten sacraments of mantras, which bestow success, are now declared."
Those mantras, when properly refined, quickly attain a state free from defects.
Birth, vivification, striking, awakening, consecration, then purification and nourishment,
as well as satiation, illumination, and concealment— these ten are the purificatory rites of mantra.
The extraction of mantras from the yantra of the Mātṛkās is known as their "birth."
The wise one should recite the syllables of the mantra with the Praṇava (Om) interspersed between them;
for they declare that this practice, performed according to the number of the mantra's syllables, is indeed "Jīvana" (the life-giving).
Having inscribed the syllables of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water;
striking each one individually with the seed-syllable of Vāyu is what is called "striking" (tāḍana).
Having written the syllables of the mantra with oleander flowers (karavīra), one should strike them with as many flowers as there are syllables in the mantra; this is known as "awakening" (bodhana).
Following the procedure prescribed in his own Tantra,
the mantra-practitioner should consecrate the mantra with pipal (aśvattha) sprouts, equal in number to the syllables of the mantra, for the sake of purification.

Having reflected upon the mantra with the mind, the practitioner of mantra should burn away the three impurities within the mantra by means of the Jyotir-mantra; for that is indeed the purification of the mantra.
The mantra of light is declared to consist of the syllables *tāra*, *vyoma*, *agni*, *manu*, and *yug*.
With this mantra, one should perform a sprinkling with water from kusha grass, reciting it for each individual syllable of the mantra.
This nourishment is considered to be performed according to rule by means of the water-seed [syllable];
the satiation of the mantra with consecrated water is known as *tarpaṇa*.
The conjunction of *tāra*, *māyā*, and *ramā* is called the "illumination" (*dīpana*) of the mantra;
the "concealment" (*gopana*) of the mantra being recited is its non-disclosure.
These ten consecrations of the mantras are secreted in all tantras;
by performing them according to the tradition, the mantra-practitioner attains his desired goal.
Even those [mantras] that are obstructed, pinned down, severed, dormant, or cursed—
such defects of mantra are destroyed by these supreme consecrations.
Therefore, enough with this premature, frantic proclamation of the secrets of the Mantra-śāstra!

What is called "devotion to the Lord" (īśvarapraṇidhāna) is the dedication of all actions—both those explicitly mentioned and those not mentioned—to the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Teacher, without regard for their fruits. Regarding this, it has been said: "Whatever I do, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whether intentionally or unintentionally," [I offer that all to You].
All that has been entrusted to you; impelled by you, I perform it.
Even the renunciation of the fruits of action is indeed *praṇidhāna*—a synonym for a particular form of devotion—because it consists in performing action without aiming for results.
Thus it is sung by the Blessed One in the *Gītā*: "Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits;
let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction."

Thus it is said in the Bhagavadgītā (2.47). The venerable Nīlakaṇṭhabhāratī has stated that the desire for results acts as a corruption [of spiritual practice]: "Even penance accomplished with great effort, if corrupted by desire, does not lead to the satisfaction of Maheśvara, just like milk-rice licked by a dog."

And that practice, consisting of austerity (tapas), self-study (svādhyāya), and devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna), is designated as "yoga" because it is a means for achieving yoga; this is determined by resorting to the definition of *śuddhasāropalakṣaṇā*, as in the expression "clarified butter is life.
*Śuddhasāropalakṣaṇā* is a specific variety of *lakṣaṇā*.
*Lakṣaṇā* is the indication of another meaning through the sublation of the primary sense and its connection [to that other meaning].
It is of two kinds:
