As it has been said: "In the perception of a yellow conch, the yellowness residing in the bile located within the sense organ is apprehended through a defect as if it were devoid of its substance."
Due to a defect in the sense organ, the whiteness of the conch is not perceived;
only the substance itself appears, devoid of its color.
When a quality dependent on a substance and a substance requiring a quality appear [simultaneously],
the cognition of those two does not perceive their lack of connection.
Even when there is the appearance of truth, these two cognitions appear as equal;
likewise, conventional practice is similar in this case as well, and thus it is appropriate here too.
(Prakaraṇapañcikā 4.48–51).

Now, one might object: "If an erroneous cognition in the form 'this is silver' is not admitted, then since the appearance of silver would be non-existent, how could the negation 'this is not silver' convey the absence of silver? This is not a fault;

for by accepting the negation of the practical usage of silver with respect to mother-of-pearl—which was occasioned by the non-apprehension of their difference—there is the presence of conceptual parsimony (*kalpanālāghava*).

As it has been stated in the *Pañcikāprakaraṇa*: "Even though it is false, because it initiates a conventional usage identical to that [of the real object], it does not deceive a person regarding the aspect of the conventional usage of silver."
Therefore, it is held that even a subverting cognition possesses the quality of being a subverter,
because it does not prevent the occurrence of the conventional usage of "silver" that would otherwise result.
Thus [it is said in] *Prakaraṇapañcikā* (4.38–39).
By this, the doubt—namely, how there can be the established status of error for those two former cognitions if they are true—is refuted;
for that [status of error] is logically accounted for by their causing activity that does not correspond to reality (*ayathāvyavahāra*).
Furthermore, the subverting cognition "this is not silver" does not apprehend a non-existence (abhāva),
because non-existence cannot be grasped apart from a positive entity (bhāva).
If this is so, my friend, what is the objective support (ālambana) for the cognition "it does not exist"?
If it is argued that otherwise one would fall into the position of the Māhābhāṇika school, do not speak thus.

For you must necessarily admit that non-existence (*abhāva*) is defined in dependence upon the definition of its locus (*dharmin*) and its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Since the linguistic usage "it does not exist" is established by the mere cognition of the locus—whether the counter-positive is perceptible or imperceptible, or merely remembered—there is no evidence for postulating a non-existence as a distinct entity.
As it is said in the *Amṛtakalā*: "In this regard, it is said that there are two types of cognition regarding an object such as a floor."
One [type of non-perception] has a mixed object as its domain, while the other has the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) as its domain;
furthermore, that which has the subtle elements as its domain is said to be twofold:
when the counter-correlative is invisible and when the counter-correlative is visible.
In that case, this cognition of the mere locus, when the counter-correlate has been remembered,
is itself the non-existence of the counter-correlate, such as a jar, on that portion of ground.
Thus [it is said in] *Prakaraṇapañcikā* (6.37–39).
For this very reason, the followers of the Prābhākara school have elaborated upon only five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in their *Pramāṇapārāyaṇa*.
Now, one might object: "If non-existence (*abhāva*) were thus absent, would it not follow that the negative particle (*na-kāra*) is rendered useless?"

If it is argued that this would result in a contradiction with the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), that is a trivial objection; for among the forty-nine letters, no letter is observed to have the meaning of "non-existence," and thus it is impossible for the existing letter *na* to have that meaning.
Nor does this entail a contradiction with the grammatical rule.

The purpose of the instruction regarding things other than that, the absence of that, and things contradictory to that would be as follows: among sentient beings, one is the enemy of another, one is the friend of another, and one is indifferent to another; likewise, this applies even to insentient things. By the term "other than that" (*tadanya*), the meaning of the negative particle (*na*) refers to that which is indifferent to it.
By the word "contrary" (viruddha), the enemy is the meaning of the negative particle (na);

by the word "absence thereof" (tad-abhāva), the friend is the meaning of the negative particle. Thus, in the very word *abrāhmaṇa*, these three are understood: the Śūdra as the neutral, the Yavana as the enemy, and the Kṣatriya as the friend.
Thus, this should be understood to apply everywhere in instances where a negative particle (*nañ*) is employed; therefore, no absence (*abhāva*) exists as something distinct from existence (*bhāva*).

Consequently, by the aforementioned method and based on common experience, it is established that the cognitions under dispute are valid, because they are cognitions, just like the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍīti pratyaya*).
Others, however, do not accept this.
Indeed, in this world, every discerning person engages in activity upon the cognition of either the desired object itself or the means to achieve it.
However, for one who desires silver, the cognition of a fragment of mother-of-pearl is not capable of making that [silver] appear as its form,
because the fragment of mother-of-pearl is neither the desired object nor the means to achieve it.
Nor is the recollection of silver the cause of activity toward the object present before one;
for, being dependent upon experience, it can only induce activity in the very place where that experience occurred.
Nor is the non-apprehension of difference the cause of practical engagement.
[Objection: Since linguistic usage regarding consciousness is based on apprehension, one might argue:
"We do not assert that each [of these factors] individually is the cause, such that we should be reproached in this way.

Rather, it is the two cognitions—whose distinction has not been grasped—which have attained a similarity to the cognition of silver present before one; therefore, this reproach is misplaced. [Response: This too is incorrect.
Because it cannot withstand critical analysis.

To explain: that which prompts action is either (1) the similarity to a correct appearance of silver as it manifests, by its mere existence, or (2) the similarity grasped in a general manner, namely, the non-apprehension of the difference between these two cognitions—which is synonymous with "non-apprehension of distinction"—characterized by the thought, "These two cognitions resemble a correct one. Regarding the first alternative, does the similarity function as the cause of activity while being grasped in a specific form, or does it do so while being grasped in a general form, such that there exists a non-apprehension of the mutual difference between these two [cognitions] themselves, both in their own nature and in respect to their objects?
Not the first [alternative],
because it is impossible for a cognition resembling a correct cognition to initiate the appropriate practical activity (vyavahāra),
just as the appearance "the gavaya resembles a cow" does not prompt one who seeks a cow to act toward a gavaya.

Not the second, because it is self-contradictory. Indeed, when one grasps these two as "these two," there can be no cognition that "there is a non-apprehension of difference" regarding them, for they have not been apprehended as distinct.

Therefore, by process of elimination, it must be admitted that similarity—in the form of the non-apprehension of difference—serves as the cause of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) by its mere existence.

If you say, "Let it be so," then this must be considered here: does this non-apprehension of difference serve as the cause of linguistic usage through the process of producing a superimposition (*samāropa*), or does it do so by itself without having produced a superimposition?
And the second alternative is not the better one.
It should be understood that since linguistic usage arises by that much alone, the imposition [of superimposition] is marred by the fault of unnecessary complexity;
for, given the rule that specific linguistic usage is necessarily preceded by the knowledge of a qualified object, it would be untenable for it to be preceded by ignorance.

Now, if someone—failing to grasp the opponent's underlying intention—should suspect that this linguistic usage is not preceded by ignorance because it is established by his own accepted tenets, he should be answered as follows.

Since the perception of the object as a mother-of-pearl shell cannot be the cause for the activity of one seeking silver—because its object is not the desired one—and since, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is possible for the cognition of silver to be the cause of activity because its object is the desired one, it must be asserted that the recollection of silver, even when distinct from the perception of the "this" object, is the cause [of activity].
However, that cannot be asserted;
for according to the principle that "one knows, then desires, and from that one acts," knowledge, desire, and activity must necessarily have the same object.
Furthermore, for one who proceeds toward the locus of the "this" while seeking silver, [that proceeding] is based on the desire for that [silver].
Otherwise, it would be contradictory for one to act toward one thing while desiring another.
And thus, if the locus of the "this" did not come within the range of the appearance of silver, how could one who seeks silver desire it?
If one were to say, "Because of the non-apprehension of non-silver-ness," then [the opponent might ask]:

"Why would he not remain indifferent because of the non-apprehension of silver-ness? A person being pulled from the front and from behind by two factors—namely, the inclination to appropriate [the object] based on the non-apprehension of its difference from silver, and the inclination to remain indifferent based on the non-apprehension of its identity with it—is so oscillating that, without the superimposition of silver, he cannot be established in the act of appropriation alone. Thus, even one of clear intellect who does not wish to admit it must resort to the theory of superimposition (samāropa).

As it has been said: "The first position—that one proceeds toward the object by superimposing silverness upon the locus of the 'this'-cognition due to the non-apprehension of difference, then recollecting that which belongs to that class is a cause of utility, and finally inferring that this [object] also possesses that class-character and thus being desirous of it—is the commendable one.

Nor should it be argued that this path is the same even in the view that there is a memory of a detached (external) silver, because the reason (*hetu*), namely silverness, lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

Nor should it be suspected that a mark possesses the capacity to produce knowledge (*gamakatva*) by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*) alone, even in the absence of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*);

for it is accepted that only a mark possessing both pervasion and presence in the subject is a producer of knowledge. As Śabarasvāmin has said: "Inference is the cognition of one part of the property-bearer qualified by the probandum (*liṅgin*), arising from the perception of one part of the property-bearer qualified by the mark (*liṅga*) for a person who already knows the relationship [between them]."
The Teacher also said: "This very thing which is accepted as both the signified and the signifier consists of two parts;
since one part is unestablished, it does not cause the understanding of the signified because that part remains unestablished."

[Objection: But even in your own view, since the ultimate reality of "thisness" (idam-artha) standing before one does not possess silver-ness, silver-ness cannot be a property-part (ekadeśa) of that substrate. [Response: This is not so; for according to the maxim "the offering must correspond to the spirit," there exists a property-part consistent with the fallacious inference.
And thus the formal argument: the cognition of silver under dispute has the object standing before one as its content, because it invariably induces activity toward it in one who desires silver.
That which has the stated means of proof possesses the stated object of proof, as is the case with the cognition of real silver agreed upon by both disputants.

The subject of dispute, a piece of mother-of-pearl, is the object of the cognition of silver, because it is the object of activity on the part of one seeking silver without any intervention, or because it is denoted by another word co-referential with the word "silver," just like actual silver.
As for the claim that there is a contradiction with experience insofar as the cognition of silver has mother-of-pearl as its objective support, that too is incorrect.
Because it cannot withstand critical analysis.

To explain: in this case, is the contradiction with experience being raised against the fact that the mother-of-pearl is the objective referent (*ālambana*) for the cognition of the form of silver, or against the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*)?
It is not the first.
Because it is refuted by its own non-acceptance.
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;

for it contradicts your own experience that a real object—characterized by a shimmering luster and having as its locus a specific place determined by "this-ness"—is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the cognition of silver.

Furthermore, because we observe the practical activity of picking up an object and so forth, preceded by the pointing of a finger toward what is in front with the expression of grammatical coreferentiality, "This is silver.
As for the claim that defects do not produce erroneous effects because they merely obstruct the power of natural causes to produce their usual effects—
that too is incorrect.
This is because it is observed to be so in the case of the seeds of the cane plant (*vetra*) burnt by a forest fire and the like.
Nor should it be thought that the burnt thing lacks the nature of being a cane seed;
for if it were so, it would follow that the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) would cease to exist merely through the black jar’s becoming red.
If it is argued that the existence of "jar-ness" (ghaṭatva) follows from the presence of the recurring cognition and usage "this is a jar," we say no;
for here too, the two are identical to the case of "this is a cane-seed.
Likewise, the digestive fire of one afflicted by the disorder of *bhasmaka* is observed to possess the capacity to digest vast quantities of food.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that the power to digest a large quantity of food belongs only to the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) and not to the disease *bhasmaka*;

for even when that [digestive fire] has a sluggish or minimal capacity for digestion, its sudden ability to digest a great amount cannot be accounted for without the assistance of the *bhasmaka* disease.

Otherwise, such a condition would result for everyone. Moreover, you yourself ought to be questioned: if you maintain that cognitions are the causes of correct practical activity (*vyavahāra*), yet admit—under the influence of defects—that they can also be causes of incorrect practical activity.

As it has been stated in the Bhāṣya: "When a fault shines forth equally for both parties, then no one should be subjected to censure. Regarding this, it is also said: "When a fault is equal for both sides, or when the rebuttal is likewise equal, neither party should be held accountable in such an investigation of the matter."
Nevertheless, what refutation was given against my inference?
If you are not satisfied without a refutation of the inference, then alas, there is the fallacy of being "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa),
like the inference that fire is not hot.

Since, for all this time, that which appeared as "this is silver" has been revealed by the perception "this is mother-of-pearl" to be an unreal cognition, it is possible for the inference of its reality to be sublated, because its object has been removed. As for what was said— that if there were deviation regarding one's own object-domain, it would lead to a lack of confidence in everything— that is incorrect.

Even though cognitions may produce consistent practical activity (*vyavahāra*) in some instances, the fear that this might not be the case everywhere does not lead to the cessation of purposeful action; for just as in your own view, so too in mine, this path is not barred, since the two cases share an identical status regarding their security and vulnerability.

While commenting on the *Vidhiviveka* by relying on the Tautātika school, the teacher Vācaspatimiśra demonstrated in the *Nyāyakaṇikā* that intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) consists in being a means of knowledge (*bodhakatva*), and not in non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*).
Therefore, the suspicion of lack of trust finds no opportunity to arise.
If it is argued that, by following the Madhyamaka view, the objective basis (*ālambana*) for an illusion such as [the appearance of] silver is non-existent (*asat*), that has already been answered:
because what is non-existent is incapable of appearing in immediate perception (*aparokṣa-pratibhāsa*),
and because activity (*pravṛtti*) motivated by the desire to acquire that [object] would be impossible.

Now, it might be argued: "Is it not the case that consciousness itself—having acquired a specific nature established by examples through the efficacy of its own causes such as latent impressions (vāsanā)—is capable of manifesting the non-existent?

'The power to manifest the non-existent,' 'ignorance' (avidyā), and 'conventional reality' (saṃvṛti) are synonyms. Therefore, things appear as non-existent due to the power of ignorance. This too cannot be maintained.
Because that which is possible is difficult to determine.
What here is possible: is it an effect (*kārya*) or something to be made known (*jñāpya*)?
Not the first.
Because it is logically untenable for that which is non-existent to be a cause;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because only that which is capable [of action] is accepted as a cause.
Furthermore, because no cognition other than [the cognition itself] is perceived;
or, if it were perceived, there would result an infinite regress (anavasthā) due to its being an object of cognition (jñāpyatva), which would necessitate yet another cognizer (jñāpaka).

Now, if you say that—desiring to avoid this fault—you accept that consciousness (*vijñāna*), being of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) itself, is the illuminator of the non-existent, then the "Beloved of the Gods" (the fool) must be questioned again regarding this.
This relationship between the existent and the non-existent must be either the state of the defined and the definer or necessary concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
It cannot be the first, because since the non-existent cannot serve as a substratum for an auxiliary influence, it cannot be assisted; and thus, its being defined is untenable.
The last [alternative] is not tenable;

for an invariable concomitance (avinābhāva), whether characterized by origination—as between smoke and fire—or characterized by identity—as between a *śiṃśapā* tree and a tree—is impossible between what exists and what does not exist.

Therefore, the claim of the proponents of non-existence (*asadvādins*) that "consciousness alone is the illuminator of the non-existent" is a mere empty prattle; thus, that which is being superimposed is not non-existent.
Now, according to the Vijñānavāda school, the silver being perceived is of the nature of cognition.
And the reasoning for this is stated: "In whatever manner something is experienced, it is so;
any other state is accepted only due to the onset of a powerful subverting cognition"—this is a point agreed upon by both disputants.
And in that case, once the "thisness" (*idantā*) of the silver has been negated by the judgment "this is not silver," the silver remains as a matter of necessity in the form of internal cognition.

It should not be argued that since its negation occurs through "thisness," it can be established externally through "non-thisness" (*anidantā*), and thus why should it be considered a form of consciousness?
For it is impossible for something remote to be immediate; therefore, the immediacy of the cognition must be accepted.

And thus the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: "The object of dispute, which is the aspect of cognition (*vijñānākāra*), exists independently of association (*saṃprayoga*), because it is directly manifest (*aparokṣatva*), like cognition itself.
This is untenable, because it cannot withstand critical analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*).
Does the sublation (*bādhaka*) directly cognize the form of the cognition, or does it do so through implication?
Not the first:

for there is a contradiction with experience if the cognition "this is not silver"—which has as its object merely the distinction from silver—were to have as its object the non-difference [of the object] from the cognition.

If it is argued that the negation of the silver’s presence in front—expressed as “this is not silver”—presupposes its existence as a form of cognition, this is a triviality. For the subverting cognition, which consists in the negation of what was previously expected, is established precisely there [in the external object], thereby making the negation logically consistent. Furthermore, the proof for [the silver] being a form of cognition is inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*), since it applies to the positive entity of ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is external to cognition and yet directly perceived by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
Now, according to the view of those who maintain the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), silver must exist in another location;
otherwise, its status as the counter-correlate of negation would be untenable.
For no discerning person is capable of negating a rabbit’s horn.
As it has been said: "The real nature of being a qualificand consists precisely in the absence of anything to be excluded;
the nature of a thing as a counter-correlate consists in its being the essence of the absence of that [excluded] non-existence" (Nyāyakusumāñjali 3.2).
And if it is argued that its existence in another location must therefore be resorted to, even that does not stand within the path of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For it is possible for a non-existent thing—just like the contact [of silver with mother-of-pearl] or the silver itself—to be the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a negation.
Now, is this cognition "this is silver" one or many?
Not the first [alternative],
because it would entail an abandonment of one's own tenets and because it is impossible.
To explain:

From the contact of the sense organ with the "this" portion of the mother-of-pearl, there arises a single cognition in the form of an internal transformation ending with the aspect of "this. And in that case, the silver is not capable of assuming the status of an object,
because it is not in contact [with the sense organ].
If its status as an object were admitted, it would follow that [the self] is omniscient.

Nor can it be argued that because the cognition follows the presence and absence of the eye, it must be produced by it; for it is logical that the eye's role is exhausted upon the arising of the cognition of the "this" aspect.
Nor does the cognition of silver arise from a mental impression (saṃskāra),
for that would entail its being a memory;
rather, it is the defect of the sense organ that serves as its cause.
That too is incorrect,
because it is impossible for that [object] to be a cause of cognition independently;
for there exists no other mode besides perception and recollection.

If it is argued that, therefore, a single cognition whose object is the identity between this "this-ness" and silver is not possible, nor is a plurality of cognitions possible because it would entail the theory of non-apprehension (akhyāti)— to this it is replied: first, a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) arises, having as its object merely "this-ness," by means of the eye defiled by a defect.
Immediately thereafter, when the veil over consciousness is overcome by that mental mode (*vṛtti*), that consciousness becomes manifest.

Subsequently, ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in the consciousness limited by the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*), being defiled by defects such as attachment and so forth, transforms into the form of silver. Then, ignorance residing in the consciousness limited by the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of "this," accompanied by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the transformation directed toward silver, transforms into the form of a semblance of knowledge (*jñānābhāsa*) of silver.
Both of these—the silver and the mental modification—are manifested without any intervention by the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*), which serves as their substrate.
Thus, since ignorance together with its modification is admitted to be manifested by the witness, there is no infinite regress, as it is not known by another mental modification.
Although there are two cognitions here—the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the modification of ignorance—nevertheless, the fruit [of cognition] is dependent upon the object.

Because the cognition "the jar is known" is an apprehension of a result (phala) as delimited by an object, and that object consists of the "this-aspect" (idamaṃśa) and the "silver-aspect" (rajatāṃśa)—whether real or illusory—attaining oneness through their mutual identification;
therefore, due to the oneness of the result as delimited by the object, the oneness of the cognition is figuratively attributed [to it].
Thus it has been said:
Ignorance (avidyā), residing within the consciousness of this "this-portion" (idam-aṃśa) of the mother-of-pearl,
manifests as silver, aided by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of defects such as passion (rāga).
Abiding as consciousness from which the activity of this mental mode has departed,
that [consciousness] likewise undergoes transformation (vivartate) into the nature of an appearance consisting of the cognition of silver.
Because of the identity between the real and the unreal self, that single object is considered [the same];
and because the fruit dependent upon it is one, the unity of knowledge is figuratively attributed to it.

In the *Pañcapādikā* as well, with the intention that the unity of knowledge is figuratively attributed due to the unity of the result, it is stated: "And that [knowledge] produces only one knowledge which has a single result" (*Pañcapādikā*, p.

9, l. 15). Now, an objection may be raised: if the silver being meditated upon on the surface of a mother-of-pearl shell were admitted to be real in that very place, how could the negation "this is not silver" be effective?

This is not so; for even though it possesses phenomenal reality (*prātibhāsika-satyatva*), it lacks empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*), and thus its status as a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) is possible within the locus of its apprehension (*pratipannopādhau*).
This has been stated in the *Pañcapādikāvivaraṇa* (p. 31, l. 1): "Existence is threefold: absolute existence belongs to Brahman;
existence as the capacity for causal efficiency belongs to ether and the like, which have *māyā* as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)."

The existence of silver and the like is conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopādhika*). It has also been stated elsewhere: "Because there is no sublation (of objects) at the three times—namely, at the time of the knower, at the time of their own duration, and likewise at the time of their perception—the threefold nature of the existence of entities is accepted."
The existence of Brahman is held to be ultimate (tāttvika), that of ether and so forth is empirical (vyāvahārika),
and that of the class of objects such as silver [in a shell] is apparent (prātibhāsika).
That which is sublated by worldly means of valid cognition within the worldly process of sublation possesses a merely apparent reality; it is sublated while the cognizer herself still exists.
Whatever is sublated by a Vedic means of valid cognition within a Vedic context is merely conventional reality;
it is sublated along with its very measure.
And so it is said.

Therefore, by the fact that neither manifestation nor sublation would otherwise be possible, the indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*)—characterized as being distinct from both existence and non-existence—is established for the silver and such objects that are the domain of error and are composed of *māyā*.
Regarding this, the teacher Citsukha said: "That which cannot be brought within the path of inquiry as either existent or non-existent individually..."
The proponents of Vedānta declare that it is ineffable (anirvācya).
(Citsu.pṛ.79) Thus it is said.

Now, one might object: "Since the distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā* is well-established by the fact that the former causes delusion in its own substratum while the latter does not, it is improper to speak of the superimposed object as being composed of *māyā* when it must be said to be composed of *avidyā*.

This objection is incorrect; for the collection of characteristics such as indefinability (*anirvacanīyatva*) and the obstruction of the manifestation of reality (*tattvābhāsa-pratibandhakatva*) is common to both *māyā* and *avidyā*.
Furthermore, by the word "substratum" (āśraya), is the seer meant, or the agent? Not the first,
because delusion is observed in one who perceives an illusion caused by mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth.

Not the second [alternative], because Viṣṇu was deluded by the very *māyā* residing within himself during his incarnation as Rāma; thus, being a possessor of *māyā* (*māyāvitva*) is not the determining factor there.
Rather, the determining factors are the certain knowledge of sublation and the awareness of remedies such as mantras.
Otherwise, the agent too would become deluded, like a lame man or a blind man.
Nor should it be argued that the difference between the two [the agent and the instrument] consists in following or not following the will [of the agent];

for even in the case of ignorance (avidyā), just as with the employment of gems, mantras, or medicinal herbs in the context of illusion (māyā), independence is observed even in the causes of errors such as the double moon or the perception of a net of hair, namely the pressing of a finger and so forth.
For this very reason, the treatment of *māyā* and *avidyā* as non-different in various instances within the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, commentaries (*bhāṣya*), and so forth, is consistent.

In some cases, however, where they are distinguished according to the predominance of projection (*vikṣepa*) or the predominance of concealment (*āvaraṇa*), their treatment as distinct does not contradict [the texts]. As it has been said: "Māyā is ignorance that projects, or it is that which functions under the control of the Lord's will."
Ignorance either veils reality or conforms to one's own autonomy.
Now, what is the proof for the existence of ignorance (*avidyā*)?
It is simply the direct manifestation of perception: "I am ignorant; I do not know myself and the other.

If it is argued that this [perception] has as its object merely the absence of knowledge and does not convey the intended meaning [of a positive entity], we reply: this objection does not apply to one who maintains that non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is a means of valid cognition.

If it is argued that this [perception] is also indeed a manifestation of something imperceptible because its cause is a manifestation of something imperceptible— [we reply: no, for it is not produced by a mark (liṅga), a word, or an object that is not [otherwise] possible,
since these have as their instrument that which has already been known.
Furthermore, at the time of that causal complex (*sāmagrī*), this cognition does not exist, nor is it experienced.
If you argue that it is produced by non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), we reply: this [non-apprehension] cannot be an instrument (*karaṇa*) as long as it is itself unknown.
Because there is a rule that for anything other than perception, the instrument must be known; nor is it the case that only what is known is the instrument,
because that would lead to an infinite regress regarding non-apprehension.

Nor should it be suspected that, as for others, non-apprehension of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*) in the apprehension of the absence [of an object], so it is not for us;

for there is no rule that what is a cooperative factor must necessarily be a cause of cognition, just as the instrument of cognition is. Or, let it be the case that it is the instrument in the apprehension of the absence of the object of knowledge.
It will be stated that the apprehension of the absence of knowledge cannot indeed have [knowledge] as its instrument.

However, in the theory of the perception of absence (*pratyakṣābhāvavāda*), one could not claim that through perception there is an apprehension of the mere absence of knowledge within the self while both the substratum (*dharmī*) and the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) are known;
for it is impossible to apprehend the absence of the mere existence of knowledge, just as it is impossible to apprehend the absence of a jar on a floor where a jar is present.
But when those two do not exist, it is all the more so, because of the absence of a cause.

Therefore, for this reason as well—whether by the non-apprehension of the capable or by the absence of the mark (liṅga) such as the fruit—the apprehension of the mere absence of cognition in the self is difficult to achieve; thus, this principle is the same even in the opponent's view.
Thus, it is established that it is impossible to apprehend the absence of mere cognition within the self, whether by means of perception or any other [means of knowledge].
Now, one might argue: "Let the absence of a specific cognition be apprehended by perception.
But this cannot be the absence of memory.
Because the recollection of the counter-positive is the cause for the apprehension of an absence;
nor can it be the absence of experience itself,
since that is unavoidable.

Now, if the absence of the experience of a jar in the self is indeed an object of perception, then the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*) in the cognition "I am ignorant"—which generally denotes knowledge as such—must be applied by way of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) to the specific experience that is the absence of knowledge.
And *lakṣaṇā* occurs when there is a relationship and when the primary meaning is untenable.

In this case, a relationship certainly exists between "experience-ness" (*anubhavatva*) and "knowledge-ness" (*jñānatva*), either through their coexistence in a single individual instance or through a relation of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*).
However, we see no logical inconsistency [in this].
But surely, in the absence of experience, the attainment of the object of cognition by perception is established by that very [perception], and thus its purposefulness is accomplished.
True.
This purpose is not untenable,
because [otherwise] there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Now, in the statement "I am ignorant," the negative particle (*nañ*) does not express the mere absence of knowledge in the self.
Because that [non-existence] does not exist in that which possesses knowledge;
nor is it an absence of experience,
because the mention of "knowledge" does not denote that [absence].

If it is argued that the definition [of ignorance] is established by this very same untenability—namely, that its meaninglessness is not logical—we reply: the definition of ignorance is indeed as stated, but its purpose is to address doubt.
If it is objected that this is not so because the two alternatives are unequal, we say no; for they are not equal.

For elsewhere, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is the cessation of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); but here, it is the cessation of that which is pervaded by the counter-positive. Since there can be no doubt regarding the negative particle used in conjunction with "knows" (*jānāti*) without first establishing its scope as ignorance (*avidyā*) according to the aforementioned definition, that very definition necessarily leads one to understand that the negative particle in all instances associated with "knows" has that [ignorance] as its object. It excludes the alternative possibility of a mere absence of knowledge; so where is there room for doubt?

Thus, since there is no experience of the self even in the absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and a cause (*hetu*), it is not apprehended through perception; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is established that the object of the appearance "I am ignorant" is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*) as defined above.
Or, let it be the appearance of the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*).
And this absence is not a distinct entity from its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), other than that wherein its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is negated.
Let it not be that there is the nature of being other; however, let there be the nature of being the absence of another.
[Objection: But even that is contradictory. [Response:
True, provided there is difference.
And that [non-existence] is established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And that [means of valid cognition] exists when there is a locus of the absence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), which is a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*). If it is objected: "In that case, the usage and the cognition 'there is an absence of a jar on the ground' would occur even where a jar is present"—[we reply: let these two not occur in a locus where the counter-correlate is being experienced simultaneously.

[The two] would indeed exist when there is the recollection of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) while the locus (adhikaraṇa) is being experienced. Even if this [explanation] is thus established, one should not postulate that they have a distinct ontological reality (tattvāntara). If it is asked, "What is the inconsistency [in this view]?"—the absence of any subverting evidence (bādhaka) has already been stated.
The subverting factor, however, is precisely the prolixity of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
For instance, one must first postulate that it is a distinct category of reality (*tattvāntaratva*);
furthermore, in order for that [category] to be directly perceived, a sensory contact (*indriya-saṃnikarṣa*) with it must be postulated.

Since that [substratum] cannot be a conjunction or the like, one must postulate it as a qualifier of the conjoined object; therefore, it is better to accept the substratum defined above as the object of conventional usage.
And this being so, when there is a recollection of the counter-positive, the substratum being experienced—even through the absence of cognition—is indeed known.
Moreover, that [substratum] is not merely the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
Because it is insentient;
nor is it the Self alone, because the Self is unchanging and devoid of qualities.
Therefore, there is a superimposition of non-difference between the two.
It follows that the superimposition of the Self is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) as defined above; thus, the manifestation "I am ignorant" regarding ignorance itself is the proof.

There is also an inference: the knowledge arising from a source of valid cognition under dispute is preceded by another entity residing in its own locus, which is distinct from its own prior absence, which conceals its own object, and which is removed by itself, because it illuminates an object already illuminated [by that other entity].
It is like the light of a lamp first produced in darkness.

Since it was stated that [knowledge] is preceded by an object (*vastu*), there is the fallacy of being a different thing (*arthāntara*) because it is preceded by the object that is the self (*ātma-vastu*).
To avoid this, [the sūtra says] "by another object" (*vastvantara*).
Nevertheless, since [the cognition] has another object as its domain, there would be a difference in meaning;
therefore, it is specified as "located in its own locus.
It is specified as "that which is to be removed by itself" in order to exclude unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth.
The phrase "obscuring its own object" (*svaviṣayāvaraṇa*) is used to exclude the first cognition, which is to be removed by a subsequent cognition.
The phrase "distinct from its own antecedent absence" (*svaprāgabhāvavyatirikta*) is used to reject the possibility of [the cause being] a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

If it were stated simply as "preceded by something distinct from its own antecedent absence," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*) by means of the object itself.
To that end, it is said "obscuring the object" (*viṣayāvaraṇa*); in order to exclude such darkness, it is said "removable by itself" (*svanivartya*);
and in order to refute the state of unknowability residing in the object, it is said "residing in its own locus" (*svadeśagata*).
The phrase "another object" (*vastvantara*) is used to exclude false cognition (*mithyājñāna*).
The term "unmanifested" (*aprakāśita*) is employed to prevent a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of continuous, stream-like cognitions (*dhārāvāhika-vijñāna*).

The qualifier "arisen first" (*prathamotpanna*) is included to counteract the deficiency of both the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) in the light of a lamp situated between [the observer and the object].
The term "darkness" (*andhakāra*) is used to exclude the light of a lamp situated in a place pervaded by sunlight.

Nor should one suspect a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes knowledge; for, with respect to one who is in disagreement, the function of the means of valid cognition consists merely in the removal of non-existence.
This has been stated by the authors of the *Kalpataru* in the section on the deities (*Devatādhikaraṇa*): "The negation of non-existence is effected by means of inference and other such proofs.
Now, if it is objected that the illustrative example lacks the probans (*sādhanavikala*), we say no; for by the word "light" (*prakāśa*), what is intended is a form that is opposed to darkness.

This has been stated by Sahajasarvajña Viṣṇubhaṭṭopādhyāya in the *Vivaraṇavivaraṇa*: "Nor should it be suspected here that there is a lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*) between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding the nature of light (*prakāśa*). For the word 'light' denotes a form that is opposed to darkness;
and in that form, identity exists in both cases."
But Narendragiri has stated as follows: "The meaning of the reason is 'being the cause of the conventional usage of illumination with respect to that which was previously unilluminated.
And since this [reason] is present in both cases, there is no fallacy such as 'unestablished' (asiddhi) and so forth.
This is also supported by scripture.
Furthermore, there is the scriptural text beginning with, "And finally, at the end, there is the cessation of the universal illusion" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 1.10).
"Salutation to that one whose nature is knowledge, the immeasurable, by fixing whom in the heart the yogi crosses over the widespread ignorance and illusion."
And thus:

by this, that which was stated by Bhāskara in his *Kṣapaṇakacaraṇapramāṇaśaraṇa*—namely, that for those who maintain the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābhedavādins*), there is no knowledge in the form of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa-jñāna*), but rather it is the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*)—is refuted.
To this effect is the passage from the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya* composed by Bhāskara:

The very non-perception of the supreme form is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), for if one does not accept ignorance as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) would be untenable.
Nor should it be said that the individual soul is a real part (*aṃśa*) of the Supreme Self, [for the scripture says]:
"It is without parts, without activity, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless."

(6/19) Because of the contradiction with such scriptural passages as these, certain Śāktas— accepting *Śakti*, who is the referent of the word *māyā* and acknowledged as the cause of the universe, as being real— describe Mahālakṣmī, who bears the citron, the mace, and the boar, as her first incarnation. And she, having produced two powers, *Kālarātri* and *Sarasvatī*, brought forth the male *Brāhmaṇa* and the female *Śrī*.
Having himself produced a pair, he said to his two children: "Just as I have, may you two also produce a pair.
Thereupon, Kālarātri gave birth to Mahādeva as the male and Svarā as the female;
and Sarasvatī gave birth to Viṣṇu as the male and Gaurī as the female.
Thereafter, he himself performed the marriage ceremony and caused it to be performed;
thus, having given Svarā to Brahmā, Śrī to Viṣṇu, and Gaurī to Śiva, he assigned to them—the three endowed with their respective powers—the tasks known as creation, preservation, and destruction.
This doctrine, being devoid of any foundational authority such as the Vedas and relying solely on one's own imagination, is refuted by its very definition; therefore, it should be disregarded.

Therefore, the manifold of subjectivity and so forth, which appears within the inner self (pratyagātman), is projected by beginningless, indefinable ignorance (anirvacanīyānādyavidyā); enough of this digression.

Now, for what purpose is the illusory nature (āvidyakatva) of subjectivity and the rest asserted? Is it for their cessation through the knowledge of Brahman, or for the individual soul (jīva) to attain its state as Brahman?
Not the first [alternative],
because it is established by the authority of the scripture itself that even an existing thing may be removed by knowledge,
and because such is observed in experience.
For instance: "By seeing the Setu, the slayer of a Brahmin is liberated from the sin of Brahmin-slaughter"—by such statements, sin is made to tremble.
By perceiving the defects of sense-objects, passion is consumed.
Poison is neutralized by the meditation on Tārkṣya;
likewise, even the bondage consisting of agency and so forth, though ultimately real, would be removed by the knowledge of reality. This is not the final [point].

If it is argued that the expression "bondage is caused by ignorance" (avidyā) is flawed because the state of being an individual soul (jīvatva), which is adventitious, ceases upon the cessation of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), thereby resulting in the state of Brahman— this objection is not sound. For it is logically impossible for that which is real to be removable by knowledge, as is the case with the Self (ātman).
Furthermore, that [bondage] is not established even through the authority of the scriptures, apart from its falsity;
for the scripture also states:
"A word whose capacity is understood in common worldly usage is also a means of cognition in the Veda."

Thus, according to this principle, [the Veda] proceeds by taking into account the power of words as observed in common usage and the semantic fitness of word-meanings. Otherwise, there would result the fallacy of regarding such collections of sentences as "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*) and "The grass-bundle is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*) as authoritative in their literal sense.

Furthermore, since a Vedic rite perishes immediately upon being performed, it would be impossible to accept the existence of the *apūrva* (unseen potency), because otherwise the fact that it produces results in the next world could not be logically accounted for.

Furthermore, in the world, when the true nature of a mother-of-pearl shell is revealed, the superimposed [silver] is seen to be false; by relying on that example, it is possible to infer the falsity of bondage—which is rooted in ignorance (avidyā) and is to be removed by the knowledge that directly realizes the reality of the Self—through the following inference: "The subject of dispute is false, because it is removable by the knowledge of the reality of its substratum, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Nor can there be a neutralization of this proof through an opposing argument of equal force, such as "The subject of dispute is real, because it is manifest," for the two arguments do not possess equal strength.
One should say that [the definition] is subject to one of the two faults due to the fear of contradiction;
for it suffers from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*savyabhicāra*) in cases such as the water of a mirage in the desert.
If you argue that there is no fault because the definition is qualified by the term "uncontradicted" (*abādhita*), do not speak thus.
Because the qualification is unestablished.
In this regard, being questioned, please explain:
is the qualification of the reason (*hetu*) "not being sublated by a few persons for a few times," or is it "being entirely free from sublation"?
Not the first [alternative],
for even an object that has been inferred with effort by skillful inferents may be established in an entirely different way by others who are more proficient.
According to the principle stated in *Vākyapadīya* 1.34, even that which has been established by three or four cognizers may be presented by another cognizer by adopting a different perspective;
nor is the last alternative tenable,
because the total absence of sublation (*bādhavai dhurya*) is difficult for anyone who is not omniscient to ascertain.
If it is argued that, "In that case, alas, even the reality of the nature of knowledge is not apprehended," do not think so;
for this is understood through the corroboration of scripture in such passages as, "That is the True, He is the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7).
Nor should it be thought that this same logic applies to the phenomenal world (prapañca).
Because no such scripture is found;
on the contrary, the Veda, which proclaims non-duality, is inclined precisely toward the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

[Objection: But since categories such as the thesis (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) have their bodies consisting of mere imagination, they are easily available to everyone; how then can debate proceed, given the impossibility of establishing victory or defeat?
What is the point of further inquiry here?

For, according to the principle stated [in Ślokavārttika 1.1.2]: "Thus, no higher cognition arises beyond three or four cognitions," it is accepted that for one who has come to rest after three or four stages and is no longer embraced by the characteristics of various fallacious appearances (*ābhāsa*), such factors as refutations and ornaments (*dūṣaṇa-bhūṣaṇa*) constitute the very limbs of the debate (*kathā*).
For this very reason, the author of the *Khaṇḍana* stated: "The commencement of inquiry takes place by resorting to the empirical existence of the means of valid cognition" (*Khaṇḍana*, p. 44).
Nor should it be suspected that the non-dualistic Śruti is subordinate to the means of valid cognition that apprehend difference;

for since the Śruti—which reveals Brahman as having ultimate reality and thus possesses the validity characterized by revealing the truth—has a different object from perception and other means of valid cognition which possess only empirical validity, there can be no relationship of sublation between them.
That too has been stated by that very same author: "The sublation of the scripture of non-duality (advaita-śruti) by perception is thus refuted;
neither inference nor other means of knowledge is capable of effecting such sublation even in your own system."
O you whose wealth is wisdom, if you then desire to cast away the wish-fulfilling gem obtained in your hand into the ocean, then bestow your insight upon this [work] to dispel its refutation.

Therefore, it must be admitted that this bondage, being imagined by ignorance (*ajñāna*), is removed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). For it has been stated that "knowledge is the remover of ignorance. As for what was said—that even real demerit (*durita*) is observed to cease through the sight of the Setu bridge—that is [addressed as follows]:

That is incorrect; for it is certain that dharma produced by the performance of enjoined actions has the power to remove adharma, according to the Vedic scripture: "By means of dharma they dispel evil" (Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad 6.30).

This is because an act of seeing, which depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object (*vastu*), cannot be enjoined, as it lacks dependence on the exertion of a person prompted [by scripture].

Furthermore, [the passage] "By bathing in that great ocean, one is released from the murder of a Brahmin" is intended as praise for bathing at the Setu, which achieves the fruit of ceasing the murder of a Brahmin— an act accomplished by traveling to a distant land accompanied by the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) prescribed in such Smṛti texts.
For if even the mere sight of him brings about the pacification of evil, how much more so bathing?
Otherwise, it would follow that traveling to a distant place is purposeless;
in that case, the cessation of misfortune would apply even to donkeys and the like.

And for one who is blind, it would not even exist. But surely it is said: "The fire-altar builder, a tawny cow, a king, a virtuous mendicant, and the great ocean—these purify merely by being seen; therefore, one should look upon them constantly."
If it is argued that in some instances the act of seeing itself is enjoined, do not speak thus;

for even there, by this very same logic of inconsistency, one determines that the intended meaning (tātparya) lies precisely in the honoring, service, and so forth, directed toward those such as the Agnicit.
As for what was said—that passion is consumed by the perception of defects in the object—[that too is untenable].

In that case, because the cessation of passion occurs through the singular emergence of detachment—known as "disinterest"—which is the opposite of passion and arises from seeing the defects in sense objects, it is merely the non-perception of those objects; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule].
As for the claim that poison and the like truly perish through the meditation on Tārkṣya (Garuḍa) and so forth, that does not hold together.
Even in that case, it is the very performance of ritual actions such as the application of mantras that removes poison and the like;
furthermore, meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) lacks the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).

As for what was previously stated—that since the state of being a living soul (*jīva-bhāva*), which is adventitious, ceases upon the cessation of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the state of Brahman is thereby established, and thus there is no need to explain the unreality of objects for that purpose—[that argument is refuted].
That too is like grasping at a mere straw;
for it cannot withstand critical analysis.
Do you intend for the limiting adjunct (upādhi) to be real, or do you consider it false?
Not the first,
because there is a lack of valid evidence;
nor the other.
This is because it would lead to an undesirable conclusion.
Therefore, it is stated in the Śruti that difference is due to ignorance (avidyā) for the sake of establishing non-duality, and not out of mere whim.
If the reality of the Self is in fact free from all afflictions, then how is it that it repeatedly enters the prison of the body and so forth?
That is extremely weak,
because it has already been answered by the fact that ignorance is beginningless.
Therefore, a discerning person must seek only the means for its cessation.
One should not, however, feel astonishment.

Consequently, through the cessation of that ignorance by means of the knowledge "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and other such teachings, the supreme human goal—consisting in the attainment of the Self which is unsurpassed bliss—will be accomplished.
Thus says the *Āpastamba-smṛti*: "There is nothing higher than the attainment of the Self."
But is it not the case that this [nature] is eternally attained?
For it is not the case that something is unattained by itself to itself.
True.
However, due to its connection with beginningless illusion (māyā), it does not attain a state of distinct manifestation, like milk mixed with water.

And so, just as a prince who has been raised from childhood among Śabaras and others with their sons comes to perceive himself as belonging to that same class, yet upon being informed by his kinsmen, "You are that very king who is such-and-such," he becomes as if he has recovered his true nature; in the same way, the Self, which has been led to a different state of being by ignorance—standing in the place of a courtesan—is led back to its own true nature by the Vedic texts beginning with "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), which stand in the place of a mother. Regarding this, the elders learned in the three Vedas have said: "A prince who has lived for a long time among low-born people and has grown up together with their sons clearly perceives even his own self as belonging to that [low] class."

Living in association with the great principle (mahat) and the rest, the person becomes like them; though his own self is actually free from the net of pleasure and pain, he falsely considers it thus, crying "Fie! in regret.

Just as that man, having heard from the mouth of the protector, "You are that very king who is a donor devoted to enjoyment, possessed of complete wealth, and the punisher of evildoers," duly becomes a king and strives for victory; so too, the person enlightened by the Śruti "That thou art" (tat tvam asi), casting off all evil, becomes Brahman itself.
By this, that which was stated by others is refuted: "Is there identity between the two, or of one [of them]?
Not the first, because it would entail the collapse of non-duality (advaita).
The second [alternative] is not [tenable],
because it is impossible;
that is not so.
For the validity of the doctrine of identity expressed in statements such as "That thou art" is established by its purpose of removing the distinctions imagined through ignorance.
And these two—the objection and its refutation—should be understood by the wise as follows:
"There is no identity between two [distinct] things, nor can there be identity for a single thing because of its non-duality."
Thus, the lack of authority belongs to the scripture itself, and not merely from the destruction of superimposition.

Consequently, through the direct realization born from the power of hearing, reflecting upon, and meditating on the meanings of the terms *tat* and *tvam* in the Great Saying "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), there occurs the manifestation of Brahman as the single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss upon the cessation of beginningless ignorance; thus, it is logical that Brahman is the object of inquiry as stated in the first aphorism.
Brahman, when unknown, is the subject matter (*viṣaya*); when known, it is the purpose (*prayojana*).
The seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) is the qualified candidate (*adhikārī*); and the relationship (*saṃbandha*) follows from the capacity [of the means] as revealed by scripture.
In the second aphorism, "janmādy asya yataḥ" (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.2), Brahman was defined by means of both essential (svarūpa) and incidental (taṭastha) characteristics.

Among these, the essential characteristic—which, while being included within the very nature [of the thing], serves to differentiate it—is propounded by such Vedāntic texts as "satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1.1).
This is because it differentiates [Brahman] while remaining inherent within its nature consisting of truth, knowledge, and so forth.

The "indirect definition" (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) is that which defines [Brahman] through its being the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, as in such passages as, "From whence indeed these... (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1).
This has been stated in the *Vivaraṇa*: "That cause from which the origin, subsistence, and dissolution of the world are established..."
That [Brahman] is demonstrated by means of two types of definitions: the essential (svarūpa) and the incidental (taṭastha).

In the first interpretation (*varṇaka*) of the third sūtra, *śāstrayonitvāt* (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.3), omniscience was established by relying on a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). In the second interpretation, by accepting a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*), it was asserted that Brahman has the Vedāntas as its source of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In the first interpretation of the fourth sūtra, *tattu samanvayāt* (Brahma-sūtra 1.1.4), the purport (*tātparya*) of the Vedāntas regarding Brahman was established.
In the second section, it was not even suggested that the Upanishads (Vedantas) establish Brahman as subordinate to injunctions for realization;
here, only a mere indication has been shown.
The remainder is clear within the scripture itself, and thus everything is consistent.
May there be prosperity.
Thus ends the illustrious Śāṅkara-darśana, the jewel that is the crest-ornament of all philosophical systems, within the *Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha* composed by the venerable Sāyaṇa Mādhava.
This Compendium of All Philosophical Systems is hereby completed.
